scoring.rule: Five statements, each true or false, 1 point each. The student checks the statements they believe are true. A statement scores 1 point if it is checked and true, or unchecked and false; otherwise 0.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.source: Sensitivity, false positive rate, positive predictive value, prevalence
questions.stem: A fraud team says its transaction classifier "catches 90% of fraud" and "wrongly flags 4% of legitimate transactions". Which statements name these quantities correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For a fixed sensitivity and false positive rate, the prevalence (base rate) of fraud leaves the positive predictive value unchanged.
statements.explanation: The positive predictive value rises with prevalence even when the two error rates stay fixed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Catches 90% of fraud" is the sensitivity of the classifier, also called recall or the true positive rate.
statements.explanation: Sensitivity is the share of actual positives that the classifier flags.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Sensitivity and positive predictive value are two names for one quantity.
statements.explanation: They condition on different events: sensitivity on actual positives, positive predictive value on flagged cases.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Wrongly flags 4% of legitimate transactions" is the false positive rate, which equals 1 minus the specificity.
statements.explanation: The false positive rate is the share of actual negatives flagged, the complement of specificity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The probability that a flagged transaction is fraudulent is the sensitivity.
statements.explanation: That probability is the positive predictive value (precision); sensitivity conditions on fraud, not on the flag.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.stem: A help desk logs tickets by type (billing or technical) and by whether each was escalated. Which statements use the probability terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: P(escalated) over the full log is a marginal probability, a weighted average of the group-level conditional probabilities.
statements.explanation: A marginal probability ignores the grouping and equals the sum of each group share times its conditional probability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ticket type and escalation are independent when P(escalated | billing) differs from P(escalated | technical).
statements.explanation: Independence needs the conditional probability to equal the marginal for each group; differing rates signal dependence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: P(billing and escalated) is a joint probability: the share of the full log that is both billing and escalated.
statements.explanation: A joint probability is the chance that two events happen together.

statements.label: D
statements.text: P(billing | escalated) is the same quantity as P(escalated | billing) with the words reordered.
statements.explanation: Swapping the conditioning event gives a different conditional probability with a different value.

statements.label: E
statements.text: P(escalated | billing) is a conditional probability: the chance of escalation within the billing tickets.
statements.explanation: A conditional probability restricts attention to the cases where the given event holds.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.stem: Two automated checkers each miss a given defect with probability 0.10, and a reviewer asks whether the two misses are independent events. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Independence means the two events do not occur together.
statements.explanation: Events that do not occur together are mutually exclusive, which is a different property from independence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If P(second misses | first misses) equals 1, the two misses are independent events.
statements.explanation: Independence needs the conditional probability to equal the marginal 0.10; a value of 1 is extreme dependence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two events are independent when the joint probability equals the product of the two marginal probabilities.
statements.explanation: The product rule for joint probability is the definition of independence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Two checkers built with the same method that tend to miss the same defects have independent misses.
statements.explanation: Shared blind spots make the misses positively dependent, not independent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Mutually exclusive events that each have positive probability are independent.
statements.explanation: If one occurs the other has probability 0, so knowing one changes the other; they are dependent.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.source: Complement rule, pairs, and "at least one" events
questions.stem: A statistician explains the shared-birthday result for a group of people, assuming 365 equally likely birthdays that are independent. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The event "some pair in the group shares a birthday" has the same probability as the event "one named person shares a birthday with someone else in the group".
statements.explanation: The named-person event is far less likely; the pair event has many more chances to occur.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The growth of a match chance in a small group is explained by counting pairs of people instead of counting people.
statements.explanation: The number of pairs grows roughly with the square of the group size.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The complement rule computes P(at least two share a birthday) as 1 minus P(no two share a birthday).
statements.explanation: The complement of "at least one match" is "no match", which is easier to count.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Birthdays clustered on certain dates make a match less likely than under the uniform model.
statements.explanation: Non-uniform frequencies make a match more likely; the uniform case is the least likely to produce one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "At least two share a birthday" and "exactly two share a birthday" name the same event.
statements.explanation: "At least two" includes larger shared groups; "exactly two" excludes them.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.source: Prior, likelihood, posterior, likelihood ratio, odds
questions.stem: A mail filter knows that 30% of messages are spam, that the word "urgent" appears in 60% of spam and in 10% of legitimate messages, and it wants the chance that a message containing "urgent" is spam. Which statements name the pieces correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: P("urgent" | spam) = 0.60 is a likelihood and is a different quantity from the posterior probability of spam.
statements.explanation: A likelihood is the probability of the evidence given a hypothesis; the posterior is the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: P(spam | "urgent") is the posterior probability.
statements.explanation: The posterior is the updated probability of the hypothesis after the evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The likelihood ratio is the posterior probability divided by the prior probability.
statements.explanation: The likelihood ratio compares the probability of the evidence under two hypotheses, here 0.60 divided by 0.10.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Posterior odds equal prior odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio.
statements.explanation: This is the odds form of Bayes' rule.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 30% share of spam before looking at the word is the prior probability.
statements.explanation: The prior is the probability assigned before the evidence is considered.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.source: Transposed conditional, base rate fallacy, positive predictive value
questions.stem: A school buys a detector that labels essays "AI-written" and states it is "98% accurate", meaning it flags 98% of AI-written essays and wrongly flags 2% of human-written essays. A teacher asks how likely a flagged essay is to be AI-written. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: When AI-written essays are rare, the positive predictive value of a flag is higher than when they are common.
statements.explanation: A lower base rate lowers the positive predictive value because false flags from the large legitimate group dominate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The vendor's "accuracy" claim reports the false discovery rate of the detector.
statements.explanation: The claim reports error rates conditional on the true class, not the share of flags that are wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Treating P(flagged | AI-written) as if it were P(AI-written | flagged) is an application of the law of total probability.
statements.explanation: That error is called transposing the conditional; it ignores the base rate and is also called the base rate fallacy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The vendor's 98% is a sensitivity, P(flagged | AI-written), and it does not answer the teacher's question.
statements.explanation: The teacher needs the reverse conditional, P(AI-written | flagged).

statements.label: E
statements.text: The teacher's question asks for the positive predictive value of a flag.
statements.explanation: Positive predictive value is the probability that a flagged case is truly positive.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.source: Prosecutor's fallacy, false positive rate versus false discovery proportion
questions.stem: A face-matching system searches a database of 2,000,000 people. It declares a match for a person who is not the source with probability 1 in 10,000. A prosecutor says: "The chance this match is a coincidence is 1 in 10,000, so there is a 99.99% chance he is the source." Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 1 in 10,000 rate is the false positive rate, so it is also the false discovery proportion among declared matches.
statements.explanation: The false discovery proportion is the share of matches that are wrong, which also depends on how many non-sources are tested.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Independent evidence about the person raises the prior odds, and posterior odds equal prior odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio.
statements.explanation: Independent evidence changes the prior odds before the match is weighed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A match found by testing one suspect already singled out by other evidence carries the same weight as a match found by trawling a large database.
statements.explanation: Trawling produces many coincidental matches, so a match from a trawl carries a lower posterior probability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Searching a large database raises the expected number of coincidental matches.
statements.explanation: The count of false matches grows with the number of non-source people tested.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The prosecutor transposed the conditional: P(match | not the source) is not P(not the source | match).
statements.explanation: The 1 in 10,000 is a false positive rate; the prosecutor read it as the reverse conditional.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.stem: Model A beats Model B on easy questions and also on hard questions, yet Model B has the higher overall accuracy because Model B was tested mostly on easy questions. Which statements name this correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The difference in question mix between the two models is a confounder of the overall comparison.
statements.explanation: The mix of easy and hard questions is linked to both which model is scored and the accuracy obtained.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Overall accuracy is a conditional accuracy given question difficulty.
statements.explanation: Overall accuracy ignores difficulty; accuracy within a difficulty level is the conditional quantity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A trend that holds in each group and reverses in the combined data is Simpson's paradox.
statements.explanation: Simpson's paradox is a reversal between group-level and aggregate comparisons.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Stratifying by question difficulty is a sound fix when difficulty is a property of the question and not an effect of the model.
statements.explanation: Stratification compares like with like on a variable that is not downstream of the treatment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overall accuracy is a weighted average of the group accuracies, with weights set by each model's own mix of questions.
statements.explanation: Different weights can reverse the order of the averages.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.source: Expected value, mode, variance, standard deviation
questions.stem: An agent retries a failing tool call before giving up. Let X be the number of retries in one run, with P(X=0) = 0.50, P(X=1) = 0.30, P(X=2) = 0.15 and P(X=3) = 0.05. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The mode of X is its most probable value, and it can differ from the expected value.
statements.explanation: Here the mode is 0 while the mean is 0.75.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The expected value of X is the probability-weighted mean of its possible values.
statements.explanation: Expected value is the long-run average, the sum of each value times its probability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding a constant to a random variable changes its variance.
statements.explanation: A shift moves the distribution but leaves its spread, and so its variance, unchanged.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Variance is measured in squared units of X, while standard deviation is measured in the units of X.
statements.explanation: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The expected value of a discrete random variable is itself one of its possible values.
statements.explanation: The mean of 0.75 is not a possible number of retries.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.source: Probability density function, cumulative distribution function, probability mass function
questions.stem: X is a continuous random variable, uniformly distributed on the interval from 0 to 0.5. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The cumulative distribution function can decrease as x increases.
statements.explanation: The cumulative distribution function P(X ≤ x) is non-decreasing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The area under the density curve between two points is the expected value of X.
statements.explanation: That area is the probability that X falls between the two points.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A probability mass function is the right description for a continuous variable.
statements.explanation: A probability mass function belongs to discrete variables; continuous variables use a density.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For a continuous variable the probability of one exact value is 0.
statements.explanation: Probability comes from the area under the density over an interval, and a single point has no width.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A probability density function value is not a probability and can exceed 1.
statements.explanation: Density is probability per unit length; for this uniform variable it is 2.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.stem: A model answers each of 20 test prompts correctly with probability 0.8, independently, and the number correct is modeled as binomial. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The binomial variance is np, which equals its mean.
statements.explanation: The binomial variance is np(1 − p); equal mean and variance is a property of the Poisson.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Overdispersion means the observed variance is smaller than the model variance.
statements.explanation: That is underdispersion; overdispersion is larger observed variance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Positively correlated trials, such as near-duplicate prompts, cause overdispersion: the count varies more than the binomial variance says.
statements.explanation: Overdispersion means observed variance exceeds the model variance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A binomial count is the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials that share one success probability.
statements.explanation: These are the defining conditions of the binomial model.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overdispersion and underdispersion both describe the sample mean differing from the population mean.
statements.explanation: They describe variance relative to the model, not a difference in means.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.source: Normal distribution, z-score, empirical rule, fat tails
questions.stem: Request latency for a service is modeled as a normal distribution with mean 200 ms and standard deviation 40 ms. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A z-score counts how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean.
statements.explanation: A 280 ms request has z = (280 − 200) / 40 = 2.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fat-tailed (heavy-tailed) distribution tends to put more probability far from the mean than a normal with the same mean and standard deviation.
statements.explanation: Heavy tails make extreme values more common than the normal curve predicts.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two distributions with the same mean and standard deviation have the same tail probabilities.
statements.explanation: Tail mass depends on the whole shape, not just the first two moments.

statements.label: D
statements.text: About 68% of a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean.
statements.explanation: About 68% lies within one standard deviation; about 95% lies within two.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 68-95-99.7 rule holds for skewed distributions as well as for normal ones.
statements.explanation: The empirical rule is a property of the normal distribution.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.source: Chebyshev's inequality, tail risk, quantile-quantile plot, Cauchy
questions.stem: A team sets an alert at the mean plus a multiple of the standard deviation, and a reviewer questions the quoted false-alarm rate. Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Chebyshev's inequality bounds tail probability for distributions with finite variance, whatever their shape.
statements.explanation: The bound P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k² needs only a finite variance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At 3 standard deviations the Chebyshev bound is 1/9, which is looser than the normal tail figure.
statements.explanation: The normal puts about 0.27% beyond 3 standard deviations, far under 11%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A quantile-quantile plot compares the data's quantiles with a reference distribution and can show whether the tails are heavier than normal.
statements.explanation: Points bending away from the line in the ends signal tail shape that differs from the reference.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The Cauchy distribution has a finite mean, so sample averages settle down as the sample grows.
statements.explanation: The Cauchy has no finite mean, and the average of Cauchy observations is as spread out as one observation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A "six-sigma" failure rate computed from the normal curve stays valid when the real distribution is heavy-tailed.
statements.explanation: The tiny figure depends on the normal shape; heavy tails put far more probability at extreme distances.

questions.section: 2. Random variables and distributions
questions.source: Binomial, Poisson approximation, compounding, end-to-end reliability
questions.stem: An agent run makes 500 tool calls. Each call fails with probability 0.002, independently, and one failed call ruins the run. A manager calls 99.8% per-call reliability "basically perfect". Which statements are correct? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A Poisson distribution with mean n × p approximates this binomial when n is large and p is small.
statements.explanation: The Poisson approximation to the binomial is the rare-event limit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Small per-step failure probabilities compound across steps and lower end-to-end success.
statements.explanation: The chance of no failure is (1 − p) raised to the number of steps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The number of failed calls per run is binomial with 500 trials and a per-trial failure probability of 0.002.
statements.explanation: Fixed number of independent trials with equal failure probability gives a binomial count.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Failures that share a cause, such as a down service, are positively correlated, so the independence-based figure for run success should be checked against observed runs.
statements.explanation: Correlated failures violate the independence assumption behind the product rule.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Per-call reliability and per-run (end-to-end) reliability are the same quantity.
statements.explanation: Per-run reliability is a product over steps and is much lower than the per-call figure.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Standard error, margin of error, confidence interval
questions.stem: An engineer runs 400 independent evaluation prompts and 320 pass, an observed pass rate of 0.80. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The standard error and the standard deviation of the individual pass-or-fail outcomes are the same quantity.
statements.explanation: The standard deviation describes single outcomes; the standard error describes the estimate and shrinks as n grows.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The standard error of a proportion is largest when p is near 0 or 1.
statements.explanation: The quantity p(1 − p) peaks at p = 0.5, so the standard error is largest there.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Doubling the number of prompts halves the standard error.
statements.explanation: The standard error falls in proportion to 1 over the square root of n, so doubling n shrinks it by about 29%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The standard error of the pass rate measures how much the sample proportion varies from one sample to another.
statements.explanation: A standard error is the standard deviation of a statistic across repeated samples.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The margin of error of a 95% interval is the critical value (about 1.96) times the standard error.
statements.explanation: Margin of error = critical value × standard error.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: p-value, effect size, statistical versus practical significance
questions.stem: An A/B test with 20,000 users per arm gives a two-sided p-value of 0.048 for a 0.6 percentage point lift in conversion. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, computed assuming the null hypothesis is true.
statements.explanation: It is a probability about data under the null, not about the hypothesis.

statements.label: B
statements.text: One minus the p-value, 0.952, is the probability that the feature truly raises conversion.
statements.explanation: That would be a posterior probability, which needs a prior and a different calculation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A p-value of 0.048 is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
statements.explanation: The p-value assumes the null; it does not give the probability that the null is true.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A small p-value shows that the effect size is large.
statements.explanation: With large samples a small effect can still give a small p-value; effect size is a separate quantity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Statistical significance and practical significance are different judgments.
statements.explanation: A result can be statistically significant yet too small to matter in practice.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Type I error, Type II error, power, false discovery rate, base rate
questions.stem: A group screens 200 independent hypotheses, 20 of them true effects, using significance level 0.05 and power 0.80. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The false discovery rate among significant results depends on the base rate of true effects, so alpha alone does not set it.
statements.explanation: Where true effects are rare, false positives from many true nulls make up a large share of discoveries.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Power is 1 minus the Type II error rate, the probability of detecting an effect that is real.
statements.explanation: Type II error is a miss, and power is its complement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A significance level of 0.05 means that 95% of significant findings are real effects.
statements.explanation: The share of significant findings that are real depends on the base rate of true effects, not on alpha alone.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The significance level is the Type I error rate: the probability of rejecting a null hypothesis that is true.
statements.explanation: Type I error is a false positive among true nulls.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A Type II error is a false positive.
statements.explanation: A Type II error is a false negative; a false positive is a Type I error.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Multiple comparisons, Bonferroni, family-wise error rate, false discovery rate
questions.stem: A team tests 20 prompt variants against a baseline, each at significance level 0.05, and none truly differs. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The family-wise error rate is the expected share of false findings among the discoveries.
statements.explanation: That describes the false discovery rate; the family-wise error rate is the probability of at least one false positive.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The false discovery rate is the expected proportion of false findings among the results declared significant.
statements.explanation: It is a weaker guarantee than controlling the family-wise error rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Testing 20 variants and reporting the best raw p-value is a multiple comparisons (multiplicity) problem.
statements.explanation: The chance of at least one false positive grows with the number of tests.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controls the family-wise error rate.
statements.explanation: Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate; Bonferroni and Holm control the family-wise error rate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The Bonferroni correction divides the significance level by the number of tests.
statements.explanation: With 20 tests the per-test threshold becomes 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Confidence interval, credible interval, coverage, prediction interval
questions.stem: A study reports an accuracy improvement of 2.0 percentage points, with a frequentist 95% confidence interval of 0.5 to 3.5 points. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A credible interval is a Bayesian interval that states the probability that the parameter lies in it, given the data and a prior.
statements.explanation: The credible interval gives a direct probability statement about the parameter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The interval describes the spread of individual query-level improvements.
statements.explanation: The interval concerns the mean improvement; the spread of individual changes is a prediction-interval or standard-deviation matter and is much wider.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The statement "there is a 95% probability that the true improvement lies between 0.5 and 3.5" is the standard frequentist reading of a confidence interval.
statements.explanation: That reading belongs to a credible interval; a computed confidence interval either contains the true value or does not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 95% in a confidence interval describes the long-run coverage of the procedure across repeated samples.
statements.explanation: About 95% of intervals built this way contain the true value.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A 90% confidence interval from the same data is wider than the 95% interval.
statements.explanation: A lower confidence level uses a smaller multiplier and so gives a narrower interval.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Sampling distribution, central limit theorem, effective sample size
questions.stem: Consider the sample mean of n independent, identically distributed observations from a right-skewed population with finite variance, such as task completion times. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The sampling distribution of the mean is the distribution of the sample mean across repeated samples of size n.
statements.explanation: A sampling distribution describes a statistic, not the raw data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Strong positive correlation among observations enlarges the effective sample size.
statements.explanation: Correlated observations carry less information, so the effective sample size is smaller than n.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The central limit theorem says the sampling distribution of the mean is normal at small n as well as at large n.
statements.explanation: The theorem is a limit statement; the approximation improves as n grows, and skewed data can need a large n.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The central limit theorem says a histogram of the individual observations becomes bell-shaped as n grows.
statements.explanation: The raw data keep the population's shape; the distribution of the sample mean is what approaches normal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The skewness of the sample mean grows as n grows.
statements.explanation: Skewness of the mean shrinks toward 0 in proportion to 1 over the square root of n.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Nonresponse bias, self-selection, standard error versus bias
questions.stem: A tutoring app invites its 1.25 million users to a satisfaction survey. A total of 50,000 respond and 92% of respondents say they are satisfied. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Respondents choosing for themselves whether to answer is self-selection, a source of nonresponse bias.
statements.explanation: Those who answer can differ systematically from those who do not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A larger number of respondents reduces random error but leaves selection bias in place.
statements.explanation: Bias depends on the response mechanism, not on the count.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The standard error quantifies the systematic bias that comes from who chose to respond.
statements.explanation: The standard error captures chance variation and cannot detect a systematic difference between responders and non-responders.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A large volunteer sample is a probability sample because it is large.
statements.explanation: A probability sample needs known selection chances, and size does not supply them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Selection bias and measurement bias are two names for the same problem.
statements.explanation: Selection bias concerns who ends up in the data; measurement bias concerns errors in how values are recorded.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Absence of evidence, statistical power, equivalence test, inconclusive result
questions.stem: A team runs 20 retrieval-quality trials, and the result is non-significant. Another analyst notes the sample was small. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Low power makes a non-significant result strong evidence that there is no effect.
statements.explanation: With low power the test would likely miss a real effect, so the result is uninformative.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Statistical power is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when a true effect of a given size exists.
statements.explanation: Low power makes a non-significant result expected even if the effect is real.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A confidence interval that includes zero and also includes large benefits marks the study as inconclusive.
statements.explanation: The data are compatible with both no effect and a sizable one.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An equivalence test is the tool for supporting the claim of "no meaningful effect".
statements.explanation: Equivalence testing sets a margin and tests that the effect lies within it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A non-significant result does not show the null hypothesis is true: absence of evidence differs from evidence of absence.
statements.explanation: Failing to reject is not the same as confirming no effect.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Exploratory versus confirmatory analysis, Holm, adjusted p-value, preregistration
questions.stem: A team compares 40 prompt variants with a baseline, announces the best variant as significant at p = 0.03, and then plans a follow-up. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A preregistered hypothesis is one chosen after the data have been examined.
statements.explanation: Preregistration fixes the hypothesis and analysis plan before looking at the outcome data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The raw p-value of a selected best result understates how easily chance produces such a result.
statements.explanation: The smallest of many null p-values is routinely small.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The Holm procedure controls the family-wise error rate and is less conservative than the Bonferroni correction.
statements.explanation: Holm is a step-down method that rejects at least as many hypotheses as Bonferroni.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A Bonferroni-adjusted p-value is the raw p-value divided by the number of tests.
statements.explanation: The adjusted p-value is the raw value multiplied by the number of tests, capped at 1.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Picking the best of many variants after seeing the data is exploratory; testing the winner once on fresh held-out data with a pre-specified hypothesis is confirmatory.
statements.explanation: Confirmatory analysis fixes the hypothesis before the data are seen.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Upper confidence bound, rule of three, representativeness
questions.stem: A safety filter passes 300 of 300 independent test prompts, and the report says "the failure rate is 0%". Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Zero observed failures give an upper confidence bound on the failure rate and do not establish a point value of zero.
statements.explanation: A rare failure can be missed by chance in a limited test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A higher confidence level gives a lower upper bound on the failure rate.
statements.explanation: Demanding more confidence widens the bound, so it rises.

statements.label: C
statements.text: By the rule of three, the 95% upper confidence bound after n failure-free tests is about 3 divided by n.
statements.explanation: For n = 300 the bound is about 1%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The bound applies to inputs outside the distribution of the test prompts.
statements.explanation: The bound speaks only to inputs like those sampled; uncovered or adversarial inputs lie outside it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Near-duplicate test prompts raise the effective number of independent tests.
statements.explanation: Near-duplicates are positively correlated and carry less independent information, so the effective sample size drops.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Sampling bias, selection bias, measurement bias, survivorship bias
questions.stem: An analyst describes four data problems in plain words. Which statements name the problem correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Measurement bias and sampling bias are synonyms.
statements.explanation: One concerns recorded values, the other concerns who is in the sample.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Measurement bias shrinks when a larger random sample is drawn.
statements.explanation: A bias in the instrument repeats in every observation, so more data do not remove it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sensor that reads two degrees too high has measurement bias.
statements.explanation: Measurement bias is a systematic error in how a value is recorded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A telephone survey that leaves out people without phones has a coverage (sampling) bias.
statements.explanation: The sampling frame does not include part of the target population.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Studying the companies that survived while ignoring those that failed is survivorship bias, a form of selection bias.
statements.explanation: Only the cases that passed a filter appear in the data.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.stem: A survey records age for each respondent and asks for income, which some respondents leave blank. Which statements use the missingness terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Missing not at random (MNAR) means missingness depends on the unobserved value itself, such as higher earners skipping because of income.
statements.explanation: The reason for the gap is the very value that is absent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Whether income is missing not at random can be confirmed from the observed values alone.
statements.explanation: The observed data cannot reveal dependence on unobserved values; it takes outside knowledge or assumptions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Higher earners skipping the income question because of their income is missing at random.
statements.explanation: Missingness driven by the value itself is MNAR, not MAR.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Missing completely at random (MCAR) means missingness is unrelated to the observed variables and to the unobserved values.
statements.explanation: MCAR is the least problematic missingness mechanism.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Missing at random (MAR) means missingness depends on observed variables, such as older respondents skipping more often, and not on the missing value itself.
statements.explanation: Conditioning on the observed variable removes the dependence.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.source: Mean imputation, multiple imputation, standard error
questions.stem: A column has 10 rows; five values are observed and five are missing. An analyst fills each blank with the observed mean and treats the 10 rows as real data. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Mean imputation removes the bias when missingness is MNAR.
statements.explanation: If missingness depends on the missing value, filling with the observed mean keeps the bias.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Median imputation preserves the original variance.
statements.explanation: A single constant at the center lowers the variance, whether it is the mean or the median.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Mean imputation leaves the sample mean unchanged and shrinks the sample variance.
statements.explanation: Adding values equal to the mean adds no spread.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Multiple imputation fills each blank once with the single best guess.
statements.explanation: Multiple imputation creates several completed datasets so the uncertainty about the imputed values is carried through.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Treating imputed values as observed data makes the standard error too small and overstates precision.
statements.explanation: The invented values add rows without adding information.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.source: Robust statistics, median, IQR, outlier rule
questions.stem: Eleven response times are 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 18, 19 and 120 seconds. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The interquartile range is the difference between the maximum and the minimum.
statements.explanation: That is the range; the interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The median and the interquartile range are robust (resistant) statistics, while the mean and standard deviation are sensitive to extreme values.
statements.explanation: One extreme value moves the mean and standard deviation much more than the median and IQR.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 1.5 × IQR rule flags candidate outliers for inspection.
statements.explanation: A flag marks a value to examine, not a verdict.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The mean of 24.9 seconds is a reliable summary of the typical response time here.
statements.explanation: The single extreme value pulls the mean far above the central bulk of the data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A value flagged by the 1.5 × IQR rule is a data error and is deleted automatically.
statements.explanation: A flagged value can be a genuine rare event; deletion depends on how the value arose.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.source: Row reconciliation, anti-join, stratified check, silent data loss
questions.stem: A pipeline joins an orders table to a customer table. The orders table has 50,000 rows and the joined table has 47,500, and the dropped rows belong to one region. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Row reconciliation compares counts by source, stage and group before and after a join against what is expected.
statements.explanation: A mismatch in counts exposes rows that were dropped.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Checks on null values, types and ranges can pass on the remaining rows even though rows are missing.
statements.explanation: Checks on present rows leave no trace of rows that never arrived.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If 5% of rows are lost, the statistics computed afterward are within 5% of their true values.
statements.explanation: Lost rows can differ systematically from the rest, so a statistic can shift by much more than the share lost.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A check repeated within each group can reveal a loss that the overall total hides.
statements.explanation: A stratified check shows that one region lost a quarter of its rows.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An anti-join lists the records in one table that have no matching key in the other, which reveals dropped keys.
statements.explanation: An anti-join returns the unmatched rows.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.source: Pearson correlation, sentinel value, Anscombe's quartet, correlation versus causation
questions.stem: An analyst summarizes data with statistics and plots. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pearson correlation measures linear association, so a perfect nonlinear relationship can have a correlation near 0.
statements.explanation: Y = X² on a symmetric range has correlation 0 with X.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A Pearson correlation of 0.9 in observational data is a causal effect.
statements.explanation: Correlation is association; confounding or reverse causation can produce it without causation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A spike at exactly 0 in a measurement that should be continuous suggests a sentinel value such as a default or missing-value code.
statements.explanation: A sentinel value is a placeholder entered in place of a real measurement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Datasets with identical summary statistics produce identical scatter plots.
statements.explanation: Anscombe's quartet shows very different plots that share the same means, variances and correlation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Pearson correlation is a robust statistic that one outlier barely changes.
statements.explanation: One far point can move the correlation from near 0 to near 1.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.source: Complete-case analysis, inverse probability weighting, sensitivity analysis, missingness indicator
questions.stem: A hospital estimates 30-day readmission from follow-up calls that reach only part of the patients; poorer-health patients are reached less often, and health status is recorded for each patient. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Complete-case analysis (listwise deletion) is justified when the missingness is MCAR, meaning unrelated to the data.
statements.explanation: Dropping incomplete rows leaves an unbiased subsample only under MCAR.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When missingness depends on a recorded variable such as health status, weighting or imputing within strata can correct the bias.
statements.explanation: Inverse probability weighting and stratified imputation use the observed variable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dropping the incomplete rows gives an unbiased estimate when missingness depends on health status.
statements.explanation: Under MAR, complete-case analysis is biased because the reached patients differ from the rest.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Under MNAR, a sensitivity analysis shows how conclusions change under different assumptions about the missingness mechanism.
statements.explanation: The observed data cannot settle the mechanism, so assumptions are varied.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A missingness indicator is a technique that makes MNAR data identifiable from the observed values.
statements.explanation: A missingness indicator is a column that records which values were missing; it does not make the mechanism identifiable.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.source: Skewness, mean versus median, mode, histogram versus scatter plot
questions.stem: An analyst describes the shape of a response-time variable and the best plot for it. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Standard deviation and variance are measures of central tendency.
statements.explanation: They measure spread, not center.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The median is the middle value of the sorted data, while the mean is the balance point of the data.
statements.explanation: They are two different measures of center.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In a right-skewed distribution the mean exceeds the median.
statements.explanation: A long right tail pulls the mean upward more than the median.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The mode is another name for the average.
statements.explanation: The mode is the most frequent value; the average is the mean.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A histogram shows the distribution of one variable, and a scatter plot shows the relationship between two variables.
statements.explanation: Histograms display shape; scatter plots display association.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.stem: A classifier for a rare event is scored at three thresholds, and a missed positive costs far more than a false alarm. Which statements use the metric terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accuracy is a dependable summary when the positive class is rare.
statements.explanation: With a rare class, accuracy is dominated by the majority class and can be high for a useless model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recall is the share of actual positives that the classifier flags.
statements.explanation: Recall = true positives / (true positives + false negatives).

statements.label: C
statements.text: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
statements.explanation: F1 combines the two into one number that is low when either is low.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising the decision threshold tends to raise precision and lower recall.
statements.explanation: A stricter cutoff flags fewer cases, mostly confident ones, and misses more positives.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Precision is the share of flagged cases that are truly positive.
statements.explanation: Precision = true positives / (true positives + false positives).

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.source: Overfitting, underfitting, regularization, training versus generalization error
questions.stem: Polynomial regressions of increasing degree are fit to 40 training points, and errors are measured on the training points and on held-out points. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Underfitting shows as low training error and high held-out error.
statements.explanation: Underfitting shows high error on both sets with a small gap between them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An overly flexible model has high bias and low variance.
statements.explanation: Overly flexible models have low bias and high variance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Regularization increases the flexibility of a model by adding more parameters.
statements.explanation: Regularization penalizes large coefficients to limit the effective flexibility.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Training error is a dependable estimate of generalization error.
statements.explanation: Training error falls as flexibility rises and says little about performance on new data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overfitting shows as low training error together with high held-out error.
statements.explanation: The model has fit noise in the training set.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.stem: A data scientist has 60 examples and 5,000 pure-noise features. They pick the 20 features most correlated with the label using all 60 examples, run 5-fold cross-validation on those features and report 92% accuracy. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Selecting features using the labels of the full dataset before cross-validation is leakage.
statements.explanation: The held-out labels shaped which features were chosen.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Fitting a label-dependent step such as target encoding on the full data before splitting is also leakage.
statements.explanation: Any step that sees held-out labels contaminates the estimate; such steps belong inside each training fold.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Data leakage means information from the held-out data influences model training or selection.
statements.explanation: Leakage makes the held-out estimate optimistic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With noise features and fair-coin labels, an honest evaluation should show accuracy near chance.
statements.explanation: A model has no signal to learn, so honest accuracy is about 50%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Using more folds removes the leakage from the feature selection done before the split.
statements.explanation: The selection already used every label, so the number of folds does not change the leak.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.source: Log-odds, odds, odds ratio, predicted probability
questions.stem: A logistic regression predicts whether an account is flagged: log-odds of being flagged = −2.0 + 0.9 × x, where x is the number of prior incidents. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The coefficient 0.9 is the change in log-odds of being flagged for one more prior incident.
statements.explanation: Logistic regression is linear in the log-odds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The exponential of the coefficient, about 2.46, is an odds ratio per additional incident.
statements.explanation: Each added incident multiplies the odds by exp(0.9).

statements.label: C
statements.text: Odds are the probability p divided by 1 minus p.
statements.explanation: Odds compare the chance of the event with the chance of its complement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Each additional prior incident multiplies the predicted probability of being flagged by 2.46.
statements.explanation: The coefficient acts on the odds, not on the probability.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The effect of one more incident on the predicted probability is constant across the range of x.
statements.explanation: The probability curve is S-shaped, so the change in probability depends on where you start.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.stem: A scorer assigns probabilities of being positive to nine cases, and an analyst compares AUC, calibration and log loss for it. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Cubing the scores leaves the AUC unchanged.
statements.explanation: A monotonic transformation preserves the ranking, and AUC depends only on ranking.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A high AUC guarantees that the scores are well calibrated.
statements.explanation: AUC measures ranking, so a well-ranked scorer can still have scores that do not match observed frequencies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Log loss treats a confident wrong prediction the same as an unsure wrong one.
statements.explanation: Log loss grows steeply as the probability given to the true outcome approaches 0.

statements.label: D
statements.text: AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored above a randomly chosen negative, so it measures discrimination (ranking).
statements.explanation: AUC uses only the order of the scores.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Calibration means that predicted probabilities match observed frequencies, such as 70% of cases scored 0.7 being positive.
statements.explanation: Calibration compares predicted probability with the actual rate.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.source: Confusion matrix, false negative, specificity, majority-class baseline, cost-based threshold
questions.stem: A vendor says its screening model is "99.3% accurate" on a test set where 0.8% of cases are positive. The model flags 300 cases, of which 200 are truly positive. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A baseline that flags nothing can score high accuracy when the positive class is rare, which is why a majority-class baseline is a comparison point.
statements.explanation: Accuracy reflects mostly the common class.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A false negative is an actual positive that the model failed to flag.
statements.explanation: False negatives are the missed positives.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Specificity is the share of actual negatives that the model correctly leaves unflagged.
statements.explanation: Specificity = true negatives / (true negatives + false positives).

statements.label: D
statements.text: Sensitivity and specificity are the same pair of quantities as precision and recall.
statements.explanation: Sensitivity equals recall, but specificity is a different quantity from precision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A 0.5 cutoff minimizes expected cost regardless of the relative costs of the two error types.
statements.explanation: The cost-minimizing threshold depends on the relative cost of false negatives and false positives.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.source: Winner's curse, validation set, nested cross-validation, distribution shift
questions.stem: A team tries 200 hyperparameter configurations, scores each on the same fixed test set, and reports the best score as the expected accuracy in production. Which statements use the terms correctly? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tuning belongs on a validation set or in cross-validation, and the test set is used once at the end.
statements.explanation: Keeping the test set untouched gives an independent estimate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Nested cross-validation uses an inner loop for tuning and an outer loop for estimating performance.
statements.explanation: The outer folds never influence the choices made in the inner loop.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Choosing the best of many configurations on the test set makes the reported score optimistic, a selection effect called the winner's curse.
statements.explanation: The maximum of many noisy scores is biased upward.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Distribution shift between the test data and production data leaves the test accuracy a valid estimate of production accuracy.
statements.explanation: Under distribution shift, test accuracy can overstate performance in production.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Near-duplicate examples shared between training and test splits make the score pessimistic.
statements.explanation: Shared near-duplicates leak information and make the score optimistic.

questions.stem: A reviewer rewrites the vague claim "the assistant is reliable" so that it can be tested, and asks for the exact terms for each part. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An assumption is a result observed after the test has been run.
statements.explanation: An assumption is a condition taken as given, and stated beforehand, for the claim to hold.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A falsifier is a statement of how confident the team is that the claim will hold.
statements.explanation: A falsifier is an observation that would count against the claim, not a statement of confidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A claim that no possible observation could contradict is called unfalsifiable.
statements.explanation: Unfalsifiable claims are compatible with every outcome, so they carry no testable content.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A falsifier names an observation, with a threshold and a time window, that would count against the claim.
statements.explanation: A checkable falsifier says in advance which result would show the claim to be wrong.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "The assistant performs well in the situations that matter" is a falsifier because it names the goal.
statements.explanation: Naming a goal without a metric or threshold leaves no observation that could contradict the statement.

questions.stem: A team says that adding a retrieval step makes its assistant hallucinate less, and a reviewer asks for the claim in testable form on a held-out question set. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An assumption is a condition taken as given, such as that the held-out questions resemble real use.
statements.explanation: Assumptions are the conditions under which the prediction is expected to hold.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A falsifier could be a hallucination rate with retrieval that is no lower than the rate without it, at a stated threshold.
statements.explanation: It names a result that would count as failure of the claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A falsifier is the prediction repeated in different words.
statements.explanation: A falsifier is the result that would refute the prediction, not a restatement of it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A held-out set is data used to train the retrieval step.
statements.explanation: A held-out set is data withheld from training and tuning so it can test the claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The prediction states a measurable direction of change, such as a lower hallucination rate, on a named held-out set.
statements.explanation: A prediction is a specific, measurable statement made before the test.

questions.stem: A vendor says its content filter lets through no step-by-step instructions for listed hazardous compounds. As evidence it reports that 10,000 prompts written by its own staff to look like ordinary requests produced none. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Zero failures in a test prove that the true failure rate is zero.
statements.explanation: Zero observed failures gives an upper bound on the rate that is above zero.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Prompts written to resemble ordinary requests are a non-adversarial sample and say little about deliberate attempts to get past the filter.
statements.explanation: The test inputs differ in kind from the inputs the claim is about.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A universal claim of this kind is refuted by a single counterexample.
statements.explanation: One observed instance of the forbidden output is enough to contradict a claim stated as a universal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 10,000 passing prompts verify the universal claim.
statements.explanation: A finite set of passing cases supports the claim to a limited degree and does not verify it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Red teaming means repeating the vendor's ordinary prompts at larger volume.
statements.explanation: Red teaming is deliberate, adversarial effort to make the system fail.

questions.stem: A manager wants her team to practise methodical skepticism, and asks which words describe what she wants and what she wants to avoid. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Methodical skepticism is a procedure applied to a specific claim, whose use can be seen.
statements.explanation: Methodical skepticism is a repeatable method, such as writing the failure criterion first.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to favour evidence that agrees with what one already believes.
statements.explanation: It makes a reviewer accept outputs that match prior judgment.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Cynicism is a procedure that can be performed on one particular claim.
statements.explanation: Cynicism is a general attitude of distrust, not a procedure applied to a claim.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Writing down what a wrong answer would look like before reading the output fixes the criterion in advance.
statements.explanation: A criterion set beforehand cannot be bent to fit whatever the output says.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Agreement between an output and the reviewer's own earlier judgments is independent evidence that the output is right.
statements.explanation: That agreement is not independent of the reviewer, and can repeat the reviewer's mistakes.

questions.source: Distribution shift, extrapolation, reproducibility versus accuracy
questions.stem: A loan-scoring system outputs "default risk 0.82, decline" for an applicant, and a reviewer lists the conditions under which that score would be wrong for this person. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If few training examples resemble this applicant, the score is an extrapolation and deserves less trust.
statements.explanation: Extrapolation means predicting in a region the training data covers thinly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Submitting the same application twice and receiving the same score shows that the score is accurate.
statements.explanation: Reproducibility shows consistency, not accuracy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Writing the list of conditions is itself the test that shows which conditions hold.
statements.explanation: The list names suspects; each condition still needs its own inspection.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A unit mismatch between two source systems is a modelling error, not an input data fault.
statements.explanation: Entering income in thousands in one system and in units in another is a data-quality fault in the input.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If applicants now arriving come from a different population than the validation sample, the validation result may not carry over; this is distribution shift.
statements.explanation: Distribution shift is a change between the data a model was validated on and the data it now sees.

questions.source: Pre-registration, inconclusive result, moving the goalposts
questions.stem: Before an experiment a researcher writes in a dated file: the new prompt will raise exact-match accuracy by at least 2 points, and a gain below 0.5 points or any drop means the claim has failed. The run shows a gain of 1.2 points. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Moving the failure line to 1 point after seeing the result keeps the test a pre-registered test.
statements.explanation: Changing the rule after the result removes the protection pre-registration gives.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Shifting a threshold after seeing the result is called moving the goalposts.
statements.explanation: The criterion is adjusted to fit the outcome instead of the outcome being judged against the criterion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A gain between the failure line and the predicted size leaves the claim neither confirmed nor refuted, which is an inconclusive result.
statements.explanation: The pre-set rule marks the claim as failed or supported only outside this middle band.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Recording the prediction and failure rule in a dated file before the run is pre-registration.
statements.explanation: Pre-registration fixes the prediction and decision rule before the data are seen.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A gain of 1.2 points meets the stated prediction.
statements.explanation: The prediction was a gain of at least 2 points, so the result falls short of it.

questions.source: Multiple comparisons, p-value, post hoc explanation
questions.stem: After a prompt change shows no overall gain, an analyst compares 20 customer segments, finds one with p = 0.03, and says the change works there because that segment uses shorter queries. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The explanation about shorter queries, written after the result, is a prediction.
statements.explanation: An explanation written after the result is post hoc, since it can be fitted to the data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chance of at least one false positive across a set of tests is the familywise error rate, and it rises with the number of comparisons.
statements.explanation: Each added test adds another chance of a spurious result.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A correction for multiple comparisons makes the per-test threshold looser.
statements.explanation: A correction makes the per-test threshold stricter.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% probability that the change has no effect in that segment.
statements.explanation: A p-value is the probability of data this extreme if there is no effect, not the probability that there is no effect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reporting the one significant segment out of 20 comparisons is an example of multiple comparisons, and of p-hacking when the others are not reported.
statements.explanation: Many tests inflate the chance of at least one small p-value arising by chance.

questions.stem: An LLM assistant with no access to a company's systems is asked why a query is slow, and replies with a confident, well-organised account naming a specific table and setting. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A confident tone is a measure of calibration.
statements.explanation: Calibration is agreement between stated confidence and the observed fraction correct, and tone does not measure it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Naming a specific table is evidence that the model had access to the system.
statements.explanation: Specific detail is easy to generate and does not show access.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An explanation not grounded in access to the system is a hallucination, sometimes called confabulation.
statements.explanation: The model produces plausible text without evidence about this database.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The right status for the account is a hypothesis that still needs a test.
statements.explanation: A hypothesis becomes a finding only after an observation that could have contradicted it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fluency describes the style of the text and not the evidence behind it.
statements.explanation: A well-written answer can be unsupported.

questions.stem: An LLM given only a table of weekly revenue writes a specific account blaming a competitor's price cut for an 8% fall, though a shifted billing date or a moved holiday fits the table equally well. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The account the model wrote should be chosen because it is the most fluent.
statements.explanation: Fluency is not evidence and does not break a tie between accounts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When several accounts fit the same data equally well, the data underdetermine the cause.
statements.explanation: Underdetermination means the evidence does not single out one explanation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Restating the same table in more detail in the prompt breaks the tie.
statements.explanation: More detail of the same data does not separate accounts that already fit it equally.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Telling the accounts apart takes a discriminating observation, such as billing-date records, that the rival accounts predict differently.
statements.explanation: A discriminating observation is one whose outcome differs under the rival accounts.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Rival accounts that fit the data equally well are called confounders.
statements.explanation: They are rival or alternative hypotheses; a confounder is a variable linked to both cause and outcome.

questions.stem: An LLM assistant states at least 90% confidence on 200 answers, and an audit finds 150 of them correct. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The audit measures discrimination, the ability to rank correct answers above incorrect ones.
statements.explanation: Comparing stated confidence with hit rate measures calibration.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Stating the same confidence on each answer is required for a model to count as calibrated.
statements.explanation: A model can vary its confidence and still be calibrated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Accuracy and calibration are different properties.
statements.explanation: A model can be accurate overall and still state confidence that is too high or too low.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calibration is agreement between stated confidence and the fraction of answers that are correct.
statements.explanation: A calibrated 90% statement is right about 90% of the time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Stated confidence above the observed fraction correct is overconfidence.
statements.explanation: The model's confidence statements are higher than its hit rate.

questions.stem: An analyst wants a second check on a model-written answer to a question about a company's revenue in a given year. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Looking up the figure in the company's filed annual report is a check independent of the model's recall.
statements.explanation: A primary source has errors unrelated to the model's errors.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A check is independent when its errors do not move together with the errors of the first check.
statements.explanation: Independence of errors is what makes a second check add evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A second model trained on largely the same data gives errors that are uncorrelated with the first model's.
statements.explanation: Shared training data makes the two models' errors move together.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking the same model the same question again and getting the same answer is an independent check.
statements.explanation: Repeating a source gives a correlated answer, not independent evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Agreement among checks that copy the same source strengthens the evidence in proportion to the number of checks.
statements.explanation: Copies of one source count as one source.

questions.source: Redundancy, correlated errors, recall versus precision
questions.stem: Two reviewers inspect the same batch for a defect, and a manager asks how redundancy helps and what terms describe the reviewers' performance. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the reviewers' misses are independent, the chance that both miss a defect is lower than for either alone.
statements.explanation: Independent failures combine so that joint failure is rarer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Correlated errors reduce the benefit of adding a second reviewer.
statements.explanation: If both tend to miss the same defects, the second adds little.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Redundancy improves detection whatever the correlation between reviewers.
statements.explanation: The gain from redundancy shrinks as errors become more correlated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Two reviewers who use the same checklist and the same examples have independent errors.
statements.explanation: Shared method and training make errors correlated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Precision is the share of real defects that a reviewer finds.
statements.explanation: The share of real defects found is recall, also called sensitivity.

questions.stem: A team has a language model answer 500 support questions and then grades each answer pass or fail by prompting the same model as a judge, reporting a 94% pass rate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Using the same model to generate and to grade creates circularity, because the two share blind spots.
statements.explanation: A judge with the same weaknesses as the generator tends to approve its mistakes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A 94% pass rate from the judge is an estimate of accuracy against ground truth.
statements.explanation: It measures agreement with the judge, which is not ground truth.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A model judge's verdicts are ground truth labels.
statements.explanation: Ground truth comes from an independent, trusted source, not from another model's opinion.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Self-preference bias is a judge's tendency to prefer outputs from other models.
statements.explanation: Self-preference bias is the tendency to prefer its own outputs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Comparing the judge's verdicts with human labels on a sample checks the judge against an independent reference.
statements.explanation: Human labels from a domain expert supply a reference the judge did not produce.

questions.stem: A reporter finds the statistic "62% of firms have adopted technology X" in five articles that cite different outlets, but all five trace to one press release from a vendor that sells X, with no sample size or method given. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number of articles that repeat a statistic is a measure of its reliability.
statements.explanation: Repetition measures spread, not accuracy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Provenance is the record of where a claim or dataset originated.
statements.explanation: Provenance answers the question of origin.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Five articles repeating one release is circular reporting, which is one source and not five.
statements.explanation: Circular reporting is repetition of a single origin that looks like several.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A vendor that sells the technology has no conflict of interest in reporting its adoption.
statements.explanation: A source with a stake in the result has a conflict of interest, which is a reason to seek the primary data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Lineage names the original source of a claim, while provenance records the transformations applied to it.
