statements.explanation: Provenance records where a claim or dataset came from, and lineage records the chain of transformations it went through.

questions.stem: A migration job logs "Migrated 12,000 rows: SUCCESS" and exits with status 0, but a row count run directly on the destination table returns 11,400. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing the destination count with the source count is validation, meaning a check that the right system was built.
statements.explanation: Comparing against the specification or source is verification; validation asks whether the system meets the real need.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A claim of success is evidence of the same kind as an observed outcome.
statements.explanation: A claim reports an outcome and an observation shows it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Exit status 0 shows that the output is correct.
statements.explanation: It shows only that the process ended without reporting an error.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The log line is a report about the job, while the row count is a direct observation of the destination state.
statements.explanation: A report and an observation are different kinds of evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Verification checks the artifact itself instead of relying on the process's own account.
statements.explanation: Direct inspection of the output is what makes a check independent of the job's claim.

questions.stem: A nightly backup job has written "backup completed" and exited with status 0 on 400 nights in a row, and the goal is that data can be restored after a loss. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A restore test checks the goal, that data can be recovered, directly.
statements.explanation: Restoring from a backup is the observation that matches the goal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: 400 completion log lines are 400 independent verifications of recoverability.
statements.explanation: Each line is a report from the same job and says nothing about whether a restore works.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The "backup completed" log line is a proxy for recoverability.
statements.explanation: A proxy is a measurable stand-in for the quantity that matters.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A proxy is a measure that stands in for the goal without being the goal.
statements.explanation: Proxies can come apart from the goal they represent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A restore test can still miss conditions it did not exercise, such as a partial loss.
statements.explanation: A check covers only the cases it actually exercised.

questions.source: Discriminating test, regression test, edge case
questions.stem: A developer says her patch fixes a crash when a customer's name contains an apostrophe. Her test exports a record for "Olivia Smith" and passes after the patch. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An input at the boundary of normal variation, such as a name with an apostrophe, is an edge case.
statements.explanation: Edge cases are where defects tend to hide.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The "Olivia Smith" test is a regression test for the apostrophe bug.
statements.explanation: It does not exercise the failing condition, so it cannot catch a return of the bug.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A passing test suite proves that the bug is fixed.
statements.explanation: A pass shows only that the tested inputs behave correctly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A test that passes both before and after the patch does not discriminate between fixed and unfixed code.
statements.explanation: A useful test is one whose result differs between the two states.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test that fails on the unpatched code and passes on the patched code is a discriminating test.
statements.explanation: Fail-before, pass-after shows the test responds to the fault.

questions.source: Zero events, confidence bound, statistic versus parameter
questions.stem: A safety evaluation runs a chatbot on 100 prompts drawn at random from expected traffic and records 0 harmful responses. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The observed rate of zero in the sample is the population parameter.
statements.explanation: A sample statistic estimates the population parameter and can differ from it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Random sampling from expected traffic lets the result describe adversarial traffic.
statements.explanation: A random sample describes the traffic it was drawn from.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Zero events in 100 trials gives an upper confidence bound on the harmful-response rate that is above zero.
statements.explanation: A small sample cannot rule out a modest rate; the rule of three gives roughly 3 divided by the number of trials.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A confidence interval around an observed rate of zero is a single point at zero.
statements.explanation: The interval has an upper end above zero when the sample is finite.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Zero observed harmful responses means the true rate is zero.
statements.explanation: The observed frequency is an estimate and has uncertainty.

questions.stem: A static-analysis tool finds each instance of a vulnerability class with probability 0.6 and raises no false alarms. It reports nothing for a module. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Failing to report a real vulnerability is a false negative.
statements.explanation: A false negative is a real case that the test misses.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Precision is the share of real instances that the tool finds.
statements.explanation: Precision is the share of reported instances that are real; the share found is recall.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising no false alarms corresponds to a specificity of 0.
statements.explanation: No false alarms corresponds to a specificity of 1.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 0.6 chance of finding a real instance is the tool's sensitivity, also called recall.
statements.explanation: Sensitivity is the share of real instances the tool detects.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A silent report establishes that the module contains no instance.
statements.explanation: With sensitivity below 1, a silent report leaves some chance that an instance is present.

questions.stem: A team injects 50 small deliberate faults into its code, one at a time, and reruns its passing test suite for each. The suite detects 31 of the 50. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Injecting deliberate faults to see whether tests catch them is mutation testing.
statements.explanation: Mutation testing measures the strength of a test suite.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A passing suite means less when its mutation score is low.
statements.explanation: A suite that misses many injected faults could also miss real ones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The share of injected faults detected is the suite's false positive rate.
statements.explanation: It is the mutation score, also called the kill rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The share of injected faults that the suite detects is called the mutation score.
statements.explanation: A higher score means the suite responds to more kinds of faults.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A mutant that changes behavior on no possible input is an equivalent mutant, and it does not show a gap in the tests.
statements.explanation: No test could detect it, since the program's behavior is unchanged.

questions.stem: A discussion compares the effort needed to produce an answer with the effort needed to check it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Solve-verify asymmetry names a gap between the effort to produce an answer and the effort to check it.
statements.explanation: The gap can be large in either direction, depending on the task.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For open-ended text such as summaries, verifying is cheaper than generating.
statements.explanation: Checking a summary against its source can cost as much as writing it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Checking a proposed factorisation by multiplying is a case where verifying is cheaper than solving.
statements.explanation: Some tasks are hard to solve and easy to check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When the cost of generating falls toward zero, the cost of verifying falls with it.
statements.explanation: Cheap generation does not make checking cheaper.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The gap between solving and checking runs in one direction across task types.
statements.explanation: The direction varies with the task.

questions.stem: A model drafts 2,000 contract summaries a day at negligible cost, and a lawyer needs 10 minutes to check one summary against its contract. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Outputs that were not checked are unverified, not verified-correct, even if no error was reported.
statements.explanation: Lack of a reported error is not evidence of correctness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A random-sample audit catches each material error in the batch.
statements.explanation: A sample finds only the errors that fall inside it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Auditing a random sample estimates the error rate of the batch without checking each item.
statements.explanation: Sampling trades coverage for cost while keeping an estimate of the rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Directing more checking effort toward higher-risk items is risk-based sampling.
statements.explanation: Risk-based sampling spends scarce review effort where errors cost the most.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When generation is cheap and checking is expensive, verification becomes the bottleneck.
statements.explanation: Throughput is limited by the slowest step, which here is checking.

questions.stem: A support team rewards agents, and its AI drafting assistant, for average handle time. Handle time falls from 11 to 7 minutes while repeat contacts about the same issue rise from 14% to 26%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reward hacking means an agent improves the true goal beyond what the metric asked.
statements.explanation: Reward hacking is scoring high on the specified metric without achieving the intended goal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Average handle time is a proxy for service quality.
statements.explanation: It stands in for quality without being quality.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The rise in repeat contacts is evidence that handle time measures resolution well.
statements.explanation: Rising repeats show that handle time and resolution have come apart.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A proxy validated once still tracks the goal after the incentives change.
statements.explanation: Incentives can change behavior and break a relationship that held before.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure; this is Goodhart's law.
statements.explanation: Optimising a proxy directly breaks its link to the goal.

questions.source: Proxy label, concept drift, covariate shift, label shift
questions.stem: Team 1 trains a model on past healthcare spending as a stand-in for medical need. Team 2's demand forecaster had low error for two years, until a new competitor changed customers' buying habits and the error began to rise. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Team 1 used a proxy label, and the proxy was not the target to begin with.
statements.explanation: A proxy label is a measured stand-in for the quantity that matters.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Concept drift is a change in the distribution of inputs while the relation of outcome to inputs stays fixed.
statements.explanation: That description fits covariate shift.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Team 2's rising error after the competitor appeared is concept drift, since the relation between inputs and outcome changed.
statements.explanation: Concept drift is a change in how inputs relate to the outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Label shift is a change in the proportion of outcome classes between training and use.
statements.explanation: It is also called prior probability shift.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retraining Team 1's model on newer data with the same proxy label closes the gap between label and need.
statements.explanation: The same flawed label reproduces the same gap.

questions.source: Covariate shift, in-distribution versus out-of-distribution, external validity
questions.stem: A delivery-time predictor was within its stated margin on 98% of 50,000 orders in a year of normal operation. The company opens a new region with a different road network. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: External validity is whether a result carries over to settings other than the one tested.
statements.explanation: The new region is a setting outside the tested one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Covariate shift means that the relation of the outputs to the inputs changes.
statements.explanation: That describes concept drift; covariate shift changes the input distribution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Accuracy on held-out data from the same period is an in-distribution estimate.
statements.explanation: It describes performance on data like the data it was tested on.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Inputs from the new region differ from the earlier inputs, which is distribution shift, specifically covariate shift if the relation of outcome to inputs holds.
statements.explanation: Covariate shift changes the input distribution while the outcome relation stays the same.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 98% figure is an out-of-distribution estimate for the new region.
statements.explanation: It was measured on the old region and does not describe the new one.

questions.stem: A pneumonia classifier is trained and tested on pooled images from two hospitals with very different pneumonia rates, and each image carries a visible scanner tag that identifies its hospital. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The hospital is a confounder, since it is linked to both the tag and the pneumonia rate.
statements.explanation: A confounder is related to both the cue and the outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Pooling the data from two hospitals does not remove the confounding.
statements.explanation: The hospital remains linked to both the tag and the label.

statements.label: C
statements.text: High accuracy on the pooled test set shows that the model generalises to a third hospital.
statements.explanation: The pooled test set shares the same shortcut, so it does not show generalisation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A spurious correlation is a link in the training data, here between tag and label, that does not reflect the disease.
statements.explanation: The association comes from how the data were pooled.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A model that relies on the hospital tag as a cue instead of the lung image is shortcut learning.
statements.explanation: Shortcut learning means using an easy cue that happens to predict the label.

questions.stem: A pipeline lets an AI reviewer approve routine configuration changes proposed by an AI agent, and the record reads "Approved by ReviewBot." One approved change causes an outage. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Responsibility transfers to the AI model because it performed the review.
statements.explanation: A software component cannot be held answerable, so responsibility stays with the people who deployed it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Rubber-stamping is a meaningful review carried out at speed.
statements.explanation: Rubber-stamping is approval given without real examination.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An approval attributed to a software component assigns accountability.
statements.explanation: Accountability needs an identifiable person who can answer for the decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An audit trail records who decided what and when.
statements.explanation: An audit trail supports later review even though it does not prevent errors.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Accountability needs a person who accepted the risk, can explain the decision, and had the authority to make it.
statements.explanation: Without such a person nobody answers for the outcome.

questions.stem: Reviewers approve 4,850 of 5,000 AI recommendations, at a median of 4 seconds each. An independent audit finds that 400 of the 5,000 were wrong. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The approval rate measures how many of the recommendations were correct.
statements.explanation: The approval rate describes reviewers' decisions, which the audit shows can differ from correctness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Automation bias is the tendency to over-rely on suggestions from an automated system.
statements.explanation: It can lead reviewers to approve without examining.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A human-in-the-loop step is meaningful when the person has the time, the information and the authority to reject.
statements.explanation: A reviewer lacking any of these cannot provide a real check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Rejecting 150 items when 400 were wrong means the reviewers' sensitivity to errors was below 100%.
statements.explanation: At most 150 of the 400 wrong items could have been caught.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Approvals given without examination are called rubber-stamping.
statements.explanation: A very high approval rate with very short review times is consistent with it.

questions.source: Scope of a claim, unverified status
questions.stem: A test report reads: "Tested 40 of 40 sample invoices: all processed correctly. Not tested: handwritten scans, invoices in languages other than English, behavior under production load." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The scope of a claim is the set of conditions under which it was tested.
statements.explanation: The claim extends only as far as the conditions that were exercised.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 40 correct invoices support the claim that the system handles handwritten scans.
statements.explanation: Handwritten scans are outside the scope that was tested.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sample of 40 clean invoices is representative of behavior under production load.
statements.explanation: The sample differs in kind from the load conditions it is meant to stand for.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Absence of a failure in untested conditions counts as a pass.
statements.explanation: No test was run there, so there is no result either way.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Conditions that were not tested should be labelled unverified.
statements.explanation: Unverified means unknown, which differs from tested and passed.

questions.stem: A vendor reports 91% accuracy for its model on a benchmark. Eight training runs that differ only in random seed scored between 83% and 91%, and the vendor reported the best run, picked by looking at test accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reporting the best of several runs, chosen using the test score, is cherry-picking.
statements.explanation: The reported number is selected for being high.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reporting the mean and spread across seeds, with selection done on a validation set, is p-hacking.
statements.explanation: That reporting separates selection from testing and shows the variability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The spread of results across random seeds is called bias.
statements.explanation: The spread across seeds is variance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The best of eight runs is an upward-biased estimate of the expected accuracy of a fresh run, an effect called the winner's curse.
statements.explanation: Selecting the maximum of noisy results overstates the typical result.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Choosing a run by test accuracy uses the test set for model selection, which is a form of leakage.
statements.explanation: The test set no longer gives an unbiased estimate once it guides choices.

questions.stem: A deployment team wants its skeptical checks to happen reliably instead of depending on whether one engineer remembers to be careful. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A checklist item phrased as a yes-or-no question makes a general worry something that can be inspected.
statements.explanation: A specific question can be assigned, answered and audited.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Setting a threshold in a monitoring alert before launch applies the criterion without relying on memory.
statements.explanation: A pre-set alert runs whether or not anyone is thinking about it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A named person with authority to hold a release gives a failed check consequences.
statements.explanation: Authority to act is what makes the check effective.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Once a check is written into the process, the check does not need review.
statements.explanation: Checks drift away from the real risk as the system and its use change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A check is a gate when its failure can halt or delay a release.
statements.explanation: A check that cannot stop anything only records a problem.

questions.source: Post hoc explanation, HARKing, decision rule
questions.stem: A data scientist trains several variants, looks at validation results, and then writes a plausible explanation of why one variant won. A colleague writes a prediction and a decision rule before running the same comparison. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing many variants on the validation set and picking the best leaves the validation estimate unbiased.
statements.explanation: Repeated selection on the validation set makes its estimate optimistic, a form of overfitting to it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A decision rule fixed before the comparison keeps the analyst from choosing the criterion after seeing results.
statements.explanation: The rule is set without knowledge of the outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An explanation written after seeing results is post hoc, since it can be fitted to whatever the data showed.
statements.explanation: Post hoc accounts are easy to produce for any outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: HARKing means forming the hypothesis before the results are known.
statements.explanation: HARKing is hypothesizing after the results are known.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A prediction written before the run is weaker evidence because the data had not been seen.
statements.explanation: A prediction that could have failed is stronger evidence when it succeeds.

questions.source: Data drift, concept drift, label delay, nonstationarity
questions.stem: A credit-risk model has been accurate for two years, and the team is designing post-deployment monitoring. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Past accuracy is inductive evidence and does not guarantee future accuracy when conditions change.
statements.explanation: Conditions that held in the past can stop holding, which is nonstationarity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Data drift monitoring compares the distribution of live inputs with the distribution of the training inputs.
statements.explanation: It flags changes in the inputs before outcomes are known.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Concept drift can be detected from the input distribution alone.
statements.explanation: Concept drift is a change in the relation of outcome to inputs, which inputs alone can miss.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A drift alert tells the team the cause of a drop in performance.
statements.explanation: An alert signals that something changed, not why.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Monitoring performance needs ground-truth outcomes, which often arrive late; this is label delay.
statements.explanation: Loan defaults appear long after the decision.

questions.source: Judge agreement, recall, precision, Cohen's kappa
questions.stem: People relabel a random sample of 50 answers from a model judge. In the sample the judge passed 45 answers and the humans passed 38; the judge failed 5 answers, of which 4 the humans also failed. The team wants terms for how well the judge matches the humans. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The share of judge-pass answers that humans also pass is the judge's recall.
statements.explanation: That share is the precision of the judge's pass verdicts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A judge that passes answers humans fail is lenient, producing false passes.
statements.explanation: A false pass is a judge pass where the reference says fail.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Agreement between two raters corrected for chance agreement is measured by Cohen's kappa.
statements.explanation: Kappa discounts the agreement expected from chance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raw percent agreement already adjusts for chance agreement.
statements.explanation: Raw agreement ignores chance, which is why kappa is used.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The share of answers that humans fail and the judge also fails is the judge's sensitivity, or recall, for failures.
statements.explanation: Sensitivity for a target class is the share of true members of that class that are detected.

questions.stem: A vendor claims its meeting-summary assistant "saves managers time", and an evaluator turns this into a measurable test. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Saves time" is already an operational definition.
statements.explanation: It names no measurable quantity or unit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A control group is the group that receives the tool.
statements.explanation: A control group is the comparison group that does not receive the tool.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Operationalising a claim means choosing a measurable quantity that stands for it, such as minutes spent on meeting follow-up.
statements.explanation: An operational definition makes a vague term measurable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Counting how many managers say they like the tool measures time saved.
statements.explanation: A satisfaction rating measures a different construct than minutes saved.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A baseline is the number reported after the tool has been introduced.
statements.explanation: A baseline is a measurement taken before the change, or in a comparison group without it.

questions.source: Negative finding, sensitivity, false negative, prevalence
questions.stem: An AI reviewer scans 400 pull requests for security flaws, reports none, and a manager concludes that the code base is secure. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Seeding known flaws and counting how many the reviewer flags estimates its sensitivity, or recall.
statements.explanation: Seeded flaws give the denominator needed to measure detection.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reporting no findings establishes that the code is secure.
statements.explanation: No findings is consistent with a reviewer that misses flaws.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A reviewer with high specificity has high sensitivity as a result.
statements.explanation: Specificity and sensitivity are separate properties.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A true negative is a flaw that the reviewer missed.
statements.explanation: A missed flaw is a false negative; a true negative is a clean item correctly passed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The prevalence of flaws is a property of the reviewer.
statements.explanation: Prevalence is a property of the code being reviewed.

questions.source: Approval design, segregation of duties, accountability
questions.stem: A company plans for an AI agent to prepare production price changes, with one Approve button for a person beside the agent's own summary of the change. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Approval by a person with no ability to reject the change is meaningful oversight.
statements.explanation: Oversight needs the practical ability to stop the action.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A named approver whose identity is recorded makes the decision attributable to a person.
statements.explanation: Attribution to a person is a precondition of accountability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Segregation of duties means that the same agent proposes and approves a change.
statements.explanation: Segregation of duties means that different parties propose and approve.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Showing the agent's own summary alone has the approver review the agent's account instead of the change itself.
statements.explanation: The summary is a report, and the diff of the change is the observation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Showing the actual difference and its expected impact lets the approver judge the change on independent evidence.
statements.explanation: Independent evidence is what makes the approval a check.

questions.stem: A reviewer picks words for three requests to an analyst: confirm the build matches its specification, confirm the system serves the real need, and look for a result that would refute the claim. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Falsification means collecting more cases that agree with the claim.
statements.explanation: Falsification seeks an observation that would contradict the claim.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Verification asks whether the system was built to its specification.
statements.explanation: Verification compares the artifact with its specification.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Validation asks whether the system meets the real need it was built for.
statements.explanation: A system can pass verification and still fail validation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Verification and validation are interchangeable words for this purpose.
statements.explanation: They answer different questions: built right versus right thing built.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test designed to falsify looks for cases expected to agree with the claim.
statements.explanation: A falsifying test targets cases where the claim could fail.

questions.source: Coherence, normalization and the Dutch book
questions.stem: A forecasting service publishes P(outage) = 0.70 and P(no outage) = 0.40 for the same day. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Coherence is judged on a set of probabilities taken together, not on one number alone.
statements.explanation: Probabilities are coherent when they satisfy the axioms jointly, such as normalization and additivity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The figures violate normalization, because the probabilities of an event and its complement should sum to 1.
statements.explanation: Normalization and the complement rule require P(event) + P(not event) = 1, and here the sum is 1.10.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The complement rule says P(no outage) should equal P(outage).
statements.explanation: The complement rule says P(not A) = 1 - P(A), which is different from equality.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A bettor treating the figures as fair prices could build a Dutch book, a set of bets that wins whichever outcome occurs.
statements.explanation: A Dutch book is a guaranteed-profit set of bets that exploits probabilities that are not coherent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The figures are coherent, because each one lies between 0 and 1.
statements.explanation: Coherence is a property of the whole set of probabilities; each number being in range is not enough.

questions.stem: An assistant is asked for P(rain or snow) given P(rain) and P(snow) for a day on which both can occur, and it simply adds the two numbers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The overlap term P(A and B) is called the marginal probability of A.
statements.explanation: P(A and B) is a joint probability; the marginal is P(A) on its own.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Simple addition of the two probabilities is valid for mutually exclusive events.
statements.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot co-occur, so there is no overlap to subtract.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For events that can co-occur, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), which is inclusion-exclusion.
statements.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion removes the overlap that addition counts twice.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Rain and snow that can fall on the same day are mutually exclusive.
statements.explanation: Mutually exclusive means the events cannot both happen; rain and snow here can.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding without subtracting the overlap double counts the outcomes where both events occur.
statements.explanation: The overlap is included once in each term, so it appears twice in the sum.

questions.stem: In a log of past cases, 70% carry an abnormal-lab flag, 40% are high-acuity, and 25% are both flagged and high-acuity. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 0.70 flag rate is a marginal probability.
statements.explanation: A marginal probability describes one variable without conditioning on another.

statements.label: B
statements.text: P(flag | high-acuity) is the same quantity as P(high-acuity | flag).
statements.explanation: Reversing the conditioning changes the denominator, so the two conditionals differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: P(high-acuity | flag) is found by dividing the marginal probability of the flag by the joint probability.
statements.explanation: A conditional probability divides the joint by the marginal of the conditioning event, not the other way round.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The flag and high acuity are independent because the joint probability is smaller than each marginal.
statements.explanation: Independence needs the joint to equal the product of the marginals, not merely to be smaller than each.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 0.25 figure is a joint probability.
statements.explanation: A joint probability is the probability that both events occur together.

questions.stem: For the same log, an analyst compares the joint probability 0.25 with the product of the two marginals, 0.70 x 0.40 = 0.28. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Independence means the joint probability equals the product of the marginal probabilities.
statements.explanation: That equality is the definition of independence for two events.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Independent events and mutually exclusive events are the same thing.
statements.explanation: Independent events can co-occur; mutually exclusive events cannot.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Since 0.25 differs from 0.28, the flag and high acuity are not independent.
statements.explanation: A joint that does not match the product of the marginals signals dependence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For independent events, conditioning on one leaves the probability of the other unchanged.
statements.explanation: If A and B are independent, P(A | B) = P(A).

statements.label: E
statements.text: A joint below each marginal shows the two events are mutually exclusive.
statements.explanation: Mutually exclusive events have a joint of zero, which is a different condition.

questions.stem: An agent completes three tool calls in sequence. An analyst estimates the chance that all three succeed by multiplying each call's success rate measured separately on fresh inputs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chain rule requires the steps to be independent.
statements.explanation: The chain rule is valid for dependent events; independence only lets the conditionals simplify.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chain rule multiplies P(first) by P(second | first) by P(third | first and second).
statements.explanation: The chain rule builds a joint probability from conditionals on the earlier steps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If each step is more reliable after earlier steps succeed than on its own, the independence product overstates the chance that the whole task succeeds.
statements.explanation: That situation would make the independence product understate the joint probability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Multiplying marginal success rates gives the joint probability when the calls are independent.
statements.explanation: The product of marginals equals the joint exactly under independence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The factors in the chain rule are the marginal probabilities of each step.
statements.explanation: The factors are conditional probabilities given the earlier steps, not marginals.

questions.stem: A fraud-screening service routes each case to one of three model versions, each with its own error rate and share of traffic. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: P(version | error) comes from Bayes' theorem applied to the traffic shares and the version error rates.
statements.explanation: Bayes' theorem inverts P(error | version) into P(version | error) using the shares as priors.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A version's share of the errors is its traffic share times its error rate, divided by the overall error rate.
statements.explanation: That is Bayes' theorem written with the law of total probability in the denominator.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Changing the traffic mix changes the overall error rate even when no model changes.
statements.explanation: The overall rate is a weighted average, so its weights matter.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The overall error rate is the plain average of the three versions' error rates.
statements.explanation: The plain average ignores the weights; the correct combination weights each rate by its share.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The overall error rate is the sum over versions of traffic share times that version's error rate, by the law of total probability.
statements.explanation: The law of total probability decomposes an overall probability into a weighted sum over cases.

questions.stem: A team updates its belief that a transaction is fraudulent after an alert fires. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The posterior is the probability of fraud before the alert is taken into account.
statements.explanation: The posterior is the updated belief after the evidence; the quantity described is the prior.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The likelihood P(alert | fraud) is the same quantity as the posterior P(fraud | alert).
statements.explanation: The two are conditionals in opposite directions and generally differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The prior is the probability computed after the evidence has been included.
statements.explanation: That describes the posterior; a prior comes before the evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The likelihood is P(alert | fraud).
statements.explanation: A likelihood is the probability of the observed evidence given a hypothesis.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The prior is the probability of fraud before the alert is taken into account.
statements.explanation: A prior is the belief held before seeing the evidence.

questions.stem: A vendor calls its fraud tool 98% accurate, meaning it flags 98% of fraudulent transactions and clears 98% of legitimate ones. Fraud is rare in the target market. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 98% of legitimate transactions cleared is the specificity.
statements.explanation: Specificity is P(clear | legitimate).

statements.label: B
statements.text: Precision depends on the prevalence of fraud as well as on sensitivity and specificity.
statements.explanation: A rarer condition gives more false flags relative to true flags, lowering precision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The share of flagged transactions that are truly fraud is the precision, also called positive predictive value.
statements.explanation: Precision is P(fraud | flag).

statements.label: D
statements.text: The vendor's 98% figure is the precision of the tool.
statements.explanation: The 98% describes behaviour given true status, so it is sensitivity and specificity, not precision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 98% of fraudulent transactions flagged is the sensitivity, also called the true positive rate.
statements.explanation: Sensitivity is P(flag | fraud).

questions.stem: An analyst writes in a report: "The test is 99% accurate, so a positive result means a 99% probability of disease." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The quantity the sentence needs is the posterior P(disease | positive), which depends on the prevalence.
statements.explanation: The posterior combines the test's likelihood with the base rate through Bayes' theorem.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Replacing the word accurate with the word calibrated fixes the sentence.
statements.explanation: Calibration is a different property, agreement of stated probabilities with frequencies, and does not repair the confusion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A precise rewrite is: "The test has stated sensitivity and specificity; at this prevalence the positive predictive value is X."
statements.explanation: The rewrite uses the exact terms and states the base rate dependence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The sentence confuses sensitivity and specificity with positive predictive value.
statements.explanation: Accuracy-style figures condition on true status; the claim needs the probability of disease given a positive.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The figure 99% accurate names the posterior probability of disease.
statements.explanation: It names behaviour given true status, which is a different conditional.

questions.stem: An expert testifies: "The chance an innocent person matches this DNA profile is 1 in 100,000, so the chance the defendant is innocent is 1 in 100,000." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The random-match probability and the probability of innocence given a match are equal when the same profile is involved.
statements.explanation: They are different conditionals and are equal only by coincidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The quantity the court needs is P(innocent | match).
statements.explanation: The court conditions on the observed match and asks about innocence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Swapping P(A | B) for P(B | A) is called transposing the conditional, also known as the prosecutor's fallacy.
statements.explanation: The two conditionals are linked only through Bayes' theorem and the prior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The prior probability for the posterior calculation can come from the size of the pool of possible sources.
statements.explanation: A larger pool gives a smaller prior probability that any one person is the source.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The random-match probability is P(match | innocent).
statements.explanation: It conditions on innocence and asks about a match.

questions.stem: A diagnostic test has a positive likelihood ratio computed from its sensitivity and specificity, and a user wants to update a prior to a posterior. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The positive likelihood ratio is sensitivity divided by (1 - specificity).
statements.explanation: It compares P(positive | condition) with P(positive | no condition).

statements.label: B
statements.text: Posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio.
statements.explanation: This is Bayes' theorem on the odds scale.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Sensitivity divided by specificity is the positive likelihood ratio.
statements.explanation: The denominator is the false positive rate, 1 - specificity, not the specificity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Odds of 1 to 3 correspond to a probability of one third.
statements.explanation: Odds of 1 to 3 correspond to a probability of one in four.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Odds and probability are the same scale and take identical values.
statements.explanation: Odds are a ratio of chance to complement, so they differ from probability.

questions.stem: A test is run twice on the same person and both results are positive. An analyst combines the two results. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Conditional independence means the two results are independent in the population without conditioning on true status.
statements.explanation: The two results are usually dependent without conditioning because both depend on the true status.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reversing the order of two positive results changes the final posterior.
statements.explanation: Odds updates multiply, and multiplication is commutative.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If both positives come from the same specimen with the same interference, treating them as independent overstates the evidence.
statements.explanation: Shared error sources break conditional independence, so the second result adds less.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Multiplying likelihood ratios across the two results is valid when they are conditionally independent given true status.
statements.explanation: Conditional independence lets the likelihood of both results factor into a product.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The posterior after the first positive result serves as the prior for the second update.
statements.explanation: Sequential updating treats each posterior as the next prior.

questions.stem: A detector with fixed sensitivity and specificity is moved from a setting where 20% of cases are positive to one where 2% are positive. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A probability score calibrated at the old prevalence stays calibrated after the prior shift.
statements.explanation: Calibration depends on the base rate, so the score is now too high.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sensitivity and specificity stay the same under pure prior shift, since they condition on the true class.
statements.explanation: They are conditionals given class, so a change in class proportions does not move them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Precision of the flags falls, because precision depends on prevalence.
statements.explanation: A lower base rate produces more false flags per true flag.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The fall in precision shows the detector's discrimination between classes has worsened.
statements.explanation: Discrimination is unchanged by assumption; the base rate changed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A change in the prevalence of the target class, with class-conditional behaviour unchanged, is called prior shift (label shift).
statements.explanation: Prior shift alters P(class) but leaves P(input | class) unchanged.

questions.source: Covariate shift, concept drift and label shift
questions.stem: Four situations are described to a model-monitoring assistant, each to be named with the correct term for the type of shift. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The same inputs now lead to different outcomes because behaviour changed: concept drift.
statements.explanation: Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and outcomes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A change in the input distribution with the same input-outcome relationship is called concept drift.
statements.explanation: That is covariate shift; concept drift changes the relationship.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The share of fraud among transactions rises while each class looks the same as before: concept drift.
statements.explanation: A change in class proportions alone is label (prior) shift.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Customers start sending longer messages than in the training data, while the rule linking message to outcome is unchanged: covariate shift.
statements.explanation: Covariate shift changes the distribution of inputs but not the input-outcome relationship.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The share of positive cases falls while class-conditional inputs stay the same: covariate shift.
statements.explanation: That pattern is label shift, a change in the prior, not in the input distribution.

questions.stem: A classifier was found calibrated on data from an earlier year, and the user population has since changed in undocumented ways. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A calibration curve measured earlier remains valid after the population changes, provided the model weights are unchanged.
statements.explanation: Calibration is a property of a model on a population, so it can go stale when the population shifts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Monitoring the distribution of inputs can flag covariate shift without waiting for labels.
statements.explanation: Input drift is visible in features alone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Unchanged overall accuracy implies unchanged calibration.
statements.explanation: Accuracy at a threshold ignores the size of the probability, so calibration can decay unseen.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Monitoring inputs alone is the most direct way to detect calibration decay.
statements.explanation: Calibration compares stated probabilities with realized outcomes, so it needs labels.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Concept drift can occur while the input distribution looks unchanged.
statements.explanation: The relationship between inputs and outcomes can change with the same inputs.

questions.stem: An evaluation team computes a 95% confidence interval for a model's accuracy on each of 100 independent test sets drawn from the same population. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 95% refers to the long-run coverage of the procedure over repeated samples.
statements.explanation: A confidence level describes how often the method captures the true value across repetitions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using much larger test sets would raise the coverage of the intervals above 95%.
statements.explanation: Larger samples narrow the intervals while coverage stays at the nominal level.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Nominal coverage is guaranteed even when the independence assumption behind the interval fails.
statements.explanation: Actual coverage can fall short of nominal when assumptions such as independence do not hold.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A single computed interval has a 95% probability of containing the true accuracy.
statements.explanation: For a fixed computed interval the true value is either inside or outside; the probability statement belongs to the procedure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A very narrow interval shows the test set is representative of the deployment population.
statements.explanation: Width reflects sampling noise, not bias or representativeness.

questions.stem: A team observes 19 correct answers out of 20 test items and computes both a confidence interval and a credible interval for the model's accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 95% confidence interval states a 95% probability that the parameter lies inside it, given the data.
statements.explanation: That reading belongs to a credible interval.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A credible interval depends on the prior, while a confidence interval has no prior.
statements.explanation: The prior enters the posterior, so a different prior can change the credible interval.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A confidence interval is a statement about the coverage of a procedure across repeated samples.
statements.explanation: Its guarantee concerns the method, not one realised interval.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A credible interval is a posterior probability statement about the parameter, given the model and the prior.
statements.explanation: A 95% credible interval holds 95% of the posterior probability.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A credible interval and a confidence interval are the same quantity and agree numerically in small samples.
statements.explanation: They answer different questions and can differ, especially with small samples or informative priors.

questions.source: Confidence interval, prediction interval and standard error
questions.stem: An engineer times 25 requests (mean 100 ms, standard deviation 15 ms) and writes: "The 95% interval is 93.8 to 106.2 ms, so there is a 95% chance the next request falls in that range." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The interval that answers the engineer's question about one new request is a prediction interval, and it is wider.
statements.explanation: A prediction interval adds the variability of a single new observation to the uncertainty about the mean.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The engineer's sentence is correct, because a confidence interval describes the spread of individual observations.
statements.explanation: A confidence interval describes the mean, not individual observations.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The standard error of the mean shrinks as the sample grows, while the spread of individual requests does not.
statements.explanation: Standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n; the standard deviation itself is a property of the data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation of individual requests.
statements.explanation: Standard error describes the sampling distribution of the mean, not the spread of individual values.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The interval 93.8 to 106.2 ms is a confidence interval for the mean response time.
statements.explanation: It expresses uncertainty about the average, built from the standard error.

questions.source: Effective sample size and non-sampling error
questions.stem: A test set of 400 items is in fact 40 distinct items, each reworded ten times, and an analyst computes an accuracy interval as if the 400 items were independent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reworded copies of one item add independent information in the same way as new items.
statements.explanation: Rewordings of the same item are strongly dependent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A confidence interval for accuracy accounts for sampling noise and for bias from an unrepresentative test set alike.
statements.explanation: An interval reflects sampling noise; a biased sample can still give a narrow interval around the wrong value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Leakage of test items into training data is a non-sampling error that a confidence interval captures.
statements.explanation: Leakage biases the estimate and the interval does not reflect it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An interval computed as if the 400 items were independent is too narrow.
statements.explanation: Treating correlated items as independent understates the uncertainty.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Near-duplicate items are correlated, so the effective sample size is smaller than the nominal sample size.
statements.explanation: Correlated observations carry less independent information.

questions.source: Central limit theorem and heavy tails
questions.stem: Independent draws come from a heavy-tailed distribution, and an analyst reports a mean with a standard-error interval. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean.
statements.explanation: That is the definition of standard error.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The standard error formula sigma / sqrt(n) does not apply when the variance is infinite.
statements.explanation: The formula presumes a finite standard deviation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The central limit theorem for the sample mean needs finite variance, among other conditions.
statements.explanation: Without finite variance the usual normal approximation does not hold.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Strong positive correlation among observations makes sigma / sqrt(n) understate the variability of the mean.
statements.explanation: Correlated observations reduce the effective sample size.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For heavy-tailed data the sample mean approaches a normal shape quickly.
statements.explanation: Rare large values can make convergence very slow or absent.

questions.stem: A deployed model's mistakes cost 1 unit in most cases and a very large amount in rare cases. An audit sample contains no rare large mistake, and the report says the average cost has no variation and is therefore precise. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A zero-width interval from a sample with no variation reflects precise knowledge of the mean.
statements.explanation: The zero width comes from the missing rare event, not from precise knowledge.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The median is an adequate summary of the risk from rare large losses.
statements.explanation: The median ignores the tail, which can dominate the mean.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reporting the frequency and size of the largest losses, or high quantiles, alongside the mean is tail-aware reporting.
statements.explanation: Tail-aware reporting makes rare severe outcomes visible.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sample with no rare event shows that rare events are absent from the population.
statements.explanation: Absence in a sample is not absence in the population; the zero-width interval is an artifact.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The mean, or expected value, weights rare large losses by their probability.
statements.explanation: Expected cost includes the tail through probability weighting.

questions.stem: Model P gets 19 of 20 test items right and Model Q gets 940 of 1,000 right. Wilson intervals are computed for each. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An observed accuracy is a point estimate, and the interval expresses its sampling uncertainty.
statements.explanation: A point estimate is a single best guess with no stated uncertainty.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Overlapping intervals mean that the data do not establish that P is more accurate than Q.
statements.explanation: A small gap in point estimates within sampling noise is not a demonstrated difference.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Halving an interval's width needs about double the number of items.
statements.explanation: Width scales with 1 / sqrt(n), so halving it needs about four times as many items.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evaluating both models on the same items and analyzing the differences is a paired comparison.
statements.explanation: Pairing removes item-to-item variation from the comparison.

statements.label: E
statements.text: P's interval is wider than Q's because interval width scales roughly with one over the square root of n.
statements.explanation: Fewer items give a larger standard error.

questions.stem: A team compares two models by the difference in their accuracy and reports both a confidence interval for the difference and a p-value. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis.
statements.explanation: That is the definition of a p-value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A posterior probability of a hypothesis requires a prior.
statements.explanation: Bayes' theorem needs a prior to turn a likelihood into a posterior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A small p-value is the same thing as a large effect size.
statements.explanation: A p-value reflects evidence against the null and depends on sample size, so it is not an effect size.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 95% confidence interval for the difference that excludes zero corresponds to rejecting no difference in a two-sided test at the 5% level.
statements.explanation: Two-sided tests and confidence intervals are dual.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data.
statements.explanation: A p-value conditions on the null; the probability of a hypothesis given the data is a posterior.

questions.stem: A reviewer says that accuracy, discrimination and calibration are three ways to say that a probabilistic classifier is good. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A model that predicts the base rate for each case is calibrated in aggregate but has no discrimination.
statements.explanation: A constant forecast matches overall frequency and ranks nothing, so AUC is 0.5.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Calibration and discrimination are two names for the same property.
statements.explanation: A model can be calibrated without ranking cases or can rank perfectly with miscalibrated scores.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Accuracy at a threshold ignores the size of the predicted probability.
statements.explanation: Only the side of the threshold matters, not how far from it a probability lies.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calibration is agreement between stated probabilities and observed frequencies.
statements.explanation: Among cases given probability p, about a fraction p should be positive.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Discrimination is the ability to rank positives above negatives, as summarized by AUC.
statements.explanation: A discriminating model gives higher scores to positives than to negatives.

questions.source: Calibration without discrimination and the reverse
questions.stem: At 10% prevalence, model M1 outputs 0.10 for every patient, while model M2 ranks patients perfectly but outputs scores between 0.60 and 1.00. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For deciding which patients to examine first, calibration is the relevant property and discrimination is not.
statements.explanation: Prioritizing needs a ranking, which is discrimination.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A strictly increasing recalibration map leaves M2's AUC unchanged.
statements.explanation: Such a map preserves the order of scores.

statements.label: C
statements.text: M1 has no discrimination, since its scores give no way to rank patients.
statements.explanation: A constant score gives AUC 0.5.

statements.label: D
statements.text: M2 has excellent discrimination and poor calibration.
statements.explanation: Perfect ranking is compatible with scores far above the actual frequency.

statements.label: E
statements.text: M2's high AUC means its scores can be read as probabilities of disease.
statements.explanation: AUC measures ranking, not agreement of scores with frequencies.

questions.stem: A data scientist reports an AUC for a classifier and describes how it is defined. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive case scores higher than a randomly chosen negative case, with ties counted as half.
statements.explanation: That is the ranking interpretation of AUC.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Applying a strictly increasing transformation to the scores leaves the AUC unchanged.
statements.explanation: AUC depends only on the order of scores.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The expected AUC does not depend on the class proportions in the sample.
statements.explanation: It compares the positive and negative score distributions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: AUC measures calibration of the predicted probabilities.
statements.explanation: AUC measures discrimination, not calibration.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An AUC of 0.875 means 87.5% accuracy at a 0.5 cutoff.
statements.explanation: AUC is a ranking measure and accuracy at a cutoff is a separate quantity.

questions.source: Brier score, log loss and accuracy compared
questions.stem: Two forecasters each assign a fixed probability to 10 events, 8 of which occur. Forecaster P says 0.8 for each event and forecaster Q says 0.99 for each event. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The Brier score is the mean squared difference between the forecast probability and the outcome.
statements.explanation: It is a mean squared probability error.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The Brier score is an error rate at a cutoff.
statements.explanation: It averages squared probability error and does not use a cutoff.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Forecaster Q is better, because it states higher confidence.
statements.explanation: Q is overconfident; proper scores favour P, whose probabilities match the frequency.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Log loss caps the penalty for a confident miss at 1.
statements.explanation: Log loss is unbounded as the probability given to the true outcome approaches 0.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two forecasters have the same accuracy at a 0.5 cutoff.
statements.explanation: Both are on the correct side of 0.5 for the same events.

questions.source: Proper and strictly proper scoring rules
questions.stem: A statistician discusses scoring rules that reward honest probability reports. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accuracy at a cutoff is strictly proper.
statements.explanation: Any report on the correct side of the cutoff earns the same expected score.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Brier score and log loss are strictly proper.
statements.explanation: Each is uniquely optimized by reporting the true probability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A proper scoring rule has its expected score optimized by reporting one's true belief.
statements.explanation: That is the definition of properness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Absolute error is proper because it penalizes the distance from the outcome.
statements.explanation: Its expected value is minimized by reporting 0 or 1, so it rewards exaggeration.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A strictly proper rule is one in which many different reports earn the same expected score.
statements.explanation: Strict properness means the true belief is the unique optimum.

questions.source: Brier skill score and reference forecast
questions.stem: A model's Brier score is compared with that of a reference forecaster who predicts the base rate for every case. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reference forecaster has a Brier score of 0 because it is calibrated.
statements.explanation: Calibration without discrimination still leaves a positive Brier score.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Brier scores from test sets with different base rates are directly comparable without a reference.
statements.explanation: The score of a trivial forecast depends on the base rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reference forecast is calibrated in aggregate and has no discrimination.
statements.explanation: A constant base-rate forecast matches overall frequency but ranks nothing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A forecast of the base rate for each case is a climatological reference.
statements.explanation: Such a constant forecast is the standard no-skill baseline.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A Brier skill score measures improvement relative to a reference forecast.
statements.explanation: It is 1 minus the ratio of the model's score to the reference score.

questions.stem: A classifier's probabilities are scored with log loss, defined as the mean negative natural logarithm of the probability given to the true class. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Log loss is unbounded above, while the Brier score for a binary outcome is bounded by 1.
statements.explanation: The log penalty grows without limit as the probability given to the true class nears 0.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Log loss is computed from the labels alone and ignores the predicted probabilities.
statements.explanation: It is computed from the probability assigned to the true class.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A confident miss costs more under the Brier score than under log loss.
statements.explanation: Log loss punishes a confident miss more heavily because it has no upper bound.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A forecast of exactly 0 for a case that turns out positive gives a large but finite penalty.
statements.explanation: The negative log of zero is infinite, which is why implementations clip probabilities.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Log loss averages the squared difference between forecast and outcome.
statements.explanation: That describes the Brier score.

questions.stem: A reliability diagram shows four bins as pairs (mean predicted probability, observed fraction of positives): (0.15, 0.22), (0.45, 0.47), (0.75, 0.62), (0.95, 0.80). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reliability diagram plots observed frequency against mean predicted probability by bin.
statements.explanation: A calibrated model lies near the diagonal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A point above the diagonal at low predicted probability shows the model understates risk in that bin.
statements.explanation: Events occur more often than predicted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A curve that rises with predicted probability establishes that the model is calibrated.
statements.explanation: A rising curve shows sensible ranking; calibration needs points near the diagonal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Points below the diagonal at high predicted probability indicate overconfidence.
statements.explanation: Stated probabilities exceed observed frequencies there.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Small bins give noisy observed frequencies, so bin counts or intervals belong alongside the points.
statements.explanation: Sampling noise grows as the number of cases per bin falls.

questions.stem: An evaluation reports a single expected calibration error (ECE) for a classifier, with predictions grouped into bins. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: ECE is the misclassification rate at a 0.5 cutoff.
statements.explanation: ECE measures probability gaps, not classification errors.

statements.label: B
statements.text: ECE is the count-weighted mean absolute gap between mean predicted probability and observed frequency across bins.
statements.explanation: Weighting by bin count makes ECE an average over cases.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A perfectly calibrated model has a measured ECE of zero on a finite test set.
statements.explanation: Sampling noise gives a positive expected ECE even for a perfectly calibrated model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Maximum calibration error is the count-weighted average of the bin gaps.
statements.explanation: Maximum calibration error is the largest gap among the bins, not a weighted average.

statements.label: E
statements.text: ECE does not depend on the number and placement of bins.
statements.explanation: Different binning schemes give different ECE values.

questions.stem: A classifier reports confidence 0.90 for every held-out case. Group X is 80% correct and group Y is 100% correct, in equal numbers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pooled calibration implies each group is calibrated.
statements.explanation: The pooled average can be correct while each group is miscalibrated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A pooled calibration check suffices to show each group is calibrated.
statements.explanation: Calibration should be checked within subgroups because offsetting errors hide in the aggregate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A single global rescaling fitted on the pooled data would find nothing to correct.
statements.explanation: The pooled point already lies on the diagonal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Overconfidence means stated confidence is below observed accuracy.
statements.explanation: Overconfidence is stated confidence above observed accuracy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Pooled calibration at 0.90 coexists with overconfidence for group X and underconfidence for group Y.
statements.explanation: Opposite gaps average out in the pool.

questions.stem: A team applies temperature scaling to a classifier that outputs sigma(z) from a logit z. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Temperature scaling changes the ordering of cases, so the AUC changes.
statements.explanation: Dividing by a positive T preserves order and AUC.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Temperature scaling is a regularizer applied during training.
statements.explanation: It is fitted after training on held-out data, as a recalibration step.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Temperature scaling repairs a classifier whose ranking is poor.
statements.explanation: It rescales confidence without changing the ranking.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Temperature scaling divides the logit by a single parameter T fitted on held-out data.
statements.explanation: It is a one-parameter post-hoc recalibration.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A T greater than 1 softens the probabilities toward 0.5.
statements.explanation: Dividing the logit by a larger number moves the sigmoid output toward one half.

questions.stem: A language model answers factual questions and appends "Confidence: 95%" to each answer, and a team wants to treat the number as a probability of being correct. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Higher stated confidence tracking higher accuracy is discrimination, even when the stated levels are too high.
statements.explanation: Ranking information can remain when the levels are off.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Stated confidence is calibrated if, among answers stated at 95%, about 95% are correct.
statements.explanation: Calibration compares stated values with observed frequency.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A precise stated figure shows the model computed that probability internally.
statements.explanation: Precision of display is not evidence of how the number was produced.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Verbalized confidence is a number written in the model's text and is not necessarily an internally computed probability.
statements.explanation: Fluent stated figures need not reflect a calculated probability.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Verbalized confidences are too unreliable to be recalibrated with labeled data.
statements.explanation: A recalibration map can be fitted on held-out labeled answers.

questions.stem: A clinic can follow up a flagged patient at a small cost, while a missed positive case is much more costly, and the model gives calibrated probabilities. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 0.5 cutoff minimizes expected cost because it minimizes the number of errors.
statements.explanation: Minimizing error count treats both mistakes as equally costly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A cost-derived threshold stays valid when the probabilities are miscalibrated.
statements.explanation: The threshold assumes stated probabilities equal true frequencies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the cost of a missed case falls, the cost-minimizing threshold rises.
statements.explanation: A smaller miss cost justifies following up only more probable cases.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A threshold chosen from costs treats a false negative and a false positive as equally costly.
statements.explanation: It is chosen precisely because the two errors have different costs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With calibrated probabilities the cost-minimizing decision threshold comes from the costs of the two error types, not from 0.5.
statements.explanation: Following up pays when the probability of a positive times the miss cost exceeds the follow-up cost.

questions.stem: A team checks whether the confidence scores of a deployed classifier can be read as probabilities and plans a fitting and evaluation procedure. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A calibration check done once stays valid as the population changes.
statements.explanation: Calibration can drift, so it is rechecked over time.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A held-out set is data that were used to fit the model.
statements.explanation: A held-out set is data kept out of fitting.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Calibration is a property of a model on a population, so it is measured on data resembling the deployment population.
statements.explanation: Scores calibrated on one population can be miscalibrated on another.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A recalibration map judged on the same data used to fit it gives an honest estimate of calibration.
statements.explanation: A held-out set is needed because the fit data flatter the map.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The Brier score depends on the choice of bins.
statements.explanation: The Brier score is computed per case and does not use bins.

questions.source: False precision and the meaning of a probability
questions.stem: A loan dashboard shows each decision with a score such as "87.3% likely to repay". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number of displayed decimal places is a formatting choice and is not evidence of accuracy.
statements.explanation: Digits shown say nothing about validity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The meaning of a score as a probability comes from the model's architecture rather than from observed outcomes.
