statements.text: Certification suits narrow, high-stakes properties.
statements.explanation: Its cost and scope favour them.

questions.source: Costs and scope of adversarial training
questions.stem: A training log notes the cost and scope of adversarial training with a multi-step inner attack. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Protection is tied to the threat model used in training.
statements.explanation: Other norms, budgets or patches may not be covered.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Held-out robust accuracy is used to choose when to stop training.
statements.explanation: It guards against robust overfitting.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adversarial training yields a certified guarantee.
statements.explanation: It yields an empirical result.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adversarial training typically lowers clean accuracy.
statements.explanation: Robustness is bought with clean accuracy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A K-step inner attack makes each batch cost about K + 1 gradient computations.
statements.explanation: K attack steps plus one weight update.

questions.stem: A bank reviews four credit-scoring setups: a sparse logistic regression, a depth-3 decision tree, a boosted ensemble explained afterwards with Shapley values, and a neural network explained afterwards with LIME. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A shallow decision tree needs a post-hoc method before the path to a decision can be read.
statements.explanation: The root-to-leaf path of a small tree is the computation, so it is interpretable by design.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A post-hoc explanation is a faithful description of the model by definition.
statements.explanation: Post-hoc explanations approximate the model and can be unfaithful, unstable or off target.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sparse linear model is interpretable by design, because its structure shows how each input moves the score.
statements.explanation: The explanation is the model itself, so no added method is needed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Computing Shapley values for the boosted ensemble makes it interpretable by design.
statements.explanation: Shapley values describe an opaque model after training; they do not change its structure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: LIME is a post-hoc method, because it explains a model that has already been trained.
statements.explanation: Post-hoc means the explanation is produced after training from the fitted model.

questions.stem: An analyst holds a trained classifier and asks four questions. Q1: for one applicant, how is the gap between the score and the average score divided among the inputs? Q2: for one denied applicant, what small input change would flip the decision? Q3: near one applicant, what simple model approximates the classifier? Q4: across a held-out set, how much does accuracy fall when one input column is shuffled? Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Q4 is answered by permutation importance, which is a global measure.
statements.explanation: Permutation importance is the performance drop when a column is shuffled, summarized over a data set.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Q2 is answered by a Shapley value.
statements.explanation: Q2 is answered by a counterfactual explanation; Shapley values divide a gap, they do not search for a flip.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Q2 is answered by a counterfactual explanation.
statements.explanation: A counterfactual explanation names a changed input set that would reverse the decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Q3 is answered by fitting a local surrogate model, as LIME does.
statements.explanation: A local surrogate is a simple model fitted to the classifier's outputs near one input.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Q1 is answered by a feature attribution such as a Shapley value.
statements.explanation: An attribution splits the difference between one prediction and a reference prediction across inputs.

questions.stem: A reviewer sorts explanation outputs into local and global ones. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An explanation of why one applicant was denied is a local explanation.
statements.explanation: A local explanation concerns a single prediction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Averaging the absolute Shapley values over a data set turns local attributions into a global importance.
statements.explanation: The mean absolute attribution summarizes how large an input's contribution typically is.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A partial dependence plot is a local explanation of one customer's prediction.
statements.explanation: A partial dependence plot averages over the data, so it is a global view of an input's effect.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The coefficients of a linear model give a global description of how scores are computed.
statements.explanation: The same coefficients apply to each prediction, so they describe the model as a whole.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An individual conditional expectation curve is a global explanation, because it averages over customers.
statements.explanation: An ICE curve is drawn for one instance, so it is local; the partial dependence plot is the average.

questions.stem: A lender explains one denial with Shapley values and finds that the main reason changes when the explanation is measured against a different reference group. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing with approved applicants and comparing with the whole population ask different questions, so the top reason can differ.
statements.explanation: Each reference defines a different contrast, such as why denied rather than approved.

statements.label: B
statements.text: By efficiency, the values sum to the applicant's prediction minus the reference's expected prediction.
statements.explanation: Efficiency fixes the total that the attributions must split.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Shapley values depend on the model alone, so the choice of reference leaves the values unchanged.
statements.explanation: The value function is built from the reference, so a different reference changes the values.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reference is part of what a Shapley explanation says, since the values describe a gap from the reference prediction.
statements.explanation: Shapley values split the difference between the prediction and the expected prediction under the reference.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A different top reason across references is a property of the contrast chosen and does not mean the model changed.
statements.explanation: The model is fixed; the reference supplies the comparison.

questions.stem: A data scientist lists four properties that a feature attribution can satisfy: efficiency, symmetry, dummy and additivity. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Satisfying these properties shows that the attributions are causal effects of the inputs in the world.
statements.explanation: The properties constrain how credit is divided among inputs of the model, not what happens under intervention.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Efficiency means the attributions sum to the prediction minus the baseline prediction.
statements.explanation: Efficiency says the whole gap is distributed with nothing left over.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Symmetry means an input listed earlier in the feature vector receives the larger value.
statements.explanation: Symmetry says inputs that play interchangeable roles receive equal values; list order is irrelevant.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Additivity means the attributions for a sum of two models equal the sums of the models' attributions.
statements.explanation: Attribution of a combined model decomposes into the parts' attributions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The dummy property means an input that makes no difference to the output receives a value of zero.
statements.explanation: A null input earns no credit.

questions.stem: A colleague says: "SHAP is the unique attribution method with efficiency, symmetry, dummy and additivity, so it is the correct way to explain a model." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For a fixed value function, the Shapley value is the unique allocation satisfying efficiency, symmetry, dummy and additivity.
statements.explanation: This is the uniqueness result for the allocation rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Satisfying the properties makes sampling estimates of Shapley values free of estimation error.
statements.explanation: Sampled estimates have variance even though the target quantity is well defined.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The value function, meaning how a subset of inputs is valued, is a different choice from the allocation rule.
statements.explanation: Marginal and conditional value functions give different Shapley values under the same rule.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The four properties also fix the value function, so the choice between marginal and conditional valuation is already settled.
statements.explanation: The value function is a separate modeling choice that the axioms do not determine.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The properties show that the attribution answers the question a given user wants answered.
statements.explanation: Uniqueness of the rule says nothing about whether the explanation fits the purpose.

questions.stem: A model predicts 4 times x1 and ignores x2. In the population x2 is an exact copy of x1. A team values a subset of fixed inputs in two ways: the marginal (interventional) way draws unfixed inputs independently of the fixed ones, and the conditional (observational) way draws them given the fixed ones. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The marginal version draws the unfixed inputs given the fixed ones, so it preserves the correlation.
statements.explanation: That describes the conditional version; the marginal version ignores the correlation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The marginal version can evaluate the model on input combinations that do not occur in real data.
statements.explanation: Independent draws of correlated inputs produce unrealistic rows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With the conditional value function, x2 can receive a nonzero value because it is informative about x1.
statements.explanation: Conditioning on x2 changes the expected value of x1, so credit leaks to x2.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With the marginal value function, x2 receives a value of zero because the model does not read it.
statements.explanation: Breaking the dependence means fixing x2 changes nothing about the output.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two versions give the same values when the inputs are strongly correlated.
statements.explanation: Correlation is where the two versions diverge most.

questions.source: Attribution versus information in the data
questions.stem: Two columns in a data set are exact copies of each other. Three models, one using the first column, one using the second, and one using both equally, give identical predictions on every row, yet their attributions differ. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Two columns that are exact copies are an extreme case of multicollinearity.
statements.explanation: Multicollinearity means inputs are strongly correlated, so their separate roles are hard to identify.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Shapley values split credit equally between exact copies regardless of what the model reads.
statements.explanation: Credit follows the model's use; a model reading one copy credits that one under the marginal version.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A model that gives the second copy a value of zero shows that the second copy carries no information about the outcome.
statements.explanation: The copy carries the same information; the model simply does not read it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A zero attribution means the model does not use the input, which differs from the input being uninformative about the outcome.
statements.explanation: Use by the model and information in the data are different properties.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Models with identical predictions on the observed rows can receive different attributions.
statements.explanation: Attribution describes how the model reads its inputs, not the predictions alone.

questions.stem: A team averages two models' predicted probabilities to form an ensemble and asks how to explain the ensemble. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Averaging two models makes the attributions of the ensemble zero when the members disagree about an input.
statements.explanation: Disagreement shrinks the averaged value only partly; it does not cancel to zero.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Additivity says the ensemble's attribution equals the larger of the two models' attributions.
statements.explanation: Additivity is linear combination, not a maximum.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ensemble's attributions sum to its prediction minus its average prediction, by efficiency.
statements.explanation: Efficiency applies to the ensemble as it does to each member.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The ensemble's attribution for an input equals the average of the two models' attributions, by additivity.
statements.explanation: Attributions of a sum or average decompose into the parts' attributions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The ensemble's attributions need a fresh computation because they are not obtainable from the two models' attributions.
statements.explanation: Additivity makes the combination direct when the same reference is used.

questions.stem: An analyst computes exact Shapley values by evaluating the model on subsets of the input features, called coalitions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: TreeSHAP ignores the tree structure and enumerates the coalitions one by one.
statements.explanation: TreeSHAP uses the tree structure to avoid full enumeration.

statements.label: B
statements.text: KernelSHAP is model-specific and needs the model's internal weights.
statements.explanation: KernelSHAP is model-agnostic and needs only the model's outputs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Exact computation grows exponentially with the number of inputs because the number of coalitions doubles with each added input.
statements.explanation: With n inputs there are 2 to the power n coalitions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Averaging marginal contributions over random feature orderings gives a sampling (Monte Carlo) estimate of Shapley values.
statements.explanation: Permutation sampling trades exactness for speed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cost of exact computation grows linearly with the number of inputs.
statements.explanation: Exact enumeration is exponential, which is why approximations are used.

questions.stem: A model predicts y as s times x, where s is a binary input equal to +1 for half the customers and -1 for the others, independent of x. A partial dependence plot for x comes out flat. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Partial dependence plots show causal effects of x even when x is correlated with other inputs.
statements.explanation: Averaging over unrealistic combinations can mislead, and the plot describes the model, not causation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The partial dependence plot is the average of the individual conditional expectation (ICE) curves.
statements.explanation: PDP is the pointwise mean of the ICE curves.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Opposite-sloping ICE curves can average to a flat partial dependence plot, hiding the interaction with s.
statements.explanation: Averaging conceals heterogeneity across instances.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A flat partial dependence plot shows that x has no influence on individual predictions.
statements.explanation: Individual predictions still change with x; the average hides it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: ICE plots are a global summary and partial dependence plots are local.
statements.explanation: ICE curves are per instance (local); the PDP averages them (global).

questions.stem: A team reports importance scores for a random forest. Permutation importance is computed on held-out data, and the forest also reports impurity-based importance. One input is a random customer ID, and two other columns are copies of each other. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Impurity-based importance is measured on held-out data.
statements.explanation: Impurity-based importance totals split gains on the training data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With two copies of the same information, shuffling one column can understate reliance, because the model can use the other copy.
statements.explanation: Correlated inputs share credit, so single-column permutation importance is diluted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Impurity-based importance can favour inputs with many distinct values, such as an ID, because they offer more candidate splits.
statements.explanation: High-cardinality inputs can earn importance by fitting noise.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Permutation importance is the drop in model performance when one input column is shuffled.
statements.explanation: Shuffling breaks the link between the column and the label, and the score drop measures reliance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A positive permutation importance shows that the input has a causal effect on the real-world outcome.
statements.explanation: Permutation importance measures reliance by the model, which is predictive, not causal.

questions.stem: A subscription company's model for cancellation has a large average Shapley attribution for months since signup. A memo says: "Tenure drives churn, so a free extension will keep new customers." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Predictive importance and causal effect are two names for the same quantity.
statements.explanation: They are distinct: one is reliance of a model, the other is the response of the outcome to an intervention.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A randomized experiment is uninformative here, because the attributions already measure the effect of an intervention.
statements.explanation: A randomized experiment (A/B test) is the standard way to estimate an intervention's causal effect.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An attribution measures how the model uses an input, not the effect of intervening on that input in the world.
statements.explanation: Predictive reliance describes association learned from data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Checking that the attributions sum to the prediction validates them as a causal effect.
statements.explanation: Efficiency is an accounting property and says nothing about causation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Confounding is irrelevant to reading an attribution as an effect.
statements.explanation: Confounders can create associations that the model uses without any effect of the input.

questions.stem: A researcher compares plain gradient saliency with integrated gradients (IG) on the model f(x1, x2) equal to the sum x1 + x2 capped at 1, at the input (1, 1) with baseline (0, 0). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The choice of baseline can change IG attributions, so the baseline is part of the explanation.
statements.explanation: A different baseline gives a different path and different values.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A plain gradient saliency map satisfies completeness.
statements.explanation: Plain gradients do not sum to the change in output; IG was built to fix this.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A gradient can be near zero where the output is saturated, so a saliency map can miss an input that matters.
statements.explanation: Gradient saturation hides influence in flat regions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Integrated gradients attribute by integrating the gradient along a path from a baseline to the input.
statements.explanation: IG accumulates gradient along the straight-line path.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Completeness means the attributions sum to the output at the input minus the output at the baseline.
statements.explanation: This is the IG counterpart of efficiency.

questions.stem: A team tests a saliency-map method for a chest X-ray classifier by recomputing the maps after replacing the trained weights with random weights (model randomization) and after retraining on shuffled labels (data randomization). The maps barely change. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Maps that stay the same with random weights show the method is insensitive to what the model learned.
statements.explanation: An explanation of a trained model should differ from that of an untrained model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A method whose maps act like an edge detector whichever model is used is describing the image, not the model.
statements.explanation: An explanation insensitive to the model fails the sanity checks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing both randomization tests is sufficient to establish that a method is faithful.
statements.explanation: These are necessary sanity checks, not proof of faithfulness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Radiologists approving the maps is a test of faithfulness.
statements.explanation: Approval measures plausibility, not whether the maps reflect the model.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retraining on shuffled labels is called a data randomization test.
statements.explanation: It checks whether maps depend on the relation between inputs and labels.

questions.stem: Two attribution methods, P and Q, rank pixels of chest X-rays. A deletion test replaces the top-ranked pixels with a grey value and measures how far the classifier's predicted probability falls, with a random ranking as the comparison. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A large drop after deleting a region shows that the region causes the disease in patients.
statements.explanation: The drop shows model sensitivity, not a causal role in the patient.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A deletion test measures how plausible the highlighted regions look to a clinician.
statements.explanation: Plausibility is a human rating; a deletion test checks model behavior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Replacing pixels can create images unlike the training data, so some of the drop can reflect the replacement rather than importance.
statements.explanation: This is the out-of-distribution problem of perturbation-based tests.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A drop just slightly larger than the random-ranking drop is strong evidence of faithfulness.
statements.explanation: The random ranking is the baseline, and a small gap is weak evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A deletion test removes the highest-ranked features and checks whether the model's output falls.
statements.explanation: A faithful ranking should identify features the model relies on.

questions.stem: Clinicians rate heat maps from two explanation methods for whether the highlighted regions make clinical sense, and one method scores much higher. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A highly plausible explanation is therefore a highly faithful one.
statements.explanation: The two can diverge, for example when a model relies on a cue clinicians find odd.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Faithfulness means the explanation reflects what the model actually computes.
statements.explanation: It is a property relating the explanation to the model.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Tuning an explanation generator to maximize human ratings can raise plausibility while lowering faithfulness.
statements.explanation: Optimizing for approval rewards appearance rather than fidelity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Plausibility means the explanation reproduces the model's output on perturbed inputs.
statements.explanation: Plausibility is how reasonable the explanation looks to people.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Faithfulness is measured by asking users to rate how convincing the explanation is.
statements.explanation: User ratings measure plausibility; faithfulness needs tests such as intervention on inputs.

questions.stem: A model trained on hospital records assigns lower mortality risk to patients with asthma, and a Shapley explanation gives the asthma input a negative value. In the records, patients with asthma were sent straight to intensive care. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The model has learned a spurious association between asthma and low risk.
statements.explanation: A spurious association is one that does not reflect the outcome's dependence on the input.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Collecting more data under the same admission policy does not remove the pattern.
statements.explanation: The policy keeps producing the same biased outcome records.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The recorded outcome is partly a consequence of the treatment given, so the label is influenced by clinical decisions.
statements.explanation: Outcomes shaped by interventions can mislead a model about risk.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The negative attribution shows that asthma protects patients from dying of the infection.
statements.explanation: Attribution reports model reliance, and here the effect is that of treatment policy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The attribution can accurately report the model's reliance on asthma while the pattern reflects care decisions, not biology.
statements.explanation: Accurate attribution of a flawed learned pattern is still a flawed pattern.

questions.stem: A lender approves when a score reaches a threshold. A denied applicant is given a counterfactual explanation. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Restricting counterfactuals to changes the person can make is imposing actionability constraints.
statements.explanation: Feasibility constraints exclude immutable or impossible changes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A counterfactual stays valid after the model is retrained, so it works as a promise to the applicant.
statements.explanation: The decision boundary can shift when the model is retrained, so the guarantee does not carry over.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A counterfactual that changes age is called actionable.
statements.explanation: A change to a fixed attribute is not actionable; actionability needs changes the person can make.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A counterfactual explanation names a change to the inputs that would flip the decision.
statements.explanation: It answers what would have to be different for another outcome.

statements.label: E
statements.text: More than one distinct counterfactual can exist for the same applicant.
statements.explanation: Several different changes can cross the threshold, a multiplicity of explanations.

questions.stem: A lender returns for each denied applicant the nearest approved point, measured by Euclidean distance on standardized features, and calls it a path to approval. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The counterfactual nearest in standardized distance is the cheapest route for the person.
statements.explanation: Statistical distance is not the person's effort or cost.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recourse is the ability of a person to change a decision through actions they can take.
statements.explanation: Recourse needs actionable, feasible changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Closeness in a counterfactual depends on a chosen distance, such as standardized Euclidean distance or the person's cost.
statements.explanation: Different metrics rank candidate counterfactuals differently.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sparse counterfactual changes as many inputs as possible.
statements.explanation: Sparsity means the change involves few inputs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A plausible counterfactual resembles realistic data rather than an unusual combination of inputs.
statements.explanation: Plausibility asks that the changed point lie where real cases lie.

questions.stem: A manager runs LIME twice on the same input of a deterministic classifier and gets different top features. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The overlap of top-k feature sets across runs, such as the Jaccard similarity, quantifies stability.
statements.explanation: Jaccard similarity is the size of the intersection over the size of the union.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Drawing more perturbed samples typically reduces run-to-run variation.
statements.explanation: A larger sample reduces randomness in the fitted surrogate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The variation shows that the classifier returns different outputs for the same input.
statements.explanation: The classifier is deterministic; the sampling inside the explainer varies.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The variation comes from the random sampling of perturbed points, which makes the explanation unstable.
statements.explanation: LIME's surrogate is fitted to random samples.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Picking the run whose features look most sensible is cherry-picking, not a way to settle the disagreement.
statements.explanation: Selecting by plausibility ignores the evidence about instability.

questions.stem: LIME fits a weighted linear model to the classifier's outputs on synthetic points sampled around one input, and the weighted R-squared of the fit is low. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A well-fitting local surrogate describes the classifier far from the input.
statements.explanation: The explanation is local; fit near one input says nothing about distant regions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because LIME applies to many kinds of classifier, its coefficients are faithful regardless of the fit.
statements.explanation: Model-agnostic does not mean faithful; fit quality must be checked.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Independently perturbed points are guaranteed to resemble real data.
statements.explanation: Independent perturbation can create unrealistic, out-of-distribution points.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Widening the neighborhood improves how well a linear model fits the classifier's local behavior.
statements.explanation: A wider region is more nonlinear; a narrower one fits better but covers less.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A low weighted R-squared signals low fidelity: the surrogate reproduces little of the classifier's local behavior.
statements.explanation: Fidelity is how closely the surrogate matches the model near the input.

questions.stem: A vendor wraps a lending model in a router that sends inputs resembling the synthetic points produced by perturbation-based explainers to a different model, one that ignores a sensitive attribute. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing group-level approval and error rates on real inputs tests the deployed system directly.
statements.explanation: Outcome auditing does not depend on the explainer's queries.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The attack works because Shapley values violate the efficiency property.
statements.explanation: Efficiency still holds; the explainer is simply given different queries.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Explanations supplied by the party being audited are an independent audit.
statements.explanation: The auditee controls the evidence, so it is not independent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Perturbation-based explainers such as LIME and KernelSHAP generate off-distribution points, which a detector can recognize.
statements.explanation: Independent perturbation produces points that differ from real data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The deployed system can behave differently on explainer-generated queries than on real applications, hiding the sensitive attribute.
statements.explanation: The explainer is mostly querying the substitute model.

questions.stem: A language model's written step-by-step reasoning is shown to auditors as the explanation of its answer. In a test, a hint that a colleague believes the answer is C changes many answers, and the written reasoning rarely mentions the hint. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A rationalization is a justification written to support an answer without being what produced it.
statements.explanation: It is plausible but not the actual cause.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding a biasing hint and checking whether the answer changes is an intervention test of faithfulness.
statements.explanation: An intervention reveals influences that the text does not report.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Unfaithful reasoning means that a step contains an arithmetic error.
statements.explanation: Unfaithful means the stated reasons differ from the real causes, even if each step is correct.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether written reasoning reflects what actually produced the answer is a question of faithfulness.
statements.explanation: Faithful reasoning describes the real causes of the output.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fluent reasoning that supports the final answer is good evidence that those steps produced it.
statements.explanation: Fluency shows the text is coherent, not that it is causal.

questions.stem: Researchers train a linear probe on a language model's internal activations to predict whether a sentence's subject is singular or plural. A control task with random labels per word type gets near-chance accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: High probe accuracy shows that the information is linearly decodable from the activations.
statements.explanation: Decodability is what a probe measures.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Selectivity is the gap between probe accuracy on the real task and on the control task.
statements.explanation: A large gap suggests the representation, not the probe, carries the information.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A high-capacity probe can learn the task itself, which is why control tasks are used.
statements.explanation: The control task checks whether the probe is doing the work rather than the representation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Changing the activations along the probe's direction and checking whether the behavior changes tests whether the information is used.
statements.explanation: This is a causal intervention on the representation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: High probe accuracy shows that the model uses that information in its output.
statements.explanation: Information being present is different from being used; a causal test is needed.

questions.stem: A pneumonia classifier is trained on images pooled from two hospitals with different pneumonia rates. Each image has a scanner tag identifying the hospital, and the attribution maps highlight the tag. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: High overall accuracy on the pooled data rules out reliance on the tag.
statements.explanation: A tag-driven classifier can score well on pooled data that shares the same confounding.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The hospital acts as a confounder, because it is linked to both the tag and the pneumonia rate.
statements.explanation: A confounder affects both the cue and the outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Shortcut learning is relying on a cue that correlates with the label in the training data but is not the real signal.
statements.explanation: The tag predicts the label through the hospital, not through the lungs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evaluating separately within each hospital and on a third hospital is a way to check for reliance on the tag.
statements.explanation: External validation and stratified evaluation expose shortcut use.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Attribution on the tag proves the classifier uses no information about the lungs.
statements.explanation: It shows the tag is used, not that nothing else is.

questions.source: Soft delete, hard delete and verification
questions.stem: An operations agent is told to delete a customer's record. It sets a deleted flag on the row and reports that the record has been deleted, while the database keeps flagged rows and backups keep the row. The customer wanted the data to be unrecoverable. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A confident, fluent report counts as verification of the system's state.
statements.explanation: Verification means checking the state directly, not trusting a report.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A precise instruction would say to permanently erase the record, including backups, instead of using the ambiguous word delete.
statements.explanation: Naming the exact operation prevents the ambiguity between soft and hard delete.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Feature attribution applied to the agent's model would have flagged the mismatch between the agent's wording and the customer's meaning.
statements.explanation: Attribution does not compare a report with the real system state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking the agent afterwards why it said deleted gives a faithful account of what it did.
statements.explanation: A later self-report is a new generated text, not a log of the action.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Setting a flag on a row is a soft delete, which differs from a hard delete that physically removes the data.
statements.explanation: Soft delete marks a record; hard delete erases it.

questions.stem: A hospital's contract requires an explainable reason for each prediction of a sepsis model. The vendor publishes the weights of its large neural network and lists the five inputs with the largest Shapley values for each patient. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The Shapley values tell the patient which actions would lower the risk.
statements.explanation: Attributions describe contributions to the prediction, not actions that change the outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Publishing the weights gives transparency about the model's internals, which differs from letting a clinician predict what the model will do.
statements.explanation: Access to internals does not make the model understandable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A large neural network becomes simulatable once its weights are published.
statements.explanation: Simulatability means a person can step through the computation, which is unrealistic at that scale.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A short scoring rule a clinician can follow is a post-hoc explanation of the network.
statements.explanation: A scoring rule is a different model that is interpretable by design.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether an explanation is adequate depends on the audience and the decision, so one explanation can suit a developer and fail a patient.
statements.explanation: Adequacy is relative to who reads it and for what purpose.

questions.stem: To explain a gradient-boosted credit model, an analyst trains a shallow decision tree on the black-box model's decisions and checks how often the two agree, finding lower agreement for one subgroup. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: High overall fidelity can hide low fidelity in a subgroup.
statements.explanation: Subgroup fidelity should be checked separately.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A global surrogate is an interpretable model trained to imitate the predictions of a black box.
statements.explanation: The surrogate is fitted to the black box's outputs rather than to the true labels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Perfect fidelity would show that the black box is correct about applicants.
statements.explanation: A perfect imitation copies the black box's mistakes too.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The fidelity of the surrogate is measured by its agreement with the true repayment outcomes.
statements.explanation: Fidelity is agreement with the black box; agreement with outcomes is accuracy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fidelity and accuracy are different quantities, since one compares with the black box and the other with the truth.
statements.explanation: A faithful surrogate can still be wrong about applicants.

questions.stem: A lender removes race from its approval model's inputs but keeps zip code, which is correlated with race. Shapley explanations show a large value for zip code and none for race. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing approval rates and error rates across groups, as in demographic parity or equalized odds, finds disparities that attributions can miss.
statements.explanation: Group fairness metrics measure outcomes directly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Removing the protected attribute from the inputs, called fairness through unawareness, assures equal outcomes across groups.
statements.explanation: Correlated inputs can reproduce the same disparities.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Disparate treatment and disparate impact mean the same thing.
statements.explanation: Disparate treatment is intentional use of a protected attribute; disparate impact is unequal outcomes from a neutral rule.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Zip code can act as a proxy variable, an input that carries information about a protected attribute.
statements.explanation: A proxy encodes the protected attribute indirectly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A large attribution to zip code on its own establishes that the lender discriminates on race.
statements.explanation: It shows reliance on zip code, which may or may not reflect discrimination.

questions.stem: A logistic regression for loan default uses two nearly identical inputs, balance_today and balance_yesterday. The two coefficients change sign and size across bootstrap resamples, while the predictions stay similar. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A coefficient is the change in the output per unit change in an input with the other inputs held fixed.
statements.explanation: That ceteris paribus reading breaks down when inputs move together.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Multicollinearity makes individual coefficients unstable across resamples, even while predictions stay stable.
statements.explanation: The data pin down the combined effect better than each separate coefficient.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ridge regularization stabilizes the coefficients by shrinking them.
statements.explanation: The penalty spreads weight across correlated inputs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A regression coefficient is the effect of an input ignoring the other inputs.
statements.explanation: It is a partial effect that adjusts for the other inputs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A negative coefficient on balance_yesterday shows that a higher balance yesterday lowers default risk.
statements.explanation: With a correlated input in the model, the sign can reflect an offset to its partner.

questions.stem: A team plans several uses of feature attributions such as Shapley values computed on validation data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For safety sign-off, a clean attribution pattern on validation data shows the model will perform well on a new population.
statements.explanation: Attributions say nothing about robustness under distribution shift.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For regulatory review, a list of the top three inputs for each decision shows whether the model treats demographic groups differently.
statements.explanation: Group treatment needs group-level outcome comparisons, not per-decision lists.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For debugging, heavy attribution to an input the team did not expect is a lead for data leakage or a shortcut.
statements.explanation: Unexpected reliance points to a possible artifact.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For recourse, attribution values alone tell an applicant which actions would change the decision.
statements.explanation: Recourse needs counterfactual, actionable changes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For trust, a user's increased confidence after reading an explanation is evidence that the model is more accurate.
statements.explanation: Persuasion is not evidence; trust should be calibrated to actual accuracy.

questions.stem: Two teams train models for the same task with the same data. Both reach about the same AUC and agree on most decisions, but their importance rankings put different inputs first. The two inputs are strongly correlated. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The differing rankings show that one of the two models is wrong.
statements.explanation: Both can fit the data equally well while splitting credit differently.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The importance ranking of whichever model scores higher identifies the true driver of the outcome.
statements.explanation: A ranking describes a model, not the data-generating process.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The Rashomon effect is that many different models reach similar accuracy while using the inputs differently.
statements.explanation: Equal accuracy does not pin down a single explanation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With strongly correlated inputs, credit can shift or split between them from one model to another.
statements.explanation: Correlated inputs are substitutes for each other.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal AUC means the two models rely on the same inputs.
statements.explanation: Performance is a poor guide to which inputs a model reads.

questions.stem: A skin-lesion classifier scores well in internal validation but poorly at a new clinic. Its attribution maps concentrate on a ruler and on ink marks that clinicians add near lesions they find suspicious. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The drop at a new site is an example of distribution shift between the development data and the deployment data.
statements.explanation: The new site differs in conditions from the training data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ink marks added by clinicians who suspect a lesion act as leakage, since they carry information about the label.
statements.explanation: A cue created by the labeling judgment leaks the answer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Attribution maps concentrating on the ruler are confirmation that the model uses the ruler as a shortcut.
statements.explanation: An attribution is a hypothesis to test, not a confirmation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: External validation means evaluating on a random split of the development hospital's own data.
statements.explanation: External validation uses data from a different site.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Cropping out the ruler and re-scoring is an ablation that tests a suspected shortcut without relying on the explanation.
statements.explanation: An intervention on the input confirms or refutes the hypothesis.

questions.stem: A city agency chooses between a boosted model with post-hoc Shapley explanations and a scoring rule with seven integer-weighted checks that has slightly lower accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Interpretable by design means the model is a neural network with an attention layer.
statements.explanation: It refers to structure a person can follow, such as a sparse linear model, a small tree or a scorecard.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A post-hoc explanation of the black box is as auditable as a transparent rule.
statements.explanation: Post-hoc output is an approximation produced by a method, which can itself be wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An interpretable model gives lower accuracy than a black box on tabular data.
statements.explanation: The accuracy gap is often small, and no fixed trade-off holds.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Auditability means a third party can inspect and reproduce how a decision was reached.
statements.explanation: A simple rule can be reproduced step by step.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A scorecard of integer-weighted checks is an example of a model that is interpretable by design.
statements.explanation: Its structure is the explanation.

questions.stem: A team must report importance for a random-forest model of loan default using three tools: impurity-based importance, permutation importance on held-out data, and the mean absolute Shapley value. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The mean absolute Shapley value summarizes the typical size of an input's contribution to predictions.
statements.explanation: Taking absolute values and averaging over rows gives a global magnitude.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Different importance measures answer different questions, so they can rank inputs differently.
statements.explanation: One measures split gain, one measures performance loss, one measures contribution size.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mean absolute Shapley value shows whether an input raises or lowers predictions on average.
statements.explanation: The absolute value discards direction.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Permutation importance measures how large an input's contribution to the predictions is, not its effect on accuracy.
statements.explanation: It measures the effect on performance; contribution size is what Shapley magnitudes measure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Permutation importance is computed from the training-time splits of the trees.
statements.explanation: Permutation importance uses performance after shuffling, ideally on held-out data.

questions.stem: A rule would require that a decision denying a benefit come with a clear explanation of the main factors, and a vendor proposes printing the three inputs with the largest Shapley values for each decision. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Contestability, the ability to challenge a decision, needs reasons tied to facts about the person's case that they can check.
statements.explanation: A reason that cannot be checked cannot be disputed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A top-three list is enough to detect discrimination across groups.
statements.explanation: Detecting discrimination requires group-level comparison of outcomes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A list that sums to the prediction minus the reference is, by that fact, a contestable explanation.
statements.explanation: Efficiency is accounting; it does not make reasons checkable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Interpretability and explanation are synonyms, so describing one decision after the fact makes the model interpretable.
statements.explanation: Interpretability is a property of the model; an explanation is a description of it produced by a method.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Recourse means the explanation names the inputs with the largest Shapley values.
statements.explanation: Recourse is about actions that change the outcome, not the size of attributions.

questions.stem: A reviewer notes that the words interpretability, explanation and transparency are used loosely in a vendor document. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Transparency means a method produces a reason for each prediction.
statements.explanation: Transparency means access to the model's internals, such as weights and code.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Publishing the weights makes a model interpretable.
statements.explanation: Access to weights is transparency, and a large network stays hard to understand.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An explanation is a property of the model's architecture, such as being linear.
statements.explanation: An explanation is a description produced for a purpose, often post-hoc; architecture relates to interpretability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Interpretability is a property of the model: how readily a person can understand how it maps inputs to outputs.
statements.explanation: A sparse linear model is more interpretable than a deep network.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An explanation is a description of a model or a prediction, produced by a method for a particular purpose.
statements.explanation: It can be local or global and can be faithful or unfaithful.

questions.stem: In a model, the output rises only when inputs A and B are both present, and input C never changes the output. A team explains the output with Shapley values. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Shapley values divide the joint contribution of interacting inputs between them.
statements.explanation: Averaging marginal contributions over orderings shares the interaction credit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An interaction means the effect of one input depends on the value of another.
statements.explanation: The contribution of A depends on whether B is present.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An input's marginal contribution depends on which other inputs are already present, so Shapley values average over orderings.
statements.explanation: Averaging over coalitions makes the credit independent of order.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An input with no effect alone can still have a nonzero Shapley value through interactions.
statements.explanation: Its marginal contribution can be positive in some coalitions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Removing one input at a time gives effects that add up to the total, even with an interaction.
statements.explanation: With an interaction, one-at-a-time effects can miss or double count the joint contribution.

questions.stem: An analyst groups explanation methods by how they access the model. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A saliency map assigns importance scores to input regions, often from gradients.
statements.explanation: It highlights which pixels the output is most sensitive to.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Gradient-based methods apply directly to a model made of decision trees.
statements.explanation: Tree ensembles are not differentiable in the inputs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: TreeSHAP is model-specific, because it uses the structure of tree ensembles.
statements.explanation: It exploits the tree structure for efficient computation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Integrated gradients is model-specific, because it needs a differentiable model.
statements.explanation: It uses gradients of the output with respect to the inputs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: LIME and KernelSHAP are model-agnostic, because they need just the model's outputs.
statements.explanation: They query the model as a black box.

questions.stem: A hospital runs a trial that randomizes clinicians to see an AI recommendation alone or with a feature-attribution explanation, on cases where the recommendation is wrong. More clinicians follow the wrong advice when the explanation is shown, but the interval for the difference is wide. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A confidence interval for the difference expresses how uncertain the estimated effect is.
statements.explanation: A wide interval means the estimate is imprecise.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Random assignment to arms supports a causal reading of the difference between arms.
statements.explanation: Randomization balances other differences between groups on average.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A higher following rate with the explanation shows that the explanation is an unfaithful description of the model.
statements.explanation: Following rate is a human outcome; faithfulness concerns the explanation and the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An interval for the difference that includes zero shows that the explanation has no effect.
statements.explanation: It means the data are compatible with no difference, which differs from evidence of no difference.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overreliance is following AI advice when it is wrong.
statements.explanation: It is the human-side failure that explanations are sometimes expected to reduce.

questions.stem: A survey firm estimates citywide support for a measure by sampling landline numbers only, and residents without a landline support it less often than residents with one. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Enlarging the sample shrinks the bias along with the standard error.
statements.explanation: A larger sample reduces random sampling error but leaves the systematic offset where it was.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gap is a coverage error, because part of the population is missing from the sampling frame.
statements.explanation: Coverage error arises when the frame omits people the survey is meant to describe.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The estimate is biased in the statistical sense: its expected value differs from the population value.
statements.explanation: Estimator bias is the gap between an estimator's average over repeated samples and the true value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reweighting the landline respondents to match the population's landline share repairs the estimate without sampling anyone else.
statements.explanation: Weighting adjusts the mix of people sampled, and a group with no respondents has nothing to weight up.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sampling error is a systematic offset that does not shrink as the sample grows.
statements.explanation: Sampling error is chance variation that shrinks with sample size, and a systematic offset is bias.

questions.source: Selection bias and inverse probability weighting
questions.stem: A model is trained on patients who had a lab panel in the first hours of admission. Patients who looked unstable were less likely to get the panel, so the retained patients do not represent all admissions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A baseline risk learned from the retained patients is miscalibrated for the full admitted population.
statements.explanation: Calibration means predicted risks match observed frequencies, and a skewed sample breaks that match.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Weighting retained patients by the inverse of their retention probability corrects the skew even when retention depends on an unrecorded variable.
statements.explanation: Weighting needs a recorded variable that explains who was kept.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Collecting more records under the same retention rule removes the bias.
statements.explanation: More data from the same filter reproduces the same skewed mix with less noise.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is measurement bias, because the lab values are recorded with error.
statements.explanation: Measurement bias concerns how values are recorded, whereas here the issue is who is recorded.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This is selection bias, because inclusion in the data depends on a variable related to the outcome.
statements.explanation: Selection bias arises when the rule that decides who enters the data is tied to what is being predicted.

questions.stem: A lender deletes the protected attribute from its training table but keeps neighbourhood, which closely tracks group membership. A manager says the model treats groups equally because it never sees group. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Deleting the attribute from the records leaves the lender able to compute outcome rates by group.
statements.explanation: Without a recorded attribute, outcome rates by group cannot be computed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Redundant encoding means group membership can be predicted from the remaining features.
statements.explanation: When other columns carry the same information, dropping one column does not remove the signal.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Fairness through unawareness is the practice of withholding the protected attribute, and it guarantees equal outcomes across groups.
statements.explanation: Unawareness describes the withholding, but it does not guarantee equal outcomes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Neighbourhood acts as a proxy for the protected attribute.
statements.explanation: A proxy is a feature that stands in for another variable because the two are correlated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A feature that correlates with group is, by itself, proof of disparate treatment.
statements.explanation: Correlation with group does not show improper use, since the feature may also carry legitimate information.

questions.stem: A reviewer divides the lower group's selection rate by the higher group's selection rate, gets 0.67, and compares it with 0.8. A separate two-proportion test on the same counts gives a very small p-value. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The four-fifths rule is a heuristic applied to aggregate selection rates, not a significance test.
statements.explanation: It is a rule of thumb for flagging adverse impact and carries no test statistic.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Subtracting the two selection rates gives the disparate impact ratio.
statements.explanation: A subtraction gives a difference in rates, and the impact ratio is a quotient.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ratio of selection rates is called the disparate impact ratio, also known as the adverse impact ratio.
statements.explanation: It is the standard name for the lower selection rate divided by the higher.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Statistical significance says a gap is unlikely to be sampling noise, which is a different question from whether it is large enough to matter.
statements.explanation: Statistical significance and practical significance answer different questions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A ratio of selection rates close to 1 indicates similar selection rates in the two groups.
statements.explanation: A disparate impact ratio of 1 means equal selection rates, and lower values mean a larger relative gap.

questions.stem: An audit finds a large approval gap between two groups and wants to locate the pipeline stage that produced it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A statistically significant gap names the pipeline stage that produced it.
statements.explanation: Significance says the gap is not noise but not where it arose.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Stratifying on legitimate covariates compares applicants with similar qualifications.
statements.explanation: Stratification splits the data by a variable so groups are compared within levels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An ablation reports the correlation between a component and the gap without changing the component.
statements.explanation: An ablation intervenes on a component, and a correlation does not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the gap disappears after conditioning on a variable, that variable is a legitimate explanation of the gap.
statements.explanation: The conditioning variable may itself be shaped by group, so the gap running through it is not justified by that fact.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Matching balances the measured covariates but leaves unmeasured ones free to differ.
statements.explanation: Matching can only equalise the variables that were recorded.

questions.stem: A company advanced candidates for two roles. Group B has the higher advancement rate within each role, yet group A has the higher advancement rate overall, because the two groups apply to the roles in different proportions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This reversal between subgroup and aggregate comparisons is Simpson's paradox.
statements.explanation: Simpson's paradox is a trend within strata that reverses or vanishes after pooling.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The aggregate comparison is the right one to report because it uses the most data.
statements.explanation: Using more data does not make the pooled table the answer to the causal question.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Choosing between the stratified and the pooled table is settled by whichever has the larger sample.
statements.explanation: Sample size does not decide which table answers the causal question.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A reversal like this indicates an arithmetic error in the counts.
statements.explanation: A reversal is routine when group composition differs across strata.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Group is the stratifying variable whose different mix across roles produces the reversal.
statements.explanation: Role is the stratifying variable, and the groups differ in how they spread across roles.

questions.stem: In hospital records, the drug group recovered less often overall than the untreated group, but did better within each severity level, because doctors gave the drug mostly to severe patients. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Giving a treatment on the basis of a prognostic factor such as severity confounds the raw comparison.
statements.explanation: A factor that drives both treatment and outcome confounds the comparison.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Randomised assignment breaks the link between severity and treatment, measured or not.
statements.explanation: Randomisation makes treatment independent of prior factors in expectation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Severity is a confounder because it influences both who gets the drug and how likely recovery is.
statements.explanation: A confounder is a common cause of treatment and outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Confounding by indication names the situation where sicker patients are the ones given the treatment.
statements.explanation: The reason for treatment is itself related to the outcome.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adjusting for a mediator, a variable on the path from treatment to outcome, is the standard way to remove confounding.
statements.explanation: Adjusting for a mediator blocks part of the effect, while confounders are the variables to adjust for.

questions.stem: A classifier has 90% overall accuracy, made of 95% on a large group A and 70% on a small group B. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Representation bias describes a model that predicts poorly for the majority group.
statements.explanation: Representation bias concerns a group being thinly represented in the data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Disaggregation means averaging the group metrics into one fair number.
statements.explanation: That would be aggregation, the opposite of reporting the groups separately.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Disaggregated evaluation reports metrics separately for each subgroup.
statements.explanation: Disaggregation splits a metric by group rather than averaging over them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pooled accuracy is an average weighted by group size, so the large group dominates it.
statements.explanation: A pooled metric reflects the biggest group most.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A high overall accuracy implies that each subgroup's accuracy is near the overall figure.
statements.explanation: A pooled average can hide a subgroup far below it.

questions.stem: Group B has 40 test examples with 15% error and group A has 2,000 test examples with 8% error. A 95% interval for group B's error rate is wide, and a significance test on the difference gives p = 0.13. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A Wilson interval is a credible interval computed from a posterior distribution.
statements.explanation: A Wilson interval is a frequentist confidence interval for a proportion.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A non-significant result from a small sample is inconclusive rather than evidence of equal error rates.
statements.explanation: Failing to reject a null hypothesis is not evidence that it is true.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A wide confidence interval signals that the estimate for the small group is imprecise.
statements.explanation: Interval width reflects estimation uncertainty, which is large for small samples.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Low statistical power means a test often fails to detect a real difference.
statements.explanation: Power is the chance of detecting a true effect, and it is low for small samples.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reporting just the pooled error rate hides the subgroup of interest.
statements.explanation: Pooling averages the small group into a figure dominated by the large one.

questions.stem: An auditor tests 20 independent subgroups for an error-rate gap at the 5% significance level for each test, and the model performs identically in the subgroups. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Choosing which subgroup to report after seeing the results is p-hacking, also called data dredging.
statements.explanation: Searching for a significant result after the fact inflates false findings.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A non-significant result in a small subgroup shows the model performs equally well there.
statements.explanation: A null result may reflect low power rather than equality.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Bonferroni correction multiplies the significance level by the number of tests.
statements.explanation: It divides the significance level by the number of tests.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 5% significance level applies to the group of 20 tests taken together.
statements.explanation: The level is set per test, so the combined false-positive chance is much higher.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Testing many subgroups raises the family-wise error rate, the chance of at least one false positive.
statements.explanation: The per-test rate applies to a single test, and errors accumulate across a family.

questions.stem: A face-attribute classifier is evaluated by gender and, separately, by skin tone, and the marginal error rates look equal. Evaluating the four gender-by-skin-tone cells shows error rates from 1% to 21%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal marginal error rates imply equal error rates in each gender-by-skin-tone cell.
statements.explanation: Marginal equality can mask large differences between cells.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Intersectional evaluation means evaluating each attribute separately and comparing the results.
statements.explanation: Separate evaluation produces marginal results, not joint ones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Intersectional evaluation reports metrics for combinations of attributes.
statements.explanation: It looks at joint subgroups rather than one attribute at a time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The number of cells grows multiplicatively with each attribute added, so cells become small and noisy.
statements.explanation: Combining attributes multiplies subgroups and thins out the data in each.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Dropping a thin cell from the report is more honest than showing a wide interval.
statements.explanation: Dropping a cell hides the subgroup, and a wide interval shows the uncertainty.

questions.stem: A model predicts arrest in the next year as a proxy for offending. Two neighbourhoods have the same offence rate, but the more heavily patrolled one has a higher arrest rate per offence. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Label bias is the same thing as sampling bias.
statements.explanation: Label bias concerns how the outcome is recorded, and sampling bias concerns who is included.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The label is recorded with different accuracy in different neighbourhoods, which is differential measurement bias.
statements.explanation: Differential measurement bias means measurement quality varies by group.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Collecting more arrest records fixes the label problem.
statements.explanation: More records from the same process estimate the same distorted rates more precisely.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A model that is highly accurate on the arrest label measures offending correctly.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is judged against the label and says nothing about whether the label tracks offending.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Arrest is a proxy label for offending, so the label is measured with error.
statements.explanation: A proxy label stands in for the outcome of interest and may track it imperfectly.

questions.stem: A hospital enrols patients by predicted annual cost, as a stand-in for health need. One group faces access barriers, so its cost understates its need, and the model predicts cost perfectly. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Replacing the label with a measure closer to need addresses the mismatch.
statements.explanation: Moving the label toward the construct reduces label bias.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model that predicts the label accurately shows that the label is valid.
statements.explanation: Accuracy against a label says nothing about whether the label measures the construct.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Accuracy in predicting a label is a different question from whether the label has construct validity.
statements.explanation: Predictive accuracy and construct validity answer different questions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cost is a proxy label for need.
statements.explanation: A proxy label is a measurable quantity used in place of the one that matters.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Construct validity is the question of whether the label measures the quantity of interest.
statements.explanation: A valid construct measure tracks the concept it claims to capture.

questions.stem: A lender sees repayment outcomes only for applicants it approved. It then trains a new model on those outcomes and wants to estimate how denied applicants would have performed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reject inference is the name for estimating outcomes for denied applicants.
statements.explanation: It is the term for inferring performance of applicants who were declined.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Outcomes are observed for just those who received the favourable decision, which is the selective labels problem.
statements.explanation: Selective labels arise when the decision determines whether the outcome is recorded.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Selective labels are the same problem as class imbalance.
statements.explanation: Class imbalance is about unequal class frequencies, not about which outcomes get observed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Approving a random sample of denied applicants gives outcome data that do not represent the denied group.
statements.explanation: A random draw from the denied group does represent that group.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Test accuracy computed on approved applicants is an unbiased estimate of performance on denied applicants.
statements.explanation: The approved group was selected by the earlier score, so it differs from the denied group.

questions.stem: Two districts have the same true incident rate. Patrol hours are allocated in proportion to incidents recorded in the previous cycle, and recorded incidents are proportional to patrol hours. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Proportional allocation drives the two districts toward their true rates over repeated cycles.
statements.explanation: The initial split reproduces itself, because records mirror patrol hours.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Allocating more patrol hours to the district with more records breaks the loop.
statements.explanation: That allocation rule is the loop, so it reinforces the existing split.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This is a runaway feedback loop, in which the system's decisions determine the data it later learns from.
statements.explanation: A feedback loop occurs when model outputs shape future training data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A feedback loop is random sampling error that averages out over time.
statements.explanation: A feedback loop is systematic and reinforces itself rather than averaging out.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Recorded incidents reflect observation effort as well as the true rate.
statements.explanation: Counts depend on where observers look, which is a measurement bias.

questions.stem: A reweighing scheme gives each combination of group and label a weight so that group and label are statistically independent in the weighted training data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reweighing leaves the recorded labels unchanged and alters how much each row counts.
statements.explanation: The weights change the influence of each row while the labels stay as recorded.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reweighing is a pre-processing method, because it changes the training data rather than the learner.
statements.explanation: Pre-processing methods adjust the data before training.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reweighing guarantees equal selection rates in the model's predictions on new data.
statements.explanation: Independence in the training sample does not carry over to predictions on new data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: After reweighing, group and label are independent in the weighted training sample.
statements.explanation: That independence is the purpose of the weights.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reweighing requires group membership to be recorded for the training rows, even when it is not a model input.
statements.explanation: The weights are computed from group, so it has to be recorded.
