questions.stem: A lender proposes setting a different score cutoff for each group after the model has produced its scores, to narrow a selection gap. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Group-specific cutoffs can be applied without recording group membership at decision time.
statements.explanation: A cutoff that depends on group needs the group to be known when deciding.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding a fairness penalty to the training loss is an in-processing method.
statements.explanation: In-processing builds the fairness criterion into the learning objective.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adjusting cutoffs by group is an in-processing method.
statements.explanation: In-processing alters the training procedure, and cutoffs act after training.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Group-specific thresholds are a post-processing method.
statements.explanation: Post-processing acts on a model's outputs after training.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Post-processing retrains the model's scores separately for each group.
statements.explanation: Post-processing leaves the learned scores in place and changes the decision rule.

questions.stem: A résumé-ranking model trained on past hiring decisions selects group B less often than group A at the same measured experience. The team considers reweighing, a fairness penalty, separate cutoffs, and changes to how reviewers use the ranking. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reweighing the training data also repairs disparity introduced by human reviewers.
statements.explanation: Reweighing changes the training sample, so a disparity created at review is outside its reach.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Pre-processing, in-processing and post-processing act on the outputs, the training and the data respectively.
statements.explanation: The order is data, training and outputs, so the stages are listed backwards here.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Historical bias means the data reflect earlier decisions that encoded disparities, even when the records are accurate.
statements.explanation: Historical bias arises from the world that produced the data, not from recording errors.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A human review stage after the model is outside the pipeline, so it adds no disparity.
statements.explanation: Review is part of deployment and can introduce disparity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Lower agreement with past decisions shows the model is of lower quality.
statements.explanation: The past decisions are suspect, so less agreement can mean less copying of earlier skew.

questions.stem: A bank buys a credit-risk model from a vendor, which trained it on records bought from a data broker with labels taken from another lender's approvals. The bank sets the approval cutoff and routes borderline cases to officers. An audit finds a large approval gap between groups. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The approval cutoff is a decision point that the bank owns.
statements.explanation: The party that sets a threshold owns its consequences.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Buying a model from a vendor transfers accountability for the lending decisions to the vendor.
statements.explanation: The bank makes the decisions and keeps accountability for them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Data provenance means the statistical distribution of the model's scores across groups.
statements.explanation: Provenance is the origin and history of the data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Assigning accountability for a disparity requires showing that someone intended it.
statements.explanation: Accountability attaches to roles that control a step and does not depend on a finding of intent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Accountability can be assigned according to which party controls a decision point in the pipeline.
statements.explanation: Control over a step is the usual basis for assigning responsibility for it.

questions.stem: A dataset's documentation records how and why the data were collected, who is represented, and how labels were produced. A separate document for the model states its intended uses, evaluation data and subgroup performance. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An audit is called external when a party independent of the developer performs it.
statements.explanation: Independence from the developer is what makes an audit external.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model card is a disclosure and does not by itself make a model fair.
statements.explanation: A card can report poor performance without correcting it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A model card reports intended uses and performance broken down by subgroup.
statements.explanation: Disaggregated performance and scope are standard model card contents.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A datasheet documents the origin, composition and collection of a dataset.
statements.explanation: A datasheet is a disclosure document for data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A model card describes the collection process and label provenance of the training data.
statements.explanation: That content belongs in a datasheet, and a model card describes the model.

questions.stem: A model is benchmarked on data that is 90% group A and 10% group B, then deployed on a population that is half group A and half group B. Each group's accuracy stays the same in deployment. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A change in group mix between benchmark and deployment is a change in the input distribution, a form of covariate shift.
statements.explanation: Covariate shift is a change in the input distribution while the relationship to the outcome stays put.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A larger benchmark sample with the same composition removes the mismatch.
statements.explanation: More data of the same mix cannot show how the model behaves on a different mix.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Overall accuracy is a property of the model alone and does not depend on the population.
statements.explanation: Overall accuracy depends on the mix of groups it is measured over.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Group-conditional accuracy has no use for predicting overall accuracy on a new mix.
statements.explanation: Per-group figures combine with the new shares to give the deployment figure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reporting accuracy by group transfers to a new mix better than a single pooled figure.
statements.explanation: Disaggregated figures remain usable when the composition changes.

questions.stem: In group A the outcome follows y = 2x and in group B it follows y = 2x + 6. A single line fitted to both groups together misses both of them. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A high R-squared on the pooled fit shows that the model fits each group.
statements.explanation: R-squared summarises the pooled fit and can hide systematic misfit within groups.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Residuals split by group reveal consistent over- and under-prediction.
statements.explanation: Disaggregated residuals expose a group-specific pattern that the pooled line hides.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Including a group indicator in the model lets the fit capture the offset between groups.
statements.explanation: An indicator variable absorbs the group-specific intercept.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Omitting a group indicator from the model is an omitted variable problem here.
statements.explanation: The missing variable explains the offset between the groups.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fitting one model to heterogeneous groups can fit neither well, which is aggregation bias.
statements.explanation: Aggregation bias arises when a pooled model assumes one relationship for different groups.

questions.stem: A screening device reads a person's true value plus noise, and the noise is larger for group B than for group A. The same cutoff is applied to everyone. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Raising the cutoff for group B removes the effect of its larger noise.
statements.explanation: A different cutoff does not reduce the noise in the readings.

statements.label: B
statements.text: More rows of readings from the same instrument reduce the noise in each reading.
statements.explanation: The noise belongs to the instrument, so each reading stays equally noisy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Measurement quality that differs by group is differential measurement error.
statements.explanation: It is measurement error whose size depends on group.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Larger measurement noise for group B produces more misclassification for group B at the same cutoff.
statements.explanation: Noise pushes readings across the cutoff more often for the noisier group.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The disparity comes from applying a different cutoff to each group.
statements.explanation: The cutoff is common to both groups, and the difference comes from the measurement.

questions.stem: A classifier has the same true positive rate and the same false positive rate in two groups, but the share of truly positive people differs between the groups. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Predictive parity means equal positive predictive value across groups.
statements.explanation: Positive predictive value is the share of flagged people who are truly positive.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Equalized odds means equal true positive and false positive rates across groups.
statements.explanation: It constrains both error rates to match between groups.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Demographic parity means equal true positive rates across groups.
statements.explanation: Demographic parity means equal selection rates, which is a different quantity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With equal error rates and unequal base rates, the positive predictive values are also equal.
statements.explanation: Positive predictive value depends on the base rate, so it differs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With unequal base rates and an imperfect classifier, equalized odds and predictive parity hold together in general.
statements.explanation: The two criteria conflict when base rates differ.

questions.stem: A model approves 30% of group A and 18% of group B. Re-scoring the same applicants with the postcode input replaced by a constant leaves a smaller gap. Group is not an input. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The test shows how the model depends on postcode and not why the groups differ in postcode.
statements.explanation: It is a statement about the model, not about the applicants.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A gap that remains after postcode is neutralised shows the model uses group directly.
statements.explanation: Other correlated inputs can carry the remaining gap without group being used.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Neutralising an input and re-scoring is an ablation of that input.
statements.explanation: Ablation removes a component to see how outputs change.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If group is not an input, no other input can carry group information.
statements.explanation: Correlated inputs can act as proxies that carry group information.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A smaller gap after neutralising postcode shows postcode causes differences in repayment.
statements.explanation: The test intervenes on the model's input, so it says nothing about causes in the applicants.

questions.stem: Three candidate models have group A error rates of 5%, 6% and 3% and group B error rates of 30%, 20% and 45%, and group A is 90% of the data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Balanced accuracy gives groups weight in proportion to their size, so it equals pooled accuracy.
statements.explanation: Balanced accuracy weights each group equally, regardless of its size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Worst-group error is a different criterion from average error.
statements.explanation: It reports the group with the highest error rather than the weighted mean.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Empirical risk minimisation optimises average loss, which weights each group by its share of the data.
statements.explanation: The average loss follows the data mix, so the large group dominates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Two models can rank differently by average error and by worst-group error.
statements.explanation: Average error and worst-group error are different criteria and can disagree.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Choosing the model with the lowest worst-group error is a minimax criterion.
statements.explanation: Minimax minimises the maximum loss across groups.

questions.stem: A model flags the same share of applicants in two groups. A human reviewer then upholds flags in one group more often than in the other. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A funnel analysis combines the stages into one overall rate.
statements.explanation: A funnel analysis reports each stage separately so the step where rates diverge can be found.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Comparing reviewer decisions on like cases is needed to attribute the gap to reviewer behaviour.
statements.explanation: Comparable cases separate case mix from reviewer treatment.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Different upheld rates establish that the reviewer is biased.
statements.explanation: The flagged cases may differ in true risk, so rates call for investigation but do not show bias.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A review stage that follows an equal flagging step leaves the selection rates equal between groups.
statements.explanation: The review step can create or remove disparity after equal flag rates.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Automation bias means reviewers ignore the model's flags.
statements.explanation: Automation bias is over-reliance on an automated output.

questions.stem: Auditors submit paired résumés to a text-generating model, identical except for a first name signalling group A or group B, and count the pairs where the model's answers differ. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Submitting paired inputs that differ in one signal is a correspondence test, also called a paired audit.
statements.explanation: It isolates dependence of the output on the varied signal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Finding that outputs depend on the name identifies the training data as the source.
statements.explanation: Dependence could come from training data, tuning or the prompt, which is a separate question.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sign test counts the concordant pairs and ignores the discordant pairs.
statements.explanation: A sign test uses the discordant pairs, those treated differently.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because outputs are sampled randomly, pairs with differing answers carry no information.
statements.explanation: Randomness is part of the null distribution, and a test on differing pairs accounts for it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Matching by construction controls for qualifications within each pair.
statements.explanation: Identical content removes qualifications as an explanation inside the pair.

questions.stem: Two annotators label 100 clinical notes. They agree on 90, and each calls 90% of the notes positive. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Cohen's kappa corrects observed agreement for the agreement expected by chance.
statements.explanation: Kappa is observed agreement minus chance agreement, scaled by the maximum possible improvement over chance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Kappa can be low even when raw agreement is high.
statements.explanation: A dominant category inflates chance agreement, which lowers kappa.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Inter-annotator agreement measures consistency of labelling, not validity.
statements.explanation: Annotators can agree with each other and share the same systematic error.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Chance agreement is high when one category dominates, so kappa falls below raw agreement.
statements.explanation: A skewed class balance inflates the chance term.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Agreement between annotators is a measure of label validity.
statements.explanation: Validity asks whether labels capture the true condition, which agreement does not show.

questions.stem: A skin-lesion classifier has a higher error rate on darker skin. A test set labelled by the same process as the training data and a separate audit set labelled by independent experts using biopsy results show the same gap. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The audit set shows that the gap comes from under-representation in the training data.
statements.explanation: Under-representation is consistent with the gap but untested, and other causes remain.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Collecting more images of the same kind removes a label-quality problem.
statements.explanation: Label quality does not improve with more images produced by the same labelling process.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Biopsy results serve as a reference standard, also called ground truth, for the lesion labels.
statements.explanation: A reference standard is the best available measure of the true condition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An independent labelling source addresses the possibility that test and training labels share errors.
statements.explanation: Independent labels remove shared label error as an explanation of the gap.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Image capture conditions can still differ by group, even with independent labels.
statements.explanation: Independent labelling does not control for how images were produced.

questions.stem: A causal framework describes three rungs: association (seeing), intervention (doing) and counterfactual (imagining). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A counterfactual question is a rung 2 question about an average effect.
statements.explanation: Counterfactuals sit on rung 3 and concern a specific case.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A counterfactual question asks what happens on average when X is set by force.
statements.explanation: That describes an intervention at rung 2, while a counterfactual concerns a specific case.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Observing a conditional probability and setting a variable by force give the same quantity in general.
statements.explanation: Confounding makes the observed and interventional quantities differ.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rung 1 question concerns the conditional probability of an outcome given an observed value, P(Y given X).
statements.explanation: Association asks what goes with what in observed data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A rung 2 question concerns the probability of an outcome under an intervention, written P(Y given do(X)).
statements.explanation: The do operator marks setting X by force rather than observing it.

questions.stem: A lender trains a model on past loans to predict default from 30 recorded features, and it ranks risk well on new applicants who resemble past borrowers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Feature importance is a different thing from causal effect.
statements.explanation: Importance describes use by the model, and causal effect describes the result of an intervention.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The model estimates conditional probabilities, which is association at rung 1.
statements.explanation: Prediction fits observed relationships between features and outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A feature that is a consequence of the label can inflate accuracy, which is leakage.
statements.explanation: Leakage lets the model use information that would not be available at prediction time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A large weight on a feature shows that the feature causes default.
statements.explanation: A feature can carry weight as a proxy, an effect of default, or a shared cause.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Good prediction on similar cases shows what would happen if the lender changed a feature.
statements.explanation: A prediction describes what goes with a value, not what follows from changing it.

questions.stem: Customers who received a marketing email signed up at a higher rate than customers who did not. The email went mostly to customers who were already engaged with the app, and engaged customers sign up more often regardless. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The raw difference in sign-up rates is an association, a rung 1 quantity.
statements.explanation: It describes how rates differ across observed groups.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Random assignment of the email makes the two groups equivalent in expectation.
statements.explanation: Randomisation removes confounding by making treatment independent of prior factors.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Confounding is the same thing as measurement bias.
statements.explanation: Confounding is a shared cause of treatment and outcome, and measurement bias is an error in recording.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A larger sample removes the confounding.
statements.explanation: More data shrinks random error but leaves the offset caused by who was emailed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Engagement is a confounder, because it influences both who is emailed and who signs up.
statements.explanation: A confounder is a common cause of treatment and outcome.

questions.stem: Engaged customers sign up at 10% without the email, and the email raises everyone's sign-up probability by 1.5 points. The email was sent to most engaged customers and few others, and engaged customers sign up more often anyway. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The raw difference between emailed and non-emailed customers is an unbiased estimate of the average treatment effect.
statements.explanation: Confounding makes the raw difference biased as an estimate of the effect.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An average treatment effect describes one named customer's response.
statements.explanation: An average treatment effect is a population average, not an individual effect.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Stratifying by engagement and comparing within strata removes confounding by engagement, if no other confounder remains.
statements.explanation: Within a stratum, treated and untreated customers have the same engagement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Standardisation weights each stratum's effect by that stratum's share of the population.
statements.explanation: Standardisation averages stratum effects over a reference population mix.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The raw comparison overstates the effect, because engagement pushes the treated group's rate up.
statements.explanation: A positive confounder inflates the observed difference.

questions.stem: A dataset records two yes-or-no variables, coffee each day (X) and high resting heart rate (Y), which are associated. One story says coffee raises heart rate, another says a high heart rate leads people to drink coffee, and a third says anxiety raises both. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Randomly assigning coffee and comparing heart rates would separate them.
statements.explanation: An intervention on X removes arrows into X and tests the direct effect.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The story in which heart rate leads to coffee is reverse causation.
statements.explanation: Reverse causation means the outcome influences the supposed cause.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Under the confounder story, coffee and heart rate are not associated.
statements.explanation: A common cause creates association even when X has no effect on Y.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The story in which anxiety raises both variables involves a confounder.
statements.explanation: A common cause produces association without a direct effect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Different causal graphs can imply the same joint distribution of X and Y, so the stories are observationally equivalent.
statements.explanation: Observational equivalence means data on X and Y alone cannot choose between the graphs.

questions.stem: An analyst adjusts a comparison for a variable that is influenced by both the treatment and the outcome, and separately for a variable lying on the path from treatment to outcome. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Conditioning on a collider can create a spurious association between its causes.
statements.explanation: Adjusting for a common effect opens a path that was closed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding more adjustment variables reduces bias whatever their causal role.
statements.explanation: Adjusting for colliders or mediators can introduce or block real paths.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A variable with arrows pointing into it from two other variables is a collider.
statements.explanation: A collider is a common effect of two variables.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A mediator lies on the path from treatment to outcome, so adjusting for it blocks part of the effect.
statements.explanation: Mediators carry the effect, and conditioning on them removes that part.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A confounder is a variable caused by the treatment.
statements.explanation: A confounder is a cause of both treatment and outcome, and a variable caused by treatment is a mediator or descendant.

questions.stem: A hospital wants to know what would have happened to patients who got a follow-up call had they not been called, and it compares them with patients who were not called. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The comparison group stands in for the missing outcomes if it is exchangeable with the called group.
statements.explanation: Exchangeability means the groups would have had the same outcomes absent treatment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each patient is observed under one condition, so the other potential outcome is missing, which is the fundamental problem of causal inference.
statements.explanation: A unit cannot be observed under both the treated and untreated condition.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An average treatment effect is a group-average quantity, whereas an individual treatment effect is unobserved.
statements.explanation: Group comparisons estimate averages, not what happened to one patient.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The counterfactual outcome is observed directly by looking at the same patient twice.
statements.explanation: The same patient cannot be both called and not called at the same time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Matching on measured variables guarantees exchangeability on unmeasured variables.
statements.explanation: Matching balances only the variables used.

questions.stem: Among engaged customers, 11.5% sign up if emailed and 10% if not. One emailed engaged customer signed up, and the question is whether the email caused it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Group rates alone identify the individual-level probability without further assumptions.
statements.explanation: Many individual patterns are compatible with the same group rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Without monotonicity, the data give bounds rather than a single value, which is partial identification.
statements.explanation: Partial identification yields a range of values consistent with the data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Probability of necessity is a rung 2 quantity.
statements.explanation: It concerns a specific case and a contrary-to-fact action, so it sits on rung 3.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Under monotonicity and equivalent groups, the probability of necessity for an emailed sign-up is one minus the ratio of the two group rates.
statements.explanation: Probability of necessity is the chance the outcome would not have occurred without the treatment, given that both occurred.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Monotonicity is the assumption that the email does not make an individual less likely to sign up.
statements.explanation: Monotonicity rules out individuals who respond negatively to the treatment.

questions.stem: A retailer studies whether a discount coupon keeps customers from leaving. It considers four questions: which customers who got coupons stayed, whether this customer will stay given her usage, how many would stay if coupons went to everyone, and whether this particular customer would have stayed without her coupon. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing the stay rate of coupon recipients with non-recipients is a rung 1 question.
statements.explanation: It describes how outcomes differ across observed groups.

statements.label: B
statements.text: How many would stay if coupons went to everyone is a counterfactual, rung 3 question.
statements.explanation: It asks about an intervention on the whole population, which is rung 2.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rung 2 question can be answered from association alone without extra assumptions.
statements.explanation: Going from observed data to a causal claim needs assumptions or an intervention.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Predicting whether a customer will stay from her usage is a rung 2 question.
statements.explanation: Prediction from observed features is association, which is rung 1.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether this customer would have stayed without the coupon is a rung 3 question.
statements.explanation: It concerns a specific unit under a contrary-to-fact action.

questions.stem: A bank assigns a reminder to customers by coin flip and compares the share who pay on time between the reminded and the not-reminded. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Randomisation balances measured confounders but leaves unmeasured ones uncontrolled.
statements.explanation: Its advantage over adjustment is that it handles unmeasured factors as well.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The comparison identifies an average effect, not each customer's effect.
statements.explanation: Individual effects are not observed under randomisation either.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Self-selection into the reminder reintroduces confounding.
statements.explanation: People who opt in differ from those who do not, mixing the reminder with the drivers of opting in.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Random assignment makes the groups exchangeable in expectation, measured or not.
statements.explanation: Randomisation balances prior factors on average, including unmeasured ones.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Randomisation guarantees the two groups are balanced in each sample.
statements.explanation: Chance leaves some imbalance in a finite sample, so equivalence holds only in expectation.

questions.stem: A bank emailed every customer with income above a threshold and no customer below it, and recorded who signed up. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Without untreated customers at the same income level, a larger sample under the same rule still lacks a comparison group.
statements.explanation: The missing comparison group is a design problem, not a sample size problem.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Positivity, also called overlap, requires both treated and untreated units at each kind of customer.
statements.explanation: Without overlap there is no comparison group at the same covariate values.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Assigning treatment by a threshold on income is a randomised design.
statements.explanation: A deterministic threshold on a covariate is not random assignment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Extrapolating the effect to low incomes rests on modelling assumptions rather than on data.
statements.explanation: No observations exist in that range to support the estimate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Income is a confounder here, because it likely affects both who is emailed and who signs up.
statements.explanation: A variable that determines treatment and also affects the outcome confounds the comparison.

questions.stem: A coin lands heads with probability 0.7. A student estimates the heads probability from 20 flips and gets 0.65. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Calling the coin biased uses bias in the everyday sense of a process tilted away from a symmetric reference.
statements.explanation: The process itself departs from 0.5.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Estimator bias is the expected value of an estimator minus the true value.
statements.explanation: It is a property of the estimator's average behaviour over repeated samples.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An unbiased estimator can still miss the truth in a single sample.
statements.explanation: Unbiased means correct on average, not correct each time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The sample proportion is a biased estimator of the heads probability.
statements.explanation: Its expected value equals the true probability, so its bias is zero.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sampling error and estimator bias are the same thing.
statements.explanation: Sampling error is the miss in a single sample, and bias is the average miss.

questions.stem: In a population of 500,000 women and 500,000 men, 600 women and 1,400 men are data scientists. A separate league has a rule that only men may play. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An absolute difference and a ratio of rates carry the same information when the rates are small.
statements.explanation: Small rates can give a small difference alongside a large ratio.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A gap created by an explicit rule and a gap in occupational choice have the same cause.
statements.explanation: A rule that excludes a group is a different mechanism from differing rates of entry.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A ratio of rates hides exclusion that a small absolute difference shows.
statements.explanation: A ratio exposes exclusion that a small absolute difference can hide.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The probability of being a woman given being a data scientist differs from the probability of being a data scientist given being a woman.
statements.explanation: Transposing the conditional changes the denominator, which is a common error.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The event before the vertical bar supplies the denominator in a conditional probability.
statements.explanation: The event after the bar is the condition and supplies the denominator.

questions.source: Estimator bias and mean squared error
questions.stem: An analyst estimates a population variance using the sum of squared deviations from the sample mean divided by n, instead of n minus 1. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An unbiased estimator has the lowest mean squared error of the available estimators.
statements.explanation: A biased estimator with lower variance can have a smaller mean squared error.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The bias of the divide-by-n estimator grows as the sample size grows.
statements.explanation: The bias shrinks in proportion to one over n.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dividing by n gives a biased estimator that underestimates the variance on average.
statements.explanation: Deviations from the sample mean are smaller than deviations from the true mean.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Mean squared error equals variance plus squared bias.
statements.explanation: This decomposition holds for any estimator.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Accepting a little bias for a large drop in variance is the bias-variance trade-off, which shrinkage estimators exploit.
statements.explanation: Shrinkage lowers variance at the cost of some bias.

questions.stem: In a survey, every actual voter says they voted, and some non-voters also say they voted. Respondents were chosen by simple random sampling. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Nonresponse bias, meaning selected people declining to answer, is the cause here.
statements.explanation: Respondents answered, so the issue is accuracy of answers and not refusal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Misreporting of this kind is response bias, a form of measurement bias.
statements.explanation: Response bias arises when answers differ from the truth.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A gold standard on a validation subset lets analysts estimate the size of the recording error.
statements.explanation: The error cannot be seen from reported values alone.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Interviewing more respondents removes the misreporting offset.
statements.explanation: More respondents shrink random error around the distorted centre.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Selection bias is absent, because each resident had an equal chance of being sampled.
statements.explanation: The distortion is in what respondents report, not in who was chosen.

questions.stem: A researcher builds a map of startups from an online directory. The directory lists a startup more often if it is in Region R, and the researcher finds Region R holds a larger share than expected. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The listing probability is the inclusion probability, and it differs between regions here.
statements.explanation: Unequal inclusion probabilities distort the shares in the data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A larger directory under the same listing rule corrects the distortion.
statements.explanation: The same rule reproduces the same skew with less noise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A prior expectation that Region R should lead is a validation of the dataset.
statements.explanation: An expectation is a hypothesis, and a check compares the data against an independent source.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Inclusion that depends on the attribute being studied is selection bias.
statements.explanation: The rule for entering the data is tied to the region.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Selection bias disappears when inclusion is independent of the quantity being measured.
statements.explanation: Without a link between inclusion and the outcome, the sample is not distorted by it.

questions.stem: A poll draws 2,400,000 responses from a frame of telephone and car owners, in a period when owning those things is linked to voting intention, and reports a margin of error of 0.06 percentage points. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A very large sample cancels the bias.
statements.explanation: Sample size shrinks variance but leaves the offset.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The margin of error quantifies sampling error and not bias.
statements.explanation: It describes random variation under the sampling design.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Excluding people without telephones or cars is nonresponse bias.
statements.explanation: The frame never reached them, so it is coverage bias, not people declining to answer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tiny margin around a skewed centre describes an accurate but imprecise estimate.
statements.explanation: It describes a precise but inaccurate estimate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Weighting repairs the gap for people the frame did not reach.
statements.explanation: People with no chance of selection have no respondents to weight up.

questions.stem: X takes the values minus 1, 0 and 1 with equal probability, and Y equals 1 when X is not 0 and equals 0 when X is 0. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Zero correlation between X and Y does not imply that X and Y are independent.
statements.explanation: Correlation captures linear association, and other dependence can remain.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Independent variables can have a non-zero correlation.
statements.explanation: Independence implies zero covariance and so zero correlation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Correlation is a measure of association, which sits on rung 1.
statements.explanation: It describes co-movement in observed data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: X and Y are statistically dependent, because knowing X changes the distribution of Y.
statements.explanation: Y is a function of X, which is the strongest dependence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A correlation of zero demonstrates that X has no causal effect on Y.
statements.explanation: Correlation is an association measure and does not speak to interventions.

questions.source: Margin of error on a lead
questions.stem: A poll of 1,000 likely voters treated as a simple random sample finds candidate A at 48% and candidate B at 47%, and a headline reads that A leads. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The margin of error shrinks in proportion to one over the square root of the sample size.
statements.explanation: Quadrupling the sample halves the margin.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The margin of error includes the effect of nonresponse bias.
statements.explanation: It reflects random sampling error only under the stated design.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The margin of error on the lead is larger than the margin of error on a single share.
statements.explanation: The lead is a difference of two shares and has more variability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A lead smaller than the margin of error on a single share is evidence that the leader is ahead.
statements.explanation: A lead that small is well within the variability of the estimate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two shares are negatively related, because they come from the same respondents.
statements.explanation: More support for one candidate means fewer respondents left for the other.

questions.stem: A forecaster gives three races win probabilities of 0.9, 0.8 and 0.6 and treats the races as independent, although a shared polling error could move all three together. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A forecast probability of 0.9 means the party wins 90% of the seats in a race.
statements.explanation: It is a probability of winning, not a vote share.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For independent events, the joint probability is the product of the individual probabilities.
statements.explanation: Independence means one outcome gives no information about another.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Treating the races as independent understates the chance of extreme results when errors are correlated.
statements.explanation: Correlation fattens the tails of the joint distribution.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The expected number of wins equals the sum of the probabilities if the races are independent, and differs if they are correlated.
statements.explanation: Expectation is additive regardless of dependence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A systematic polling error shared by the races produces correlated outcomes.
statements.explanation: A common error source links the races beyond their individual probabilities.

questions.stem: A team tests 20 unrelated hypotheses at the 5% significance level, and every null hypothesis is true. It writes up only the significant results. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Conditioning on significance keeps large estimates, so reported effects are inflated, a pattern called the winner's curse.
statements.explanation: Selecting on significance favours overestimates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Unreported tests leave no trace in the paper, which is how publication bias hides.
statements.explanation: Publication bias arises when results are filtered before they are seen.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Type I error means failing to detect a real effect.
statements.explanation: A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reporting just the significant results out of many tests is selective reporting.
statements.explanation: Filtering by outcome distorts the evidence shown.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A significant result among 20 true nulls shows a real effect.
statements.explanation: At a 5% rate, some false positives are expected among many tests.

questions.stem: A classifier predicts whether each applicant is qualified. The qualified share is 30% in group A and 10% in group B, and the classifier is perfect. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Demographic parity means equal accuracy across groups.
statements.explanation: It means equal selection rates, which differs from equal accuracy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A perfect classifier satisfies demographic parity whatever the base rates.
statements.explanation: Perfect predictions mirror the base rates, so parity fails when they differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Satisfying demographic parity here would require misclassifying some applicants.
statements.explanation: Equal selection rates need some qualified people rejected or some unqualified ones accepted.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A perfect classifier satisfies equalized odds.
statements.explanation: The true positive rate is one and the false positive rate is zero in both groups.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With unequal base rates, a perfect classifier has unequal selection rates, which violates demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Selection rates equal the base rates when predictions are perfect.

questions.source: Bias types mapped to pipeline stages
questions.stem: A company trains a ranking model on ten years of its own hiring records. Disparities can enter at different stages: past hiring decisions, who appears in the data, how features and labels are measured, how the model is evaluated, and how the ranking is used afterwards. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Applicants screened out earlier have no outcomes in the data, which is a form of selection bias.
statements.explanation: Who has recorded outcomes depends on earlier decisions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Noisier or distorted features and labels for some groups are measurement bias.
statements.explanation: Measurement bias concerns how variables are recorded.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Past decisions that reflect earlier practices are historical bias.
statements.explanation: Historical bias comes from the world that produced the data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Disparity created when reviewers act on the ranking is called representation bias.
statements.explanation: That arises at use and belongs to deployment, whereas representation bias concerns thin coverage in the data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Using a pooled metric that hides weak subgroups is called deployment bias.
statements.explanation: Hiding subgroups in a pooled metric is aggregation or evaluation bias.

questions.stem: An audit finds that a triage model refers 24% of patients from group X and 15% of patients from group Y to a specialist programme, and the difference is far too large to be chance. A manager concludes the model is biased against group Y. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Clinical need can differ between the groups, so the disparity does not by itself show bias in the model.
statements.explanation: Differences in need, data, labels, cutoffs or review can each produce a gap.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gap is a disparity, a descriptive difference in outcomes between groups.
statements.explanation: A disparity records that outcomes differ without saying why.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rung 1 comparison of referral rates answers whether the model would refer more group Y patients if group membership were changed.
statements.explanation: That is an interventional question, which a descriptive comparison cannot answer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Statistical significance of the gap shows which pipeline stage caused it.
statements.explanation: Significance rules out chance and does not locate a cause.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Comparing patients of similar severity separates need from other causes, with the limit that unmeasured factors remain.
statements.explanation: Stratifying on legitimate covariates narrows the explanations.

questions.stem: A firm trains a model to predict promotion from ten years of its own records and finds it highly accurate on held-out records. In those years promotion went to one group more often than to others at comparable measured performance. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accuracy on held-out records from the same process measures how fair the labels are.
statements.explanation: Accuracy measures agreement with the labels and says nothing about their fairness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model that reproduces a biased label accurately is evidence that the label is fair.
statements.explanation: High accuracy can mean the model copied the bias.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A held-out split drawn from the same process is an out-of-distribution evaluation.
statements.explanation: A split from the same process is an in-distribution evaluation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This situation is label bias carried through historical bias.
statements.explanation: The labels encode past decisions that favoured one group.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Evaluating on records from the same pipeline detects bias in the labels.
statements.explanation: Test labels share the source of the training labels and carry the same bias.

questions.stem: A vendor claims its hiring model is not biased because it trained on 20 million records, that it has 94% accuracy for each group on held-out data from its own pipeline, and that it passes the one fairness metric tested. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A large training set shrinks variance but leaves bias from the data collection process.
statements.explanation: Volume does not correct a skewed process.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Held-out data from the same pipeline is an in-distribution test, which can miss problems that appear elsewhere.
statements.explanation: In-distribution results may not transfer to a different population.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing one fairness metric shows that the model satisfies the other fairness criteria.
statements.explanation: Fairness criteria can conflict, so passing one does not imply the rest.

statements.label: D
statements.text: External validity concerns whether results hold in the population where the model will be used.
statements.explanation: Generalising beyond the test pipeline is a separate question from internal accuracy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal accuracy across groups implies equal selection rates and equal error rates of each type.
statements.explanation: Accuracy hides how errors are split between false positives and false negatives.

questions.source: Adjusted versus unadjusted gap and mediation
questions.stem: A salary-recommendation model predicts salaries for women that are on average 8% lower than for men. Among employees at the same job level, the gap is 2%. Job level was assigned by earlier promotion decisions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A smaller adjusted gap shows the model does not discriminate.
statements.explanation: The remaining gap and the part running through job level are each open to question.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Job level can be a mediator, because group may influence promotion, which then influences salary.
statements.explanation: A mediator lies on a path from group to outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 8% figure is an unadjusted gap, and the 2% figure is a gap adjusted for job level.
statements.explanation: Adjusting for a variable compares people within its levels.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The adjusted gap is the better figure because job level is a legitimate explanation of pay.
statements.explanation: Job level was itself shaped by earlier decisions, so it may carry the bias being studied.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adjusting for job level removes the part of the gap that runs through promotion.
statements.explanation: Conditioning on a mediator blocks the effect that travels through it.

questions.stem: A company deploys a support assistant built on a language model licensed from a provider. Testers find that answer quality and tone differ across customer groups in ways that the company's own prompts, data and code do not explain. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The company can show where the disparity entered without information from the provider.
statements.explanation: Locating the source in training data or tuning needs documentation from the provider.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using a licensed model transfers accountability for the assistant's behaviour to the provider.
statements.explanation: The company deploys the system and keeps accountability for its use.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Behavioural testing with paired prompts can probe the model without access to its training data.
statements.explanation: Black-box testing relies on inputs and outputs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A model card or system documentation from the provider is useful evidence for the investigation.
statements.explanation: Documentation of intended use and subgroup performance helps the deployer judge fitness for use.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The licensed model is an upstream component, and the company's prompts and code are downstream.
statements.explanation: Upstream and downstream describe position in the supply chain of a system.

questions.stem: A city compares the end-of-year exam scores of students who attended a free after-school tutoring program with those who did not, to learn whether tutoring raises scores. Families choose whether to enrol; places are not assigned by lottery. Here the treatment is attending the tutoring program and the outcome is the exam score. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The student's grades in the previous year, which influence whether a family enrols the child and also influence this year's exam score.
statements.explanation: It affects both the treatment (whether a family enrols) and the outcome (the exam score), so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The number of tutoring sessions the student attends after enrolling, which tutoring produces and which in turn raises the exam score.
statements.explanation: It lies on the path from tutoring to the score (tutoring causes it), so it is part of how tutoring would work, not a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether the student later wins a scholarship, which is more likely both for students who were tutored and for students with high exam scores.
statements.explanation: The scholarship is an effect of both tutoring and the score, not a cause of either; a variable caused by both is not a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: How involved the parents are in schoolwork, which makes enrolment more likely and also raises exam scores.
statements.explanation: Involved parents both enrol their children and help with schoolwork, so this variable affects both the treatment and the outcome and is a confounder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The student's sleep on the night before the exam, which affects the exam score but is unrelated to whether the family enrolled the child.
statements.explanation: It affects the outcome but is unrelated to the treatment, so it cannot confound the comparison.

questions.stem: A hospital switches on an AI discharge-planning tool in some wards and not others; each ward chose whether to adopt it. Wards that adopted it have lower 30-day readmission rates, and management asks whether the tool reduces readmissions. Here the treatment is a ward adopting the tool and the outcome is its readmission rate. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number of follow-up calls made after discharge, which the tool triggers and which then lower readmissions.
statements.explanation: The tool causes the calls and the calls lower readmissions, so the variable is on the path from tool to outcome (a mediator), not a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: How sick the typical patient in the ward is, since wards with sicker patients were less likely to adopt the tool and also have more readmissions.
statements.explanation: It influences both which wards adopt the tool and the readmission rate, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The number of readmission entries that appear in next year's hospital database, which is produced by the readmissions themselves.
statements.explanation: It is an effect of the outcome, not a cause of the tool's adoption or of readmissions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The staff-satisfaction score for the tool, which is reported by wards that use the tool.
statements.explanation: It exists as a result of using the tool, so it follows the treatment; it cannot be a cause of it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The seniority of the ward's physicians, since wards led by senior physicians adopted the tool earlier and also manage patients' care more effectively.
statements.explanation: Physician seniority shapes both adoption and readmission outcomes, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: A company compares performance ratings of employees who work remotely with those who work on site, to learn whether remote work raises performance. Employees negotiate with their managers about who works remotely. Here the treatment is working remotely and the outcome is the performance rating. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Seniority, since senior staff are more likely to be allowed to work remotely and also tend to receive higher ratings.
statements.explanation: Seniority influences both who works remotely and the rating, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Hours of uninterrupted focus time, which remote work increases and which in turn raises the rating.
statements.explanation: It is caused by the treatment and then affects the outcome (a mediator), so it is part of the effect, not a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether the role is mainly software engineering, since engineers are more often remote and are rated against different norms that shift their ratings.
statements.explanation: Role influences who works remotely and how ratings come out, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The size of the year-end bonus, which is paid partly according to the performance rating.
statements.explanation: It is an effect of the outcome, not a cause of remote work or of the rating.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The employee's commute length, which affects who asks to work remotely but has no effect on the rating.
statements.explanation: It affects the treatment only. A variable related to the treatment but not to the outcome cannot confound the comparison.

questions.stem: A registry shows that adults who take a daily vitamin D supplement have fewer bone fractures than adults who do not. Researchers ask whether the supplement prevents fractures. People decide for themselves whether to take it. Here the treatment is taking the supplement and the outcome is having a fracture. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Bone density measured a year after starting, which the supplement raises and which lowers the risk of fracture.
statements.explanation: The supplement causes it and it then affects fractures, so it is on the path from treatment to outcome, not a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The brand of supplement bought by those who take it, which varies among users and has no effect on fracture risk.
statements.explanation: It is a detail of the treatment and is unrelated to the outcome, so it does not confound.

statements.label: C
statements.text: How health-conscious the person is, since health-conscious people are more likely to take supplements and also less likely to be injured.
statements.explanation: It influences both taking the supplement and the chance of a fracture, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether the person is later prescribed a walking aid, which is more likely after a fracture.
statements.explanation: It is an effect of the outcome, so it cannot be a cause of either variable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Age, since older adults are more likely to take the supplement and also more likely to fracture a bone.
statements.explanation: Age influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: A researcher collects 60 published language models and compares coding-benchmark scores for models trained with a new technique and models trained without it, to learn whether the technique improves scores. Each lab decided whether to use the technique. Here the treatment is using the technique and the outcome is the benchmark score. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Model size, since labs that adopt the new technique tend to train larger models, and larger models tend to score higher.
statements.explanation: Size is linked to the choice of technique and to the score, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The model's rank on the public leaderboard, which is assigned from the benchmark scores.
statements.explanation: Rank is computed from the outcome, so it is an effect of the outcome and cannot confound.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The amount of training text, since well-resourced labs both adopt new techniques early and train on more text, which raises scores.
statements.explanation: The amount of text is tied to the technique (through the lab's resources) and raises scores, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The experience of the lab's engineering team, since experienced teams adopt new techniques sooner and also tune their models better.
statements.explanation: Team experience influences both the adoption of the technique and the quality of the result.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The number of citations the technique's paper receives, which grows when models using it score well.
statements.explanation: Citations are a downstream effect of results, not a cause of adoption or of scores.

questions.stem: An online shop lets customers opt in to a "personalised picks" panel. Customers who opted in spent more in the following month, and the shop asks whether the panel increases spending. Customers choose whether to opt in. Here the treatment is opting in to the panel and the outcome is spending in the following month. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number of items the customer views in the panel, which appears after a customer opts in and leads to purchases.
statements.explanation: It lies between opting in and spending (a mediator), so it is part of the effect, not a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: How much the customer spent in the month before the panel was offered, which predicts both who opts in and spending afterwards.
statements.explanation: Earlier spending is linked to both the choice to opt in and later spending, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether the customer leaves a product review, which is more likely both for customers who used the panel and for customers who bought a lot.
statements.explanation: Reviewing is an effect of both variables, not a cause of either; a variable caused by both is not a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: How often the customer visits the site, which makes opting in more likely and also leads to more purchases.
statements.explanation: Visit frequency influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether the customer holds a loyalty membership, which prompts customers to try new features and also brings discounts that raise spending.
statements.explanation: Membership influences both opting in and spending, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: Researchers find that cities with more protected bike lanes have lower adult obesity rates, and ask whether bike lanes reduce obesity. Each city decides for itself how many lanes to build. Here the treatment is the number of bike lanes and the outcome is the obesity rate. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: City wealth, since richer cities can afford more lanes and also tend to have lower obesity rates.
statements.explanation: Wealth influences both lane building and obesity, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Climate, since mild-weather cities are more likely to build lanes and also have residents who exercise outdoors more.
statements.explanation: Climate influences both lane building and activity levels, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The share of residents who cycle to work, which the lanes encourage and which burns calories.
statements.explanation: The lanes cause it and it then affects obesity, so it is on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The number of news stories about obesity published in the city, which rises when obesity rates are high.
statements.explanation: It is an effect of the outcome, not a cause of lane building or of obesity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A city health department that funds active-living programs, which leads the city both to build lanes and to run other programs that lower obesity.
statements.explanation: One source drives both lane building and other obesity-reducing programs, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: A job board finds that applicants who paid for a résumé-writing service were hired more often than applicants who did not, and asks whether the service raises the chance of being hired. Applicants decide whether to pay. Here the treatment is paying for the service and the outcome is being hired. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number of interviews the applicant gets, which a polished résumé produces and which leads to job offers.
statements.explanation: The service causes it and it then affects hiring, so it is on the path from treatment to outcome, not a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Years of work experience, which affect whether an applicant seeks out the service and also how attractive the applicant is to employers.
statements.explanation: Experience influences both the choice to pay and the chance of being hired, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether the applicant accepts the job offer, which follows being hired.
statements.explanation: It comes after the outcome, so it cannot be a cause of either variable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The applicant's spare income, which makes paying for the service possible and also pays for coaching and networking that help in hiring.
statements.explanation: Spare income influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The number of open positions at the employer, which changes applicants' chances of being hired but is unrelated to who pays for the service.
statements.explanation: It affects the outcome but is unrelated to the treatment, so it cannot confound the comparison.

questions.stem: A researcher finds that counties with more police officers per resident report more crime per resident, and asks whether employing more officers increases crime. Here the treatment is the number of officers per resident and the outcome is the crime rate. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number of arrests made last year, which depends both on how many officers there are and on how much crime occurs.
statements.explanation: Arrests are an effect of both the treatment and the outcome, not a cause of either; such a variable is not a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Public satisfaction with the police, measured in a survey after the officers were hired.
statements.explanation: It follows the treatment, so it cannot be a cause of it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: How much crime the county had in earlier years, which led its government to hire more officers and also predicts crime today.
statements.explanation: Past crime drives the hiring of officers and predicts present crime, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Officers' overtime hours, which rise when there are more crimes to respond to.
statements.explanation: Overtime is an effect of the outcome, not a cause of either variable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A state grant that pays for officers' salaries, which lets a county hire more officers and has no other path to crime than through those officers.
statements.explanation: It affects the treatment (how many officers a county can hire) and reaches the outcome only through that treatment, so it is not a confounder.

questions.stem: A bank offers customers an optional budgeting app. Customers who use it have lower rates of missed loan payments, and the bank asks whether the app reduces missed payments. Customers choose whether to use it. Here the treatment is using the app and the outcome is missing loan payments. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The customer's credit score, which affects who chooses to download the app and also how likely they are to miss payments.
statements.explanation: Credit score influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The number of low-balance alerts the customer receives, which the app sends and which prompt customers to keep payments up.
statements.explanation: The app causes the alerts and they then affect payments, so they are on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Stability of the customer's income, which affects both the habit of using budgeting tools and the ability to make payments.
statements.explanation: Income stability influences both variables, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether the account is later sent to collections, which follows missed payments.
statements.explanation: It is an effect of the outcome, not a cause of either variable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: How comfortable the customer is with money matters, which makes using a budgeting app more likely and also makes missed payments less likely.
statements.explanation: Financial confidence influences both whether the app is used and whether payments are missed.

questions.stem: A survey finds that adults who eat breakfast every day have a lower body-mass index (BMI) than adults who skip it, and a writer concludes that eating breakfast lowers BMI. Here the treatment is eating breakfast and the outcome is BMI. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Working night shifts, which makes skipping breakfast likelier and also disrupts sleep in ways that raise weight.
statements.explanation: Shift work influences both breakfast habits and weight, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Snacking later in the morning, which is less likely after breakfast and adds calories.
statements.explanation: Eating breakfast changes it and it then affects weight, so it is on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A genetic tendency to gain weight, which affects BMI but is unrelated to whether the person eats breakfast.
statements.explanation: It affects the outcome but is unrelated to the treatment, so it is not a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Buying clothes in a larger size, which follows from a higher BMI.
statements.explanation: A larger clothing size is an effect of the outcome, not a cause of either variable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: How health-conscious the person is, which makes eating breakfast more likely and also leads to lower weight.
statements.explanation: Health-consciousness influences both variables, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: A university finds that students who used an AI writing assistant on their essays received higher grades, and asks whether using the assistant raises grades. Students decide for themselves whether to use it. Here the treatment is using the assistant and the outcome is the essay grade. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The student's earlier writing skill, which affects whether the student chooses to use the assistant and also affects essay grades.
statements.explanation: Skill influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The hours the student has available for the course, which make trying the assistant more likely and also leave more time to polish essays.
statements.explanation: Available time influences both variables, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether the instructor flags the essay as AI-assisted, which is more likely both when the assistant was used and when the essay reads as polished.
statements.explanation: The flag is an effect of both the treatment and the quality of the work, not a cause of either; it is not a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The student's ambition to earn a high grade, which makes using any available help more likely and also leads to more careful work.
statements.explanation: Ambition influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The student's major, since some majors encourage the assistant and also grade writing more generously.
statements.explanation: Major influences both whether the assistant is used and how grades come out, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: A registry finds that women who attend regular mammogram screening die less often of breast cancer than women who do not, and asks whether screening reduces deaths from breast cancer. Women choose whether to attend. Here the treatment is attending screening and the outcome is dying of breast cancer. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The stage at which a cancer is found, which screening shifts earlier and which affects survival.
statements.explanation: Screening causes the change in stage and stage then affects survival, so it is on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: How health-conscious the woman is, which makes attending screening more likely and also leads to healthier habits and earlier care.
statements.explanation: Health-consciousness influences both attendance and outcomes, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether the woman has health insurance that covers screening, which makes attending more likely and also gives access to better treatment.
statements.explanation: Insurance influences both attendance and treatment quality, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Having a regular doctor who reminds patients about preventive care, which raises attendance and also improves follow-up after any diagnosis.
statements.explanation: A regular doctor influences both attendance and outcomes, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The number of biopsies performed, which rises after screening finds suspicious spots.
statements.explanation: Biopsies are an effect of the treatment, so they cannot be a cause of it.

questions.stem: Parents notice that children who play a musical instrument have higher maths scores, and ask whether learning an instrument raises maths scores. Here the treatment is playing an instrument and the outcome is the maths score. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Hours of daily practice, which are accumulated by children who play an instrument and which may build focus.
statements.explanation: Playing causes the practice hours and they may then affect maths scores, so they are on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Membership in the school orchestra, which follows from playing an instrument.
statements.explanation: It is an effect of the treatment, so it cannot be a cause of it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether the child enters a maths competition, which is more likely for children who already have high scores.
statements.explanation: It is an effect of the outcome, not a cause of either variable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Family income, which affects whether a family can afford lessons and instruments and also affects the resources that support learning maths.
statements.explanation: Income influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The parents' level of education, which affects whether children are steered toward music lessons and also how well they are helped with maths.
statements.explanation: Parental education influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: An insurer finds that cars with automatic emergency braking are involved in fewer crashes per mile, and asks whether the braking system prevents crashes.
