Drivers choose which car to buy. Here the treatment is having automatic emergency braking and the outcome is crashes per mile. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The driver's usual caution, since careful drivers are more likely to choose safety options and also less likely to crash.
statements.explanation: Caution influences both the choice of the option and crash risk, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The price of the car, since more expensive cars more often include the system and are more often bought by drivers who maintain them well.
statements.explanation: Price is tied to both having the system and crash risk, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The number of hard-braking events the car logs, which the system triggers and which avoid collisions.
statements.explanation: The system causes the events and they then affect crashes, so they are on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether the car is new, since new cars are more likely to have the system and less likely to have worn brakes or tyres.
statements.explanation: Car age influences both having the system and crash risk, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The insurance premium for the next year, which rises after a crash.
statements.explanation: The premium is an effect of the outcome, not a cause of either variable.

questions.stem: A district finds that schools which give every student a laptop have higher average test scores, and asks whether laptops raise scores. Each school decides whether to buy them. Here the treatment is a school providing laptops and the outcome is the school's average test score. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The school's funding per student, which pays for laptops and also pays for teachers, books and support.
statements.explanation: Funding influences both laptop provision and scores, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The poverty rate in the school's neighbourhood, which limits both the school's ability to buy laptops and students' test scores.
statements.explanation: Neighbourhood poverty influences both variables, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An active parent association, which raises money for laptops and also supports learning at home.
statements.explanation: The association influences both laptop provision and student performance, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The time students spend on educational apps at school, which laptops make possible and which raises scores.
statements.explanation: Laptops cause the app time and it then affects scores, so it is on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The share of students with internet access at home, which makes a laptop programme workable and also helps students study.
statements.explanation: Home internet access influences both the programme and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: A company finds that teams that run an AI code scanner on every commit have fewer security breaches, and asks whether the scanner prevents breaches. Teams choose whether to run it. Here the treatment is running the scanner and the outcome is the number of breaches. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number of scanner alerts per commit, which is produced when a team runs the scanner.
statements.explanation: Alerts are an effect of the treatment, so they cannot be a cause of it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: How mature the team's security practices are, which leads teams to adopt scanners and also reduces breaches.
statements.explanation: Security maturity influences both the adoption of the scanner and the number of breaches, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The vulnerabilities fixed after scanner alerts, which the scanner prompts and which prevent breaches.
statements.explanation: The scanner causes the fixes and the fixes then affect breaches, so they are on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Bug-bounty payouts, which rise when more breaches occur.
statements.explanation: Payouts are an effect of the outcome, not a cause of either variable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether the team's code is hosted on the platform that offers the scanner as a one-click setting, which makes adoption easier and has no other path to breaches than through the scanner.
statements.explanation: It affects the treatment and reaches the outcome only through that treatment, so it is not a confounder.

questions.stem: A fitness company finds that customers who wear its step-tracking watch lose more weight over a year than customers who do not, and asks whether wearing the watch causes weight loss. Customers choose whether to buy the watch. Here the treatment is wearing the watch and the outcome is weight loss over the year. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The number of daily step goals met, which the watch's reminders increase and which burns calories.
statements.explanation: The watch causes the goals to be met and meeting them then affects weight, so it is on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: How strongly the customer wants to lose weight, which makes buying a tracker more likely and also leads to dieting.
statements.explanation: Motivation influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The customer's spare income, which pays for the watch and also for gym membership and healthier food.
statements.explanation: Spare income influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Existing exercise habits, such as running regularly, which make buying a tracker more likely and also produce weight loss.
statements.explanation: Prior habits influence both buying the watch and weight change, so they are confounders.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Membership in a running club, which leads people to buy trackers and also keeps them active.
statements.explanation: Club membership influences both variables, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: A company finds that teams using a code-review bot ship fewer bugs per release, and asks whether the bot reduces bugs. Teams choose whether to use it. Here the treatment is using the bot and the outcome is the number of bugs shipped per release. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Review comments resolved before merging, which the bot generates and which remove bugs.
statements.explanation: The bot causes the comments and resolving them then affects bugs, so they are on the path from treatment to outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The experience of the team's developers, which makes adopting new tools likelier and also leads to fewer bugs.
statements.explanation: Experience influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: C
statements.text: How much management values code quality, which leads teams to adopt tooling and also to test more.
statements.explanation: A quality-minded culture influences both adoption and the number of bugs, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Customer support tickets about bugs, which are caused by the bugs that ship.
statements.explanation: Tickets are an effect of the outcome, not a cause of either variable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: How complex the project is, since simpler projects are easier to automate with a bot and also easier to keep free of bugs.
statements.explanation: Complexity influences both the use of the bot and the number of bugs, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: Runners who wore carbon-plated shoes finished a race faster on average than runners in ordinary shoes, and a magazine asks whether the shoes make runners faster. Runners chose their own shoes. Here the treatment is wearing carbon-plated shoes and the outcome is the finishing time. Check each variable that is a confounder in this situation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Weekly training mileage, since serious runners more often buy racing shoes and also train harder.
statements.explanation: Training volume influences both shoe choice and finishing time, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Race-day weather, which changes finishing times but is the same for runners in both kinds of shoes.
statements.explanation: It affects the outcome but is unrelated to the treatment, so it cannot confound the comparison.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Years of running experience, which shape shoe choices and also pace.
statements.explanation: Experience influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Membership in a competitive club, which leads runners to racing shoes and to coaching that makes them faster.
statements.explanation: Club membership influences both variables, so it is a confounder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The runner's budget, which makes buying expensive shoes possible and also pays for coaching and race entries.
statements.explanation: Budget influences both the treatment and the outcome, so it is a confounder.

questions.stem: A health researcher lists studies that have been done on the effect of a treatment. Check each study that uses observational data.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Researchers pull a hospital's past records and compare patients who were given an antibiotic by their doctors with patients who were not.
statements.explanation: Doctors and circumstances, not the researchers, decided who got the antibiotic; the researchers only observed what happened, so the data are observational.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A survey asks adults whether they take a daily vitamin and whether they had a fracture this year.
statements.explanation: The researchers did not assign the vitamin; people chose for themselves, so the data are observational.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An analyst compares test scores of students in schools that chose to adopt a new curriculum with schools that did not.
statements.explanation: The schools chose the treatment; nobody assigned it for the purpose of the study, so the data are observational.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A website randomly shows half of its visitors a new layout and then measures purchases.
statements.explanation: The website assigns the layout by chance. Assigning the treatment at random is an experiment, not observation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A bank compares repayment of customers who chose to use its mobile app with customers who did not.
statements.explanation: Customers chose whether to use the app, so the treatment was not assigned by the investigator.

questions.stem: A policy group collects the following studies of a workplace or school program. Check each description that is observational data.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Researchers draw names from a hat to decide which of 200 employees will be offered a four-day week, then track their output.
statements.explanation: The researchers assign the treatment by chance, so this is an experiment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A transport agency compares commute times of people who chose to switch to a new train line with those of people who did not.
statements.explanation: Commuters chose the treatment, so the data are observational.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An online course randomly gives half of new learners a reminder email and measures completion.
statements.explanation: The course assigns the email by chance, so this is an experiment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A bank analyses past loan records to compare repayment for customers whom loan officers did or did not offer a payment plan.
statements.explanation: Loan officers, not the analysts, decided who was offered the plan, and the analysis looks back at records, so the data are observational.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Researchers use a random number generator to decide which schools receive tutoring grants, then compare scores.
statements.explanation: The researchers assign the grants by chance, so this is an experiment.

questions.stem: A health agency has the following sources. Check each source that provides observational data about whether a treatment works.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A trial in which a computer randomly assigns each patient to a drug or a placebo.
statements.explanation: Random assignment by the investigators makes this experimental data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Insurance claims that show which patients filled a prescription and who was later hospitalised.
statements.explanation: Patients and doctors decided who filled the prescription; the claims only record it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A national survey asking people whether they smoke and whether they have lung disease.
statements.explanation: Nobody assigned smoking; people chose it, so the data are observational.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Electronic health records of patients whose doctors chose which blood-pressure drug to prescribe.
statements.explanation: The doctors chose the treatment, not an investigator, so the data are observational.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fitness-tracker records of users who decided on their own to join a walking challenge.
statements.explanation: Users chose the treatment, so the data are observational.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about observational data.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In observational data the investigator did not assign the treatment; people or circumstances determined who received it.
statements.explanation: That is what makes data observational.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Any dataset taken from existing records is observational, even if the treatment in those records was assigned by chance.
statements.explanation: What matters is how the treatment was assigned. Records of a trial in which the treatment was assigned by chance are experimental data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A dataset with millions of rows can still be observational.
statements.explanation: Many rows do not change who chose the treatment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Observational data records the treatment but not the outcome.
statements.explanation: Observational data usually records both; what is missing is the investigator's assignment of the treatment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether data is observational depends on how the treatment came about, not on how carefully the variables were measured.
statements.explanation: Careful measurement does not turn chosen treatments into assigned ones.

questions.stem: A trial randomly assigns 2,000 patients to take a new drug or a placebo and compares recovery. Check each statement that is true about what randomization does in this trial.

statements.label: A
statements.text: On average, factors such as age and prior health end up similar in the two groups.
statements.explanation: Chance assignment spreads such factors across the groups in the same way on average.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In a trial of ten patients, it ensures that the two groups match closely on age.
statements.explanation: With very few patients, chance can leave the groups quite different; the balance holds on average and improves with size.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It breaks the link between a patient's prior health and whether the patient receives the drug, so prior health is not a confounder here.
statements.explanation: A confounder must affect the treatment as well as the outcome; chance assignment means prior health no longer affects who gets the drug.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It makes the recovery measurements more accurate.
statements.explanation: Randomization concerns who gets the treatment, not how well the outcome is measured.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It lets researchers estimate the drug's effect without having measured every factor that affects recovery.
statements.explanation: Because assignment is by chance, unmeasured factors are not tied to the treatment either.

questions.stem: A data scientist explains why most of her work uses observational data instead of randomized trials. Check each statement that is a reason she could give.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Randomly assigning a harmful exposure, such as smoking, to people would be unethical.
statements.explanation: Some treatments cannot be assigned for ethical reasons, so they can only be observed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Many questions concern events that have already happened, so who received the treatment cannot be reassigned.
statements.explanation: Past events can be studied only as they happened.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Randomized trials usually give less reliable causal answers than observational data.
statements.explanation: Randomization is what makes a trial a strong way to answer causal questions; its limits are cost, ethics and practicality.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Running a randomized trial can be slow and expensive.
statements.explanation: Cost and time often make a trial impractical.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Records of what people chose already exist in many settings and can be studied without running a new trial.
statements.explanation: Existing records are an available source of observational data.

questions.stem: A career site records whether 1,000 applicants had a personal website and whether they were interviewed. Experience is grouped as little, moderate or a lot, and more experience raises the chance of an interview. Among the 500 applicants with a website, 10% have little experience, 30% moderate and 60% a lot; among the 500 without a website, 60% have little, 30% moderate and 10% a lot. Interview rates for applicants with and without a website are: little experience 20% and 10%; moderate 40% and 30%; a lot 70% and 60%. Overall, 56% of applicants with a website and 21% of those without were interviewed. The treatment is having a website and the outcome is being interviewed. Check each statement that follows from these numbers.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The overall difference of 35 points shows that a website raises the chance of an interview by 35 points.
statements.explanation: Applicants with websites are more experienced, and experience raises the chance of an interview, so the overall difference mixes the website's effect with the effect of experience.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Within each experience group, having a website goes with an interview rate 10 points higher.
statements.explanation: The rates are 20 against 10, 40 against 30, and 70 against 60: a 10-point difference in every group.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because experience raises the chance of an interview, the website has no effect.
statements.explanation: Within each group, where experience is held about the same, applicants with websites still do better by 10 points.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The overall difference of 35 points overstates the website's effect, because website owners tend to be more experienced.
statements.explanation: Experience affects both whether someone has a website and whether they are interviewed, so it is a confounder and inflates the overall difference.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Averaging the three within-group differences gives an effect of about 10 points.
statements.explanation: Each group shows 10 points, so any average of the three is about 10 points.

questions.stem: In records of 10,000 adults, people in poor health are more likely to get a flu shot and also more likely to have a serious case of flu. The treatment is getting the flu shot and the outcome is having a serious case of flu. Check each comparison that compares like with like on health status.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing serious-flu rates of vaccinated and unvaccinated people who are all in poor health.
statements.explanation: Everyone compared has the same health status, so health cannot explain the difference.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Comparing serious-flu rates of all vaccinated people with all unvaccinated people, ignoring health.
statements.explanation: Ignoring health mixes the shot's effect with the effect of health status.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Doing the within-group comparison separately for people in poor health and for people in good health, then combining the two group results by weighting each group by its size.
statements.explanation: Comparing within each health group and then averaging across groups is how the effect is controlled for health and combined.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Comparing serious-flu rates of vaccinated and unvaccinated people who are all in good health.
statements.explanation: Again everyone compared has the same health status, so the comparison controls for it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Comparing vaccinated people in poor health with unvaccinated people in good health.
statements.explanation: The two groups differ in health status as well as in the shot, so health is not controlled for.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about controlling for a variable, which is also called adjusting for it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It means deleting that variable's column from the dataset.
statements.explanation: Controlling uses the variable to form comparison groups; deleting it would leave the confounding in place.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It means comparing treated and untreated people who have the same value of that variable.
statements.explanation: Comparing within groups of similar people is how the variable is held constant.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Controlling for" and "adjusting for" are two names for the same thing.
statements.explanation: They are used interchangeably.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It requires that the variable was measured.
statements.explanation: Without a measurement there is no way to group people by it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It requires the investigator to assign the treatment at random.
statements.explanation: Random assignment is a different way to handle confounders; controlling is done on the data after the fact.

questions.stem: Imagine a hidden fair coin U flipped for each person. Think of U as qualification, X as a referral and Y as an interview. In both of two worlds, a person's referral X equals the coin. In world 1, whether the person is interviewed (Y) follows the referral X. In world 2, Y follows the coin U directly and ignores the referral. In the data from either world, X and Y agree for every person, half zeros and half ones. Check each step that would let us tell the two worlds apart.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Collecting ten times as many rows from each world.
statements.explanation: More rows from either world show the same pattern, so they cannot separate the worlds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Measuring the coin value for each person without changing anything.
statements.explanation: X already equals the coin, so measuring it adds no new information.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Forcing everyone to receive a referral and then recording who is interviewed.
statements.explanation: In world 1 everyone would be interviewed; in world 2 only those whose coin is 1 would be. Changing the treatment reveals how the outcome is generated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Checking whether X and Y agree in the data.
statements.explanation: They agree for every person in both worlds.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Recording the referral status of more people.
statements.explanation: Referral status matches the coin in both worlds, so more of it looks the same in both.

questions.stem: A recruiter draws arrows between experience, having a website, and getting an interview to describe how these variables are related. Check each statement that is true about where the arrows come from.

statements.label: A
statements.text: They can be read directly off a table of rows by any statistical program.
statements.explanation: The same table can be produced by different arrow structures.

statements.label: B
statements.text: They come from assumptions about how the variables are generated, such as that experience comes before making a website.
statements.explanation: The arrows are assumptions about the setting, not findings from the table.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Once enough rows are collected, a single set of arrows is consistent with the data.
statements.explanation: More rows of the same kind do not rule out other arrow structures.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Different assumptions about the arrows can fit the same table equally well.
statements.explanation: That is why knowledge about how the data were generated is needed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: They are estimated from the rows by the same method that estimates an average interview rate.
statements.explanation: Averages are computed from rows, but the arrows are assumptions about how the variables are generated, which the rows alone do not contain.

questions.stem: Imagine a hidden fair coin U flipped for each person. Think of U as qualification, X as a referral and Y as an interview. In both of two worlds, a person's referral X equals the coin. In world 1, whether the person is interviewed (Y) follows the referral X. In world 2, Y follows the coin U directly and ignores the referral. Check each statement that is true about the data from the two worlds.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the data from both worlds, X and Y agree for every person.
statements.explanation: In world 1 Y equals X; in world 2 Y equals U, and X equals U, so Y equals X in both.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The data alone show that the referral caused the interview.
statements.explanation: World 2 produces the same data, and there the referral plays no role.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The data alone show that qualification caused the interview.
statements.explanation: World 1 produces the same data, and there qualification affects the interview only through the referral.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Both worlds produce the same pattern: half zeros and half ones, matching in every row.
statements.explanation: The coin is fair and X, Y and U coincide, so the pattern is identical.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Enough rows would eventually make the data from the two worlds look different.
statements.explanation: The worlds give the same data however many rows are collected.

questions.stem: Suppose that, after controlling for experience, 32% of applicants without a website and 70% of applicants with one were interviewed, and the difference is the website's effect. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The website raised the chance of an interview by 38 percentage points.
statements.explanation: 70 minus 32 is 38 percentage points.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Every applicant who made a website was interviewed.
statements.explanation: The chance rose to 70%, not 100%; the website did not guarantee an interview.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An applicant without a website had no chance of an interview.
statements.explanation: Applicants without a website were interviewed at a rate of 32%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The effect is the number of interviews divided by the number of websites.
statements.explanation: The effect is the change in the chance of an interview, not a count of interviews per website.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The effect describes how much the chance changed, not whether any single applicant was interviewed.
statements.explanation: The effect is a degree of change in the probability of the outcome.

questions.stem: Two career sites each report the change in interview rate from having a personal website, after controlling for experience. Site A: 32% without a website, 70% with. Site B: 5% without, 12% with. Assume each difference is the website's effect. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Site B's website raised the interview chance by more percentage points than site A's.
statements.explanation: Site B's change is 7 points and site A's is 38 points.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Site A's website raised the interview chance by more percentage points than site B's.
statements.explanation: 38 points against 7 points.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Site A's relative increase (70% compared with 32%) is larger than site B's (12% compared with 5%).
statements.explanation: 70 divided by 32 is about 2.2, and 12 divided by 5 is 2.4, so site B's relative increase is larger.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because site B's chances are low, its website had no effect.
statements.explanation: The chance rose from 5% to 12%, which is an effect even though both numbers are low.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The effect of site B's website cannot be expressed as a difference in percentage points.
statements.explanation: It can: 12 minus 5 is 7 percentage points.

questions.stem: A recruiter notices that applicants with a personal website get more interviews, and wonders whether the website or the applicant's experience is responsible. Check each step that would help separate the two.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Collecting ten times as many applicants in the same way.
statements.explanation: More of the same observational data keeps the website and experience tangled together.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Randomly assigning websites to applicants and comparing interview rates.
statements.explanation: Chance assignment breaks the link between experience and having a website.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Computing the correlation between having a website and being interviewed more precisely.
statements.explanation: A more precise association does not say whether experience or the website is responsible.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking the applicants which of the two they think mattered.
statements.explanation: Opinions are not a way of separating the effects in the data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Comparing applicants with and without websites within groups of similar experience.
statements.explanation: Holding experience about the same controls for it.

questions.source: Names of the group fairness criteria
questions.stem: A reviewer needs the exact name for each group fairness criterion of a binary classifier. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal precision of favorable decisions across groups is equalized odds.
statements.explanation: Equal precision is predictive parity; equalized odds concerns true-positive and false-positive rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Equal true-positive and equal false-positive rates across groups is equalized odds.
statements.explanation: Equalized odds is parity of both error-rate quantities conditional on the true outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equal true-positive rates across groups is equal opportunity.
statements.explanation: Equal opportunity is parity of the rate at which truly qualified people receive the favorable decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Statistical parity is another name for demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Both names describe equal selection rates across groups.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal shares of favorable decisions across groups, whatever the true outcomes, is demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Demographic parity compares selection rates and ignores the true outcome.

questions.stem: An analyst is sorting out common rate names for a classifier that gives a favorable decision. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Positive predictive value is the share of favorable decisions that go to people who truly qualify.
statements.explanation: Positive predictive value is a synonym of precision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Specificity names the same quantity as the true-positive rate.
statements.explanation: Specificity is the true-negative rate, one minus the false-positive rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Precision is another name for the false-positive rate.
statements.explanation: Precision is the share of favorable decisions that are correct; the false-positive rate is a different quantity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: True-positive rate is also called recall or sensitivity.
statements.explanation: Each of these names the share of truly qualified people who receive the favorable decision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The false-positive rate is computed among people who received the favorable decision.
statements.explanation: It is computed among people who truly do not qualify.

questions.stem: A reviewer lists what each fairness quantity conditions on. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A selection rate conditions on group membership and not on the true outcome.
statements.explanation: It is the share of a group's members receiving the favorable decision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Precision conditions on people who received the favorable decision.
statements.explanation: It asks what share of favorable decisions are correct.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A true-positive rate conditions on people who truly qualify.
statements.explanation: It is measured within the set of true positives plus false negatives.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A false-positive rate conditions on people who received the favorable decision.
statements.explanation: It conditions on the true outcome being negative.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Demographic parity conditions on the true outcome.
statements.explanation: It compares decisions across groups without reference to the true outcome.

questions.source: Imprecise word in a fairness prompt
questions.stem: An analyst tells an AI assistant, "Check that the model is fair by making sure accuracy is the same for men and women." Check each statement that is true. Each statement is worth 1 point (5 points total). about this prompt.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accuracy parity is another name for predictive parity.
statements.explanation: Predictive parity equalizes precision, not overall accuracy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The prompt asks for accuracy parity, a different criterion from equalized odds.
statements.explanation: Accuracy parity equalizes the share of correct decisions, while equalized odds equalizes two error rates.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Replacing "accuracy" with "demographic parity" would keep the same meaning.
statements.explanation: Demographic parity compares selection rates and does not use correctness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Equal accuracy shows that the true-positive rates match across the two groups.
statements.explanation: Accuracy blends both kinds of correct decision and can match while true-positive rates differ.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal accuracy can hide false positives in one group and false negatives in the other.
statements.explanation: Two groups can have the same count of errors of different types.

questions.source: Disparate impact ratio and four-fifths rule
questions.stem: A reviewer computes the ratio of the lower group's selection rate to the higher group's selection rate and compares it with 0.8, a screening convention often called the four-fifths rule. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The quantity is called the disparate impact ratio.
statements.explanation: It is the ratio of selection rates between groups.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The ratio compares the true-positive rates of the two groups.
statements.explanation: It uses selection rates and ignores who truly qualified.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ratio is built from the same quantities as demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Both use group selection rates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Which outcome is called favorable changes the value of the ratio.
statements.explanation: The ratio of favorable rates differs from the ratio of adverse rates for the same data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A ratio below 0.8 is a legal finding of discrimination.
statements.explanation: It is a screening heuristic that prompts further review.

questions.stem: A bank flags transactions for manual review, so being flagged is the adverse outcome. An analyst compares group flag rates and then compares group not-flagged rates. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A difference in selection rates is a ratio.
statements.explanation: A difference is a subtraction; a ratio is a division.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The disparate impact ratio and the difference in selection rates are two names for one quantity.
statements.explanation: One is a ratio and the other is a difference, and they can lead to different verdicts.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The difference in percentage points is the same whether computed on flag rates or on not-flagged rates.
statements.explanation: A difference in complementary rates has the same size.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The four-fifths convention is defined on the rate of the adverse outcome.
statements.explanation: It is defined on the rate of the favorable outcome.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The ratio of flag rates and the ratio of not-flagged rates generally differ for the same data.
statements.explanation: The two rates are complements, so their ratios are not equal.

questions.stem: A risk score between 0 and 1 is checked separately for each group. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Calibration is the same property as discrimination, the ability to separate positives from negatives.
statements.explanation: Calibration is about whether scores match outcome frequencies; discrimination is about ranking.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Calibration within groups means that among people given score s, about a fraction s have the positive outcome, in each group.
statements.explanation: This is the definition of calibration of a probability score.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Calibration is the share of correct decisions at a chosen cutoff.
statements.explanation: That share is accuracy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Predictive parity concerns precision at a cutoff, while calibration concerns outcome rates at each score value.
statements.explanation: The two criteria use different conditioning events.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A score can be well calibrated and weak at discrimination.
statements.explanation: Giving every person the group's base rate is calibrated but separates no one.

questions.stem: A team reports the expected calibration error (ECE) of a probability score. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: ECE is the weighted average gap between score and observed positive rate across score bins.
statements.explanation: Each bin's gap is weighted by the share of people in the bin.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A low ECE means the true-positive rate is high.
statements.explanation: ECE says nothing about the true-positive rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A single pooled ECE for both groups is a calibration check by group.
statements.explanation: Pooling can hide that one group is more miscalibrated than the other.

statements.label: D
statements.text: ECE can be computed without outcome labels.
statements.explanation: The observed positive rate in each bin needs the true outcomes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: ECE measures the difference in true-positive rates between two groups.
statements.explanation: It measures score-versus-outcome agreement, not a between-group difference in error rates.

questions.stem: In a calibration check, people in group B who were given a score of 0.2 turn out to have a positive-outcome rate of 0.30. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Recalibrating the score separately within each group is a way to address it.
statements.explanation: Group-wise recalibration maps scores to observed outcome frequencies in that group.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The score overstates the risk of these people.
statements.explanation: Overstating would mean the observed rate is below the score.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The score understates the risk of these people.
statements.explanation: The observed rate is above the stated score.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Detecting it needs outcome labels recorded by group.
statements.explanation: The observed rate by group is computed from true outcomes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This is a calibration failure for group B at that score value.
statements.explanation: Calibration requires the observed rate to match the score.

questions.stem: A risk model flags people at or above a cutoff. Analysts compare two criteria: predictive parity at the cutoff and calibration within groups. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Calibration within groups requires the observed positive rate to match the score at each score value in each group.
statements.explanation: This is the definition of group-wise calibration.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Predictive parity compares the precision of flagged people across groups.
statements.explanation: Precision of favorable decisions is the compared quantity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Calibration within groups at each score value implies equal precision across groups at a cutoff.
statements.explanation: Precision depends on each group's mix of scores, which can differ.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Predictive parity is defined using the people who were not flagged.
statements.explanation: It uses the people who were flagged.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Predictive parity at a cutoff guarantees calibration within groups.
statements.explanation: Equal overall precision can coexist with scores that match outcomes poorly in each group.

questions.stem: Two groups have different base rates and a classifier that is imperfect. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Collecting more labeled data resolves the incompatibility.
statements.explanation: More data estimates the rates more precisely but does not change the arithmetic.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It is a defect of the learning algorithm that a more flexible model removes.
statements.explanation: It concerns population rates, so a better learner does not remove it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This incompatibility is a result about the criteria themselves, often called an impossibility result.
statements.explanation: It follows from Bayes' rule applied to population rates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The incompatibility arises when the model uses group membership as an input, and disappears if the attribute is dropped.
statements.explanation: It holds for models that never see group membership.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal precision together with equal true-positive and false-positive rates generally fails to hold.
statements.explanation: With different base rates, precision moves with the base rate when the error rates are equal.

questions.stem: Two groups have different base rates. A reviewer compares a perfect classifier with a classifier that gives the favorable decision to each person. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The perfect classifier satisfies demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Its selection rates equal the unequal base rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Giving the favorable decision to everyone satisfies demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Both groups then have selection rate 1.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Giving the favorable decision to everyone is a useful resolution of the conflict because it meets several criteria.
statements.explanation: It carries no information about individuals and so has no predictive value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When base rates are equal, the conflict between equal precision and equal error rates goes away.
statements.explanation: Equal error rates and equal base rates give equal precision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The perfect classifier satisfies equalized odds and predictive parity.
statements.explanation: It has true-positive rate 1, false-positive rate 0 and precision 1 in each group.

questions.stem: Two groups have different base rates and the recorded labels are correct. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A perfect classifier violates demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Its selection rates equal the different base rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Maximizing overall accuracy treats a false positive and a false negative as equally costly.
statements.explanation: Accuracy counts both kinds of error the same.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A perfect classifier satisfies equalized odds.
statements.explanation: It has the same true-positive and false-positive rates in both groups.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Forcing equal selection rates moves some decisions away from the true labels.
statements.explanation: That adds misclassifications relative to the recorded outcomes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A trade-off between demographic parity and accuracy appears when base rates are equal.
statements.explanation: With equal base rates and correct labels, a perfect classifier already meets parity.

questions.stem: A product manager asks an analyst to show the trade-off between a fairness metric and accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Plotting a fairness gap against accuracy at several cutoffs displays a trade-off frontier.
statements.explanation: Each cutoff gives a point, and the set of points shows what is gained and lost.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A Pareto-optimal option is one where improving one objective means worsening another.
statements.explanation: No option dominates it on both objectives.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising the cutoff increases both the true-positive rate and the false-positive rate.
statements.explanation: A higher cutoff lowers both rates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A cutoff, also called a threshold, is a parameter of the training data.
statements.explanation: A cutoff is applied to the model's scores to turn them into decisions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Choosing the most accurate model is a neutral choice that makes no decision about who bears errors.
statements.explanation: Accuracy weights all errors equally and lets error rates fall unevenly across groups.

questions.stem: A lender compares a single cutoff for all applicants with a separate cutoff for each group. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Group-specific cutoffs are an in-processing method.
statements.explanation: They adjust decisions after training, so they are post-processing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Group-specific cutoffs chosen to equalize true-positive rates achieve demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Equalizing true-positive rates is equal opportunity, a different criterion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Group-specific cutoffs require the group attribute at decision time.
statements.explanation: The cutoff to apply depends on the person's group.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A single cutoff for everyone does not use the group attribute when deciding.
statements.explanation: The same rule is applied to each person's score.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With group-specific cutoffs, two people with the same score can receive different decisions, an individual fairness objection.
statements.explanation: Treating equal scores differently conflicts with treating similar people alike.

questions.stem: Practitioners sort bias-reduction methods into pre-processing, in-processing and post-processing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adjusting the cutoff of a frozen model is post-processing.
statements.explanation: It acts on the outputs after training.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Resampling the training data to balance groups is pre-processing.
statements.explanation: It changes the data before the model is trained.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reweighting training examples to balance group and label combinations is pre-processing.
statements.explanation: It changes the data before training.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding a fairness penalty term to the training loss is post-processing.
statements.explanation: A penalty in the loss alters training, which is in-processing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adversarial debiasing, where a second network tries to predict the group from the model's representation, is in-processing.
statements.explanation: It changes the training objective.

questions.stem: A company says its hiring model is fair because the gender field was removed from its inputs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A proxy is a feature correlated with the protected attribute that carries some of its information.
statements.explanation: Postal code standing in for ethnicity is a common example.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Fairness through unawareness guarantees equal error rates across groups.
statements.explanation: Removing an input says nothing about error rates.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Fairness through unawareness means leaving the protected attribute out of the model's inputs.
statements.explanation: That is the definition of the approach.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Features such as career gaps or postal code can let a model reconstruct the removed attribute.
statements.explanation: Correlated features act as proxies.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Auditing by group needs the protected attribute in the evaluation data even when the model does not use it.
statements.explanation: Group rates cannot be computed without group labels.

questions.stem: A legal and ethical review distinguishes kinds of unequal treatment by an algorithm. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Disparate treatment concerns decisions that differ by protected attribute.
statements.explanation: Explicit use of the attribute in deciding is the core case.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Disparate impact concerns a neutral-looking practice with disproportionate effects on a group.
statements.explanation: The practice is facially neutral but burdens one group more.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Disparate impact requires evidence that the designer intended to discriminate.
statements.explanation: It concerns effects, so intent is not required.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Group-specific cutoffs can raise disparate-treatment concerns in some jurisdictions.
statements.explanation: Decision rules that depend on group membership can be restricted.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Disparate treatment and disparate impact are two names for the same doctrine.
statements.explanation: They are distinct doctrines.

questions.stem: A practice with disparate impact is reviewed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fairness metric is a legal standard.
statements.explanation: A metric is a measurement; legal standards come from law.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A less discriminatory alternative is a practice that increases the disparity.
statements.explanation: It is a practice that serves the same goal with a smaller disparity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Satisfying equalized odds establishes legal compliance.
statements.explanation: Compliance depends on the applicable law and facts, not on one metric.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A selection-rate ratio of 0.9 is the usual trigger for review.
statements.explanation: The usual screening convention uses 0.8.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Business necessity is the kind of justification offered for a practice with disparate impact.
statements.explanation: The practice may be defended as needed for a legitimate goal.

questions.source: Individual fairness and the similarity metric
questions.stem: An auditor reviews a model against the principle that similar individuals should be treated similarly. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It can be evaluated from per-group confusion matrices alone.
statements.explanation: Confusion matrices average over individuals and lose pairwise comparisons.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The Lipschitz form bounds the difference in two people's outcomes by a distance between the people.
statements.explanation: Similar people must receive similar outcome distributions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This principle is called individual fairness.
statements.explanation: It compares how individuals are treated rather than group averages.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Applying it requires a similarity metric chosen for the task.
statements.explanation: Someone must say which differences between people are relevant.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Individual fairness implies demographic parity.
statements.explanation: Similar treatment of similar people can coexist with different group selection rates.

questions.stem: A reviewer contrasts group fairness with individual fairness. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A model that treats similar people alike under a chosen metric can still show different group selection rates.
statements.explanation: The groups may differ on features the metric counts as relevant.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Equal opportunity is an individual fairness criterion.
statements.explanation: Equal opportunity compares true-positive rates across groups.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Group fairness compares individuals pair by pair, while individual fairness compares group averages.
statements.explanation: The two descriptions are swapped.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A model can satisfy demographic parity and still treat two near-identical people very differently.
statements.explanation: Parity limits group rates, not which individuals receive the favorable decision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The choice of similarity metric is a technical detail without a value judgment.
statements.explanation: Deciding which differences are relevant is a substantive judgment.

questions.stem: In a causal model of a loan decision, a protected attribute A affects an education credential E, which is an input to a predictor. Unobserved background factors U also affect E. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The causal graph tells which paths from A to the prediction are acceptable.
statements.explanation: The graph shows which paths exist; accepting a path is a value judgment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A predictor whose inputs are variables that are not downstream of A is counterfactually fair in this model.
statements.explanation: Its inputs do not change when A is changed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Counterfactual fairness asks whether an individual's prediction would be the same had the attribute taken a different value, with the individual's background factors held fixed.
statements.explanation: It is an individual-level causal question.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Counterfactual fairness is another name for equalized odds.
statements.explanation: Equalized odds is about error rates by group, not a causal question.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Judging counterfactual fairness requires assumptions about the causal structure.
statements.explanation: Observed data alone cannot distinguish structures that imply different counterfactuals.

questions.stem: In a causal graph, a protected attribute A affects a credential E, which feeds a predictor, and unobserved background factors U affect E. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Path-specific fairness allows some paths from the attribute to the prediction and blocks others.
statements.explanation: It treats paths differently according to a judgment about which are acceptable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A counterfactual evaluation holds the background factors U fixed.
statements.explanation: The same individual is considered under a different attribute value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A counterfactual is a quantity observed directly in the data.
statements.explanation: It concerns a hypothetical alternative that is not observed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: E is a confounder of A and the prediction.
statements.explanation: A confounder is a common cause of two variables, which E is not here.

statements.label: E
statements.text: E is a mediator on the path from A to the prediction.
statements.explanation: A mediator lies on a path between a cause and an outcome.

questions.stem: A system gives a benefit to each person, and an analyst computes a generalized entropy index of the benefits, decomposed by group. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A large within-group component with a zero between-group component means individuals receive equal benefits.
statements.explanation: It means benefits are unequal inside groups even though group means match.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When two groups have equal mean benefits, the between-group component is positive.
statements.explanation: Equal means give a between-group component of zero.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The index splits into a between-group component and a within-group component.
statements.explanation: The decomposition separates group-mean inequality from inequality inside groups.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The generalized entropy index measures inequality in how benefits are distributed across individuals.
statements.explanation: Larger values mean more inequality.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The between-group component measures inequality between the groups' mean benefits.
statements.explanation: It is computed after replacing each person's benefit by the group mean.

questions.stem: An audit scores a model on whether it predicts re-arrest. One neighborhood is patrolled much more heavily than another. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Selection bias and measurement bias are two names for the same problem.
statements.explanation: Selection bias concerns who is included in the data; measurement bias concerns how outcomes are recorded.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using group-specific cutoffs removes label bias.
statements.explanation: Cutoffs change decisions, not how the label relates to the behavior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A proxy label is a recorded outcome standing in for the quantity of interest.
statements.explanation: Arrest records stand in for behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A recorded outcome that measures something other than the target quantity, such as arrests instead of offending, is a measurement bias problem.
statements.explanation: The label differs systematically from the quantity of interest.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal error rates against recorded arrests establish equal error rates against actual offending.
statements.explanation: The recorded label may encode enforcement differences.

questions.stem: A lender's model decides which applicants to approve, and repayment is recorded for approved applicants. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Selective labels make error rates for the full applicant population uncertain.
statements.explanation: Rates for declined applicants must be estimated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reject inference is the attempt to estimate outcomes for declined applicants.
statements.explanation: The term names methods for filling in missing outcomes of rejected cases.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Selective labels means the outcome is recorded for people who received the favorable decision and is missing for the rest.
statements.explanation: Declined applicants have no repayment record.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Selective labels is another name for overfitting.
statements.explanation: Overfitting concerns a model fitted too closely to training data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Repayment outcomes are observed for declined applicants as well as approved ones.
statements.explanation: Declined applicants did not receive a loan, so no repayment is observed.

questions.stem: An audit reports true-positive rates of 0.75 (400 qualified people) in one group and 0.60 (40 qualified people) in another. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 95% confidence interval for the smaller group's rate is wider than the larger group's.
statements.explanation: Interval width shrinks as the sample grows.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Low statistical power means a real gap can go undetected.
statements.explanation: Small samples give tests little ability to detect real differences.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The multiple comparisons problem is that testing many subgroups makes a chance significant gap less likely.
statements.explanation: Testing many subgroups makes a chance significant gap more likely.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A non-significant difference shows that the two groups have equal rates.
statements.explanation: Failing to detect a gap is not evidence of equality.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A p-value is the probability that the two groups have equal rates.
statements.explanation: A p-value is the probability of data this extreme if the rates were equal.

questions.stem: A reviewer checks selection rates by gender, by region and by gender-by-region combination. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Passing the check on each attribute separately implies passing on the combinations.
statements.explanation: Disparities can cancel in the margins.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Single-attribute selection rates can look equal while some combination cells differ.
statements.explanation: Opposite gaps in different cells can offset each other in the margins.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Checking combinations multiplies the number of subgroups, so samples per cell shrink and intervals widen.
statements.explanation: Each added attribute splits the sample further.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Intersectional analysis examines combinations of attributes such as gender and region together.
statements.explanation: Disparities can exist in combinations.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A gender-by-region cell is an example of an intersectional subgroup.
statements.explanation: It is defined by more than one attribute.

questions.source: Label shift, covariate shift and concept drift
questions.stem: A classifier keeps the same true-positive and false-positive rates in each group after deployment, but one group's base rate rises. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Concept drift is a change in the input distribution alone.
statements.explanation: Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Label shift changes the true-positive and false-positive rates by definition.
statements.explanation: Those rates are conditional on the class and stay the same.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Precision is stable under a change in base rate.
statements.explanation: Precision depends on the base rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Covariate shift is a change in the relationship between the inputs and the outcome.
statements.explanation: Covariate shift is a change in the input distribution.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A change in base rate with the class-conditional feature distributions unchanged is called label shift, also known as prior probability shift.
statements.explanation: The share of positives changes while the features within each class stay the same.

questions.stem: A hospital tests an assistant that states its own confidence in words for urgent-versus-not triage of messages in different languages. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A calibration check by group needs no outcome labels.
statements.explanation: It compares stated confidence with observed outcomes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Stating the same confidence level equally often in two groups shows it is calibrated in each.
statements.explanation: Calibration needs agreement with observed outcomes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A calibration check on one model version and prompt stays valid after either is changed.
statements.explanation: A change can alter the confidence statements, so the check is repeated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A confidence stated in words by a language model is a claim to test against outcomes.
statements.explanation: Fluent confidence need not match how often the model is right.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Hedged wording is evidence that the stated confidence is calibrated.
statements.explanation: Tone is not evidence of calibration.

questions.stem: An organization chooses which group criterion to prioritize for a cancer-screening aid, where a missed case is costly, and for a fraud flag that freezes payments. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: False-positive-rate parity targets wrongful flags, the main harm for the fraud flag.
statements.explanation: It compares how often people who did nothing wrong are flagged.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The false-negative rate equals one minus the true-positive rate.
statements.explanation: The two rates split the truly qualified people.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equal opportunity targets unequal rates of missed cases across groups.
statements.explanation: Equal true-positive rates mean equal false-negative rates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Demographic parity is the criterion that targets the cost of each error type.
statements.explanation: Demographic parity ignores which errors occur.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The choice among criteria follows from the confusion matrices alone.
statements.explanation: It depends on who bears the cost of each error type.

questions.stem: A team has built a loan-approval model and must report fairness. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Passing the chosen metric means the other criteria are also satisfied.
statements.explanation: Meeting one criterion can mean others fail.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model card is a plot of calibration.
statements.explanation: A model card is documentation of a model's use, data and limits.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Minimizing average loss has no effect on how errors fall across groups.
statements.explanation: Average loss weights examples equally, which shapes the distribution of errors.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A regulator naming a metric fixes the formula and leaves open the groups, cutoff and tolerance.
statements.explanation: Applying a named metric still requires decisions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tolerance states how close two rates have to be to count as equal.
statements.explanation: Equality of estimated rates is judged within a stated margin.

questions.stem: Group A has 400 true positives, 100 false positives, 0 false negatives and 500 true negatives. Group B has 300 true positives, 0 false positives, 100 false negatives and 600 true negatives. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accuracy parity holds between the two groups.
statements.explanation: Both groups have accuracy 0.90.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Group B has the higher true-positive rate.
statements.explanation: Group A's is 1.0 and group B's is 0.75.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The errors in group A are false positives and the errors in group B are false negatives.
statements.explanation: Group A has only false positives and group B only false negatives.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Equalized odds holds between the two groups.
statements.explanation: The true-positive rates are 1.0 and 0.75, and the false-positive rates differ too.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal accuracy means the two groups bear the same cost from errors.
statements.explanation: Different error types can carry different costs.

questions.source: Bayes' rule, base rate and likelihood ratio
questions.stem: An analyst studies why precision changes with base rate for a classifier. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: By Bayes' rule, the odds of a positive outcome given a positive prediction equal the prior odds times the likelihood ratio.
statements.explanation: This is the odds form of Bayes' rule applied to precision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Base rate is another word for the prevalence of the positive outcome in a group.
statements.explanation: Both name the share of the group with the positive outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Precision and the true-positive rate are two names for the same quantity.
statements.explanation: They condition on different events.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The likelihood ratio of a positive prediction is the true-positive rate divided by the false-positive rate.
statements.explanation: It compares how likely a positive prediction is for positives versus negatives.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The posterior probability of the positive outcome given a positive prediction is the true-positive rate.
statements.explanation: That posterior is the precision.

questions.stem: A manager asks an AI assistant, "Check whether our hiring model is unbiased and fix it so everyone is treated the same." Check each statement that is true. Each statement is worth 1 point (5 points total). about writing a precise prompt.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A precise prompt names the groups, the favorable outcome, the metric and the tolerance.
statements.explanation: Each of these is needed to define the check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Bias in the statistical sense is the same thing as unfairness.
statements.explanation: Statistical bias is systematic error, while fairness is a normative judgment.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Unbiased" is vague, and naming a criterion such as equalized odds fixes its meaning.
statements.explanation: Each criterion is a specific, checkable condition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Treated the same" can mean demographic parity, equal error rates or individual fairness, which are distinct.
statements.explanation: The phrase does not choose among distinct criteria.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking for post-processing names a family of methods that adjust decisions after training.
statements.explanation: It specifies where in the pipeline the fix is applied.

questions.source: Base rates and choice of criterion
questions.stem: A health system flags patients for a limited care program. The base rate of high need is higher in group X than in group Y, partly because group X has had less access to primary care. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Predictive parity holds automatically when error rates are equal.
statements.explanation: Precision also depends on the base rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A group's base rate can partly reflect unequal access to care.
statements.explanation: Observed prevalence can come from how people were treated, not only from underlying need.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equal opportunity and demographic parity coincide when base rates differ.
statements.explanation: They constrain different quantities and generally conflict then.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Equalized odds is another name for equal opportunity.
statements.explanation: Equal opportunity constrains only the true-positive rate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With equal true-positive and false-positive rates in both groups, the selection rates differ when base rates differ.
statements.explanation: Selection rate depends on base rate and the two error rates.

questions.stem: A reviewer compares equal opportunity with equalized odds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Predictive parity follows from equalized odds.
statements.explanation: Precision depends on base rates as well as the error rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Equalized odds implies equal opportunity.
statements.explanation: Equal true-positive rates are one of its two components.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equalized odds adds false-positive-rate parity to equal opportunity.
statements.explanation: It requires both error rates to match.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Equal opportunity implies equalized odds.
statements.explanation: False-positive rates can still differ.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal opportunity concerns people who truly qualify.
statements.explanation: It compares true-positive rates.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: A classifier says 0.8 and is right about 80% of the time at that score, but it ranks positive cases above negative cases poorly. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The model is well calibrated.
statements.explanation: Calibration means predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Calibration describes agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies.
statements.explanation: That agreement is the definition of calibration.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Discrimination is the ability to rank positives above negatives, often summarised by AUC.
statements.explanation: AUC measures how well scores separate the classes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The model has high discrimination.
statements.explanation: Discrimination is ranking ability, which is poor here.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Accuracy is the same quantity as calibration.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is the share of correct predictions; calibration is about probability values.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: A prompt asks an analyst for "the likelihood that the coin is fair given 8 heads in 10 flips." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A likelihood function is a probability distribution over the parameter that sums to one.
statements.explanation: A likelihood is not normalised over the parameter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The probability that the coin is fair given the data is called a likelihood.
statements.explanation: That quantity is a posterior probability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Likelihood is the probability of the observed data viewed as a function of the parameter.
statements.explanation: Likelihood treats the data as fixed and varies the parameter.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Likelihood and posterior probability answer the same question.
statements.explanation: Likelihood is about the data given the parameter; the posterior is about the parameter given the data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: P(data | hypothesis) and P(hypothesis | data) are the same quantity.
statements.explanation: They are different conditional probabilities.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: A report gives a 95% interval for a mean and a second report gives a 95% interval from a Bayesian model. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Confidence interval and credible interval are two names for the same thing.
statements.explanation: They have different meanings and different assumptions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A 95% credible interval says that, given the model and prior, the parameter lies in the interval with probability 0.95.
statements.explanation: A credible interval is a posterior probability statement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A confidence interval is a posterior probability statement about the parameter in the one interval computed.
statements.explanation: That reading belongs to a credible interval.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that captures the true parameter in about 95% of repeated samples.
statements.explanation: Confidence refers to the long-run behaviour of the procedure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A credible interval needs a prior distribution.
statements.explanation: The posterior, and so the interval, combines prior and likelihood.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: A report says "p = 0.03, so there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A posterior probability of the null needs no prior.
statements.explanation: A posterior comes from combining a prior with the likelihood.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true.
statements.explanation: That is the definition of a p-value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The p-value is the posterior probability of the null hypothesis.
statements.explanation: A posterior probability is P(null | data), a different quantity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A small p-value gives the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.
statements.explanation: It does not give a probability for either hypothesis.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The report confuses P(data | null) with P(null | data).
statements.explanation: The p-value is the first; the quoted sentence claims the second.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: A reviewer asks for exact terms for a screening test. Check each statement that is true.
