statements.label: A
statements.text: Precision is the share of positive predictions that are truly positive.
statements.explanation: Precision is also called positive predictive value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Specificity is the share of actual negatives classified as negative.
statements.explanation: That is the true negative rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Recall is another name for sensitivity.
statements.explanation: Both are the true positive rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Precision is the share of actual positives that the test catches.
statements.explanation: That describes recall; precision concerns the positive predictions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Specificity is also called the true negative rate.
statements.explanation: It measures how well negatives are cleared.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.source: Match the metric to the situation
questions.stem: A fraud model flags 100 transactions and 40 are fraud. Of 80 fraudulent transactions in total, it flagged those 40, so 40/100 is 0.4 and 40/80 is 0.5. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 0.5 figure is the specificity.
statements.explanation: Specificity concerns actual negatives.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 0.4 figure is the precision.
statements.explanation: Of the flagged cases, 40 percent are truly fraud.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 0.4 figure is the recall.
statements.explanation: Recall divides by the actual positives, not the flagged ones.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Legitimate transactions that were flagged are false positives.
statements.explanation: A false positive is a negative case predicted positive.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 0.5 figure is the recall, also called sensitivity.
statements.explanation: Of the actual frauds, half were found.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: A vendor says a rare-disease test is "99% accurate", so a positive result means the patient is almost surely ill. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Positive predictive value is unaffected by the base rate.
statements.explanation: Positive predictive value falls as prevalence falls.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sensitivity and specificity are defined by prevalence.
statements.explanation: They are properties of the test given the condition and do not depend on prevalence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ignoring the base rate is called overfitting.
statements.explanation: Ignoring the base rate is the base rate fallacy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With a low base rate, many positive results can be false positives even for a sensitive test.
statements.explanation: Few true cases means false positives from the large healthy group can dominate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The base rate is the prevalence of the condition in the population tested.
statements.explanation: Base rate means how common the condition is before testing.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: An engineer writes P(A and B) in a prompt but means the probability of A once B is known to have occurred. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: P(A | B) equals P(A and B) divided by P(B) when P(B) is positive.
statements.explanation: That is the definition of conditional probability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: P(A | B) is the probability of A given that B has occurred.
statements.explanation: The bar means conditioning on B.

statements.label: C
statements.text: P(A and B) is called the marginal probability of A.
statements.explanation: P(A and B) is the joint probability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: P(A | B) and P(B | A) are the same quantity.
statements.explanation: They condition on different events and generally differ.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A joint probability can exceed the marginal probability of one of its events.
statements.explanation: The joint is bounded above by each marginal.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: A dashboard shows "churn will be 12%" with no range, and a reviewer asks for an interval estimate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An interval estimate gives a range that expresses uncertainty.
statements.explanation: The range reflects sampling or model uncertainty.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A point estimate carries a measure of its own uncertainty.
statements.explanation: A bare point estimate is silent about uncertainty.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A point estimate is a single value reported as the best guess.
statements.explanation: It gives one number with no spread.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising the confidence level from 90% to 99% widens the interval, other things equal.
statements.explanation: A higher level needs a wider range to capture the parameter as often.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A wider interval at the same confidence level signals more uncertainty.
statements.explanation: Width is a direct reading of the uncertainty.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: A model says it is 90% confident on a set of cases and is right on 65% of them. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reliability diagram shows the gap between confidence and observed frequency.
statements.explanation: It plots observed accuracy against stated confidence in bins.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Overconfidence means stated confidence exceeds observed accuracy.
statements.explanation: The model claims more certainty than it earns.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising AUC repairs overconfidence.
statements.explanation: AUC measures discrimination and does not fix the calibration gap.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The model is underconfident.
statements.explanation: Underconfidence is the opposite gap.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Expected calibration error is a ranking metric like AUC.
statements.explanation: It averages the confidence-accuracy gap and is a calibration measure.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: A user asks a language model "how sure are you?" and it answers "95% confident." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Token probabilities are a different signal from verbalized confidence.
statements.explanation: Logprobs come from the output distribution, not from the text.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A stated 95% is a calibrated probability by construction.
statements.explanation: Stated values need to be checked against outcomes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Agreement across repeated samples is another way to estimate confidence.
statements.explanation: Self-consistency is a sampling-based confidence signal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Verbalized confidence is a probability the model states in words.
statements.explanation: It is the self-reported number in the text output.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Verbalized confidence can be checked by comparing stated values with observed correctness.
statements.explanation: That comparison is a calibration check.

questions.section: Jargon test: probability and confidence
questions.stem: An analyst prompts: "Tell me how accurate and how confident the model's 70% scores are." Choose the rewrites that use exact terms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Report discrimination as AUC and calibration as expected calibration error, as separate quantities.
statements.explanation: The two properties are distinct and need distinct metrics.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Use the word accuracy for the share of predictions that are correct.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is the proportion correct.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Report AUC to show the scores are calibrated.
statements.explanation: AUC is discrimination, not calibration.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Call the bootstrap interval for accuracy a posterior.
statements.explanation: A bootstrap interval is a confidence interval, not a posterior.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Report calibration of the predicted probabilities with a reliability diagram.
statements.explanation: That names the property of probability values the prompt is after.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: A team asks an agent to "document the provenance of the table" but really wants the steps from the raw file to the final table. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Lineage traces the transformations and movements of data from source to current form.
statements.explanation: Lineage is the path through processing steps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Lineage describes the licence terms of the data.
statements.explanation: Licence terms are separate metadata.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Provenance records the origin of data, such as who collected it and how.
statements.explanation: Provenance answers where the data came from.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For the steps from raw file to final table, the better term is provenance.
statements.explanation: The better term for processing steps is lineage.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Provenance and lineage are identical.
statements.explanation: They overlap but name different things.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: An engineer says the pipeline has been validated because the output matches the written specification. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Verification asks whether the system meets the real need of its users.
statements.explanation: That describes validation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Verification and validation answer the same question.
statements.explanation: Building it right differs from building the right thing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Validation means re-running the same code to check it gives the same output.
statements.explanation: That is reproducibility.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Validation asks whether the output conforms to the written specification.
statements.explanation: That describes verification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A pipeline can conform to its specification and still fail to serve the real need.
statements.explanation: Passing verification does not guarantee validation.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: A column named age holds the value 240 in one row, and a date column holds text such as "next Tuesday". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A semantic check is another name for a schema check.
statements.explanation: The two check different things.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An age of 240 stored as an integer passes the schema check but fails a semantic check.
statements.explanation: The type is right but the value is implausible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Text in a date column fails the schema check.
statements.explanation: The type does not match the declared type.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A schema check tests structure such as column names, types and required fields.
statements.explanation: Schema concerns shape and type, not meaning.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A semantic check tests whether values make sense in the domain, such as a plausible age.
statements.explanation: Semantic checks use domain meaning.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: A model scores very high because some test rows are also in the training set, and a separate benchmark score is high because its questions appeared in the pretraining text. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Benchmark contamination is test items appearing in a model's training corpus.
statements.explanation: The benchmark was seen before it was tested.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Data leakage is information from outside the training data, or from the target, getting into training so evaluation is inflated.
statements.explanation: Leakage breaks the separation between training and evaluation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Contamination is a type of missingness.
statements.explanation: Contamination concerns overlap with training data, not absent values.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A feature derived from the label is a source of leakage.
statements.explanation: It encodes the answer the model is meant to predict.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Leakage describes a model that memorises noise in the training data.
statements.explanation: That is overfitting.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: A cleaning step removes rows that are byte-for-byte identical, yet the train and test sets still share rows that differ only by trailing whitespace. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Removing exact duplicates also removes near-duplicates.
statements.explanation: Exact matching misses slightly different copies.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Near-duplicates shared between train and test can cause leakage.
statements.explanation: The model has effectively seen the test item.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Near-duplicates are records that differ slightly, such as a typo or whitespace, but carry the same content.
statements.explanation: They are close copies rather than identical copies.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Exact duplicates are records that are identical.
statements.explanation: Identical rows match on every field.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fuzzy matching or hashing of text shingles is a way to detect near-duplicates.
statements.explanation: Those methods score similarity instead of requiring equality.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: Income is missing more often for people with high income, and a reviewer asks for the exact missingness type. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: MCAR means the chance of a value being missing is unrelated to observed and unobserved values.
statements.explanation: MCAR is missing completely at random.

statements.label: B
statements.text: MAR means missingness depends on observed variables but not on the missing value once they are accounted for.
statements.explanation: MAR is missing at random given recorded variables.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This pattern is MNAR, missing not at random.
statements.explanation: Missingness depends on the unobserved value itself.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Older respondents skipping a question, with age recorded, is MNAR.
statements.explanation: It depends on an observed variable, so it is MAR.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Dropping incomplete rows is unbiased under MNAR.
statements.explanation: Under MNAR the remaining rows are a biased sample.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: Match each situation to a missingness type. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Respondents with low recorded education skip an income question more often, which is MAR.
statements.explanation: Missingness depends on a recorded variable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Imputing the column mean is a test that distinguishes MNAR from MAR.
statements.explanation: Imputation is a repair, not a diagnostic of the mechanism.

statements.label: C
statements.text: MCAR means missingness depends on the value that is missing.
statements.explanation: That describes MNAR.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sensor drops readings at random because of power glitches unrelated to the readings, which is MCAR.
statements.explanation: Unrelated causes give missing completely at random.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Patients with the worst symptoms miss follow-up so their symptom score is missing, which is MAR.
statements.explanation: Missingness depends on the unobserved score, so it is MNAR.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: A cleaner proposes deleting the largest transactions and calling them anomalies. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An outlier is a data point far from the bulk of the distribution.
statements.explanation: Outlier is a statement about position in the distribution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An outlier is a data entry error that should be deleted.
statements.explanation: An outlier can be a valid measurement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Anomaly detection is another name for imputation.
statements.explanation: Imputation fills missing values; anomaly detection flags unusual cases.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A value can be a statistical outlier and still be a valid measurement.
statements.explanation: Extreme values are not automatically errors.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An anomaly is an observation that does not conform to expected behaviour, and it may signal a fault or fraud.
statements.explanation: Anomaly is a statement about behaviour against expectation.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: A team monitors input features in production against the training data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A drift alarm shows that accuracy has dropped.
statements.explanation: Inputs can drift without a change in accuracy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test needs labels for production rows.
statements.explanation: It compares feature distributions and needs no labels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Population stability index compares binned distributions of a feature between two periods.
statements.explanation: It scores how much a binned distribution moved.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Data drift is a change in the distribution of input features between reference data and new data.
statements.explanation: It compares feature distributions across time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A drift check measures model accuracy on production data.
statements.explanation: Drift checks compare inputs; accuracy needs outcomes.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: A spec says the dataset has "labels" and a reviewer asks whether they are ground truth. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Label noise refers to random features added to the inputs.
statements.explanation: Label noise means wrong or inconsistent labels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ground truth is the model's predicted value.
statements.explanation: Ground truth is a reference for the real value, not a prediction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Inter-annotator agreement measures how close the labels are to ground truth.
statements.explanation: Agreement measures consistency among annotators, not correctness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Labels from a single annotator are ground truth.
statements.explanation: One annotator can be wrong or inconsistent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A label is the target value attached to an example, whether or not it is correct.
statements.explanation: Labels are assigned values and can contain errors.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: A dataset is shared with a colleague and no documentation. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A datasheet for datasets documents motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses.
statements.explanation: It is a structured description of the dataset.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recording known gaps and intended use helps downstream users judge fit.
statements.explanation: Documentation lets users decide whether the data suits their task.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A data card summarises a dataset's provenance, contents and known limitations.
statements.explanation: It tells users what the data is and where it falls short.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A model card documents a dataset's collection process.
statements.explanation: A model card documents a model.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A datasheet should state consent and licensing when they are known.
statements.explanation: Those facts affect permitted use.

questions.section: Jargon test: data validation and provenance
questions.stem: A manager asks an AI agent: "Check the data is clean and correct and from a trusted source." Choose the rewrites that use exact terms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Report lineage as the licence and the author.
statements.explanation: Lineage is the transformation path.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Record the provenance, meaning the source and collection method.
statements.explanation: Provenance covers origin.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Run a schema check on column types and required fields.
statements.explanation: That names the structural check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Verify that test rows do not leak by deleting the test set.
statements.explanation: Leakage checks look for overlap such as duplicates, and deleting the test set removes the evaluation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Run semantic checks such as plausible value ranges.
statements.explanation: That names the domain-meaning check.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.source: Covariate shift vs concept drift vs label shift
questions.stem: After a new camera model is introduced, the distribution of input images changes, but the rule that links an image to its label has not changed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Covariate shift means the labelling rule changed.
statements.explanation: A changed labelling rule is concept drift.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Concept drift and covariate shift are two names for the same thing.
statements.explanation: They change different parts of the joint distribution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This is covariate shift.
statements.explanation: Covariate shift is a change in P(x) with P(y | x) unchanged.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Label shift, also called prior shift, is a change in P(y) with P(x | y) unchanged.
statements.explanation: The class proportions moved but the class-conditional inputs did not.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Concept drift is a change in P(y | x), the relationship between inputs and target.
statements.explanation: The mapping itself has moved.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: Match each situation to a shift term. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A seasonal change in input features alone is concept drift.
statements.explanation: Changes confined to inputs are covariate shift.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A disease becomes more common while its symptoms given the disease stay the same, which is label shift.
statements.explanation: The class prior changed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A change in P(y | x) is called covariate shift.
statements.explanation: That change is concept drift.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Fraudsters change tactics so the same transaction features now mean fraud, which is concept drift.
statements.explanation: The input-to-target relationship changed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Photos arrive from a new phone model under the same labelling rule, which is label shift.
statements.explanation: Only the input distribution changed, so it is covariate shift.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: A medical imaging model trained on one hospital's scanners is tested on a different hospital's. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An out-of-distribution input is drawn from a distribution different from the training data.
statements.explanation: OOD inputs fall outside what training covered.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A held-out test set from the same source as training is out-of-distribution.
statements.explanation: Same-source data is in-distribution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A model's softmax confidence is low on out-of-distribution inputs.
statements.explanation: Confidence can stay high on inputs unlike the training data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Out-of-distribution detection aims to flag inputs unlike the training data.
statements.explanation: Detection is how such inputs are caught.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In-distribution inputs come from the same distribution as the training data.
statements.explanation: That is the meaning of in-distribution.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: A report says a model is robust because it scores well on a random held-out test set from its own source. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Good in-distribution test accuracy shows robustness.
statements.explanation: It shows generalization; robustness needs perturbed or shifted data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Robustness is performance staying acceptable under perturbation or shift.
statements.explanation: Robustness concerns conditions that differ from training.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Robustness and generalization are identical.
statements.explanation: They test different conditions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A model can generalize well in-distribution and still be fragile under shift.
statements.explanation: The two properties can come apart.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Generalization is performance on new data from the same distribution as the training data.
statements.explanation: A same-source test measures generalization.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: A team distinguishes adversarial examples from noisy inputs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Random noise is a perturbation not chosen to target the model.
statements.explanation: It is not optimised against the model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model robust to random noise is robust to adversarial examples.
statements.explanation: Targeted perturbations can succeed where random ones fail.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An adversarial example is an input deliberately perturbed, often by a small amount, to cause a wrong output.
statements.explanation: The perturbation is chosen to attack the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An adversarial example can look nearly unchanged to a human.
statements.explanation: The change can be small and still flip the output.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adversarial perturbations can be found using the model's gradients or by querying it.
statements.explanation: Attacks use model access to search for failures.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: A reviewer asks for a stress test and a perturbation test of a text classifier. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A stress test is run on the training set to measure fit.
statements.explanation: Fit on training data is not a stress test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A stress test evaluates a model under extreme or rare conditions beyond typical inputs.
statements.explanation: It probes the edges of expected use.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A perturbation test applies small controlled changes to inputs and checks that the output stays stable.
statements.explanation: It measures sensitivity to small input changes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A changed output under a label-preserving perturbation signals fragility.
statements.explanation: The label should not change, so a change shows sensitivity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Typo injection and paraphrasing are perturbations for a text model.
statements.explanation: They change the surface of the input in a controlled way.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: A demand-forecasting model scores well on a random split but poorly after deployment, and the data changes over time. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A random held-out split is the right choice when the data drifts over time.
statements.explanation: It mixes periods and hides the effect of drift.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A held-out split sets aside data that is not used for training.
statements.explanation: It provides an unseen evaluation set.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A random split is not a held-out set.
statements.explanation: A random split can still produce a held-out set.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An out-of-time split trains on earlier data and tests on later data.
statements.explanation: The test period follows the training period.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Out-of-time evaluation better mimics deployment when the distribution changes over time.
statements.explanation: Deployment always faces the future, which the split imitates.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: A team plans monitoring for a deployed classifier. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Input drift monitoring needs labels.
statements.explanation: Input drift compares feature distributions and needs no labels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Monitoring is finished once the model passes offline tests.
statements.explanation: Shift happens after release, so monitoring continues.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Performance monitoring needs ground truth, which often arrives with delay.
statements.explanation: Accuracy cannot be computed until outcomes are known.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A feature distribution alert is the same as an accuracy drop.
statements.explanation: An alert concerns inputs and accuracy concerns outcomes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Monitoring tracks inputs, predictions and outcomes of a deployed model over time.
statements.explanation: It is ongoing observation after release.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: A model that was well calibrated on its validation set is deployed on shifted data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Overconfidence under shift means accuracy exceeds stated confidence.
statements.explanation: That is underconfidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Under distribution shift, calibration often degrades.
statements.explanation: Stated probabilities stop matching observed frequencies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A model calibrated on its validation set stays calibrated under shift.
statements.explanation: Calibration is tied to the distribution it was fitted on.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calibration can be re-measured on a labelled sample of shifted data.
statements.explanation: A fresh reliability check shows the current gap.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Temperature scaling fitted on in-distribution data repairs calibration on shifted data.
statements.explanation: The fitted correction reflects the old distribution.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: A user prompts an AI: "The model got worse because the data changed." Choose the rewrites that use exact terms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Call a random perturbation an adversarial example.
statements.explanation: Adversarial means deliberately targeted.

statements.label: B
statements.text: State whether P(x) changed, which is covariate shift, or P(y | x) changed, which is concept drift.
statements.explanation: That separates the two kinds of change.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Report accuracy on the training set to show robustness.
statements.explanation: Training accuracy does not test robustness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Describe the held-out test as out-of-time if it is a random sample.
statements.explanation: An out-of-time split orders data by time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Call it covariate shift if the class proportions changed.
statements.explanation: A change in class proportions is label shift.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: Fraud rises from 1% to 3% of transactions, and fraudulent transactions look the same as before. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: P(y) has changed.
statements.explanation: The proportion of fraud moved.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The decision threshold may need adjusting because the class prior changed.
statements.explanation: The optimal threshold depends on the prior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This is label shift, also called prior shift.
statements.explanation: The class prior changed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: P(x | y) is unchanged.
statements.explanation: Fraud looks the same as before.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This is concept drift.
statements.explanation: Concept drift would need P(y | x) to change.

questions.section: Jargon test: robustness and distribution shift
questions.stem: Match each description to its term. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test image from the training source is out-of-distribution.
statements.explanation: Same-source images are in-distribution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Training on January to June and testing on July to December is an out-of-time split.
statements.explanation: The test period follows training.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Applying a random blur to an image is an adversarial example.
statements.explanation: A random blur is not targeted at the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Swapping a word for a synonym in a prompt is a perturbation.
statements.explanation: It is a small controlled input change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Testing a document model on very long documents is a stress test.
statements.explanation: It pushes the model beyond typical inputs.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: A vendor brochure calls its model "explainable, interpretable and transparent", and the buyer wants each word pinned down. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Interpretability is the degree to which a person can understand the model's own mechanism, as with a short decision tree.
statements.explanation: That is the standard meaning: understanding the mechanism itself.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The three words are synonyms for the same property.
statements.explanation: They name different things: understanding the mechanism, access to internals, and a produced account of an output.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Publishing the full weights of a large neural network makes it interpretable.
statements.explanation: Open weights make a model transparent, but a person still cannot read a large network's mechanism, so it is not interpretable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Transparency means the model, its design and its data are open to inspection.
statements.explanation: Transparency is about access to the internals, not about understanding them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An explanation is a statement or artifact offered about why a particular output came out as it did.
statements.explanation: An explanation is something produced about a model's output, which may or may not reflect the mechanism.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: An analyst reports that ice cream sales is the most important feature for predicting drownings and concludes that cutting ice cream sales will cut drownings. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Feature importance measures how much a model relies on an input to make predictions.
statements.explanation: It describes the fitted model's dependence on the input, not the world.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A causal effect describes how the outcome changes when the input is set by intervention.
statements.explanation: Causal effect is defined by an intervention, not by predictive usefulness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An input can have high importance because it acts as a proxy for the true cause.
statements.explanation: A proxy carries information about the cause, so the model leans on it without it being causal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A high feature importance shows that the input causes the outcome.
statements.explanation: Importance reflects association the model exploited, which a confounder can create.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A confounder such as hot weather can drive both variables and make one predict the other.
statements.explanation: A confounder is a common cause that produces a non-causal association.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: Four requests are sent to an analyst: why was this one applicant denied; which inputs matter most across the whole portfolio; what does the average effect of income look like across many rows; and does the answer for one applicant match the portfolio ranking. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Asking which inputs matter most across the whole portfolio asks for a global explanation.
statements.explanation: A global explanation describes behaviour in aggregate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A single-prediction attribution is a global explanation.
statements.explanation: An attribution for one prediction is local.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A local explanation for one case is guaranteed to match the global ranking of inputs.
statements.explanation: Local and global explanations can disagree, since one case need not resemble the average.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking why one applicant was denied asks for a local explanation.
statements.explanation: A local explanation covers a single prediction.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A partial dependence plot averaged over many rows is a local explanation.
statements.explanation: Averaging over many rows gives a global view of an input's effect.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: A team has to explain a credit model and is choosing between intrinsic and post-hoc approaches. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Applying a saliency method to a trained network is an intrinsic approach.
statements.explanation: A saliency method is applied after training, so it is post-hoc.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Choosing a short rule list instead of a deep network is a choice of an intrinsic approach.
statements.explanation: The model is chosen so its structure is readable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An intrinsically interpretable model is understandable by its structure, such as a sparse linear model.
statements.explanation: Intrinsic means interpretability is built into the model form.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A post-hoc explanation is produced after training by analysing a fitted model.
statements.explanation: Post-hoc methods leave the model as trained and explain it afterward.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Post-hoc methods change the trained weights to make the model readable.
statements.explanation: Post-hoc methods leave the model unchanged.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: An analyst fits a depth-3 decision tree to imitate a black-box model and reads the tree to understand the black box. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: High fidelity on held-out inputs is not proof that the black box uses the same internal logic.
statements.explanation: Matching outputs does not show matching reasoning.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The tree is a surrogate model of the black box.
statements.explanation: A surrogate is a simpler model fitted to approximate a more complex one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A surrogate fitted near one input is called a global surrogate.
statements.explanation: A surrogate fitted near one input is a local surrogate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Agreement of the tree with the true labels is the measure of surrogate fidelity.
statements.explanation: Fidelity is agreement with the black box's outputs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The tree is trained on the true labels so that it explains the black box.
statements.explanation: To explain the black box the surrogate is trained on the black box's own predictions.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: A heat map highlights regions of a chest X-ray that drove a classifier's output. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A saliency map is a counterfactual explanation.
statements.explanation: A counterfactual describes an altered input that flips the outcome; a saliency map scores existing inputs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A highlighted region shows where the disease is located in the patient.
statements.explanation: The map describes the model's reliance, not the patient's biology.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An attribution method assigns each input feature a share of a prediction.
statements.explanation: Attribution divides a prediction among inputs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Shapley values are one kind of attribution method.
statements.explanation: Shapley values attribute a prediction to features using a game-theoretic definition.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A saliency map shows which input regions most affect the model's output score.
statements.explanation: Saliency is a sensitivity of the output to the input.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: A lender tells a denied applicant: "had your income been 6,000 higher, you would have been approved." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A counterfactual explanation requires an intrinsically interpretable model.
statements.explanation: Counterfactuals are usually computed post-hoc for black-box models.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It guarantees approval after the income rises, even if the lender retrains the model.
statements.explanation: The statement is about the current model, and a retrained model can decide differently.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It is a feature importance score for income.
statements.explanation: Feature importance ranks inputs; a counterfactual gives a specific change.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is a counterfactual explanation: a change to the inputs that would flip the outcome.
statements.explanation: That is the definition of a counterfactual explanation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It describes a nearby alternative input, not the model's full internal logic.
statements.explanation: A counterfactual answers one what-if, not how the whole model works.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: Two explanation methods are compared. Clinicians rate one method's heat maps as sensible, while a test shows the other method tracks the classifier's behaviour more closely. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Clinician ratings of how sensible heat maps look measure faithfulness.
statements.explanation: They measure plausibility.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Faithfulness is how accurately an explanation reflects what the model actually does.
statements.explanation: Faithfulness is about agreement with the model's behaviour.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A plausible explanation is therefore faithful.
statements.explanation: Looking sensible to a reader says nothing about matching the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Plausibility is how closely an explanation matches the model's computation.
statements.explanation: That describes faithfulness; plausibility is how convincing the explanation looks to a person.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An explanation can be faithful and implausible if the model relies on a spurious cue.
statements.explanation: The explanation then points at the cue, which looks odd but is true to the model.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: A model trained on hospital records predicts lower pneumonia mortality for patients with asthma, because those patients were sent straight to intensive care. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Intensive care treatment acts as a confounder that explains the pattern.
statements.explanation: The treatment affects both who has the label of asthma-care and the outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The pattern shows that asthma protects patients from dying of pneumonia.
statements.explanation: The association comes from the treatment pathway, not a protective effect.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A large attribution to asthma shows its causal effect on survival.
statements.explanation: An attribution describes the model's reliance, not an intervention result.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A correlation in observational data can reflect a confounder instead of a causal effect.
statements.explanation: Confounding is the standard reason association differs from causation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The model has learned a correlation present in the records.
statements.explanation: It captured an association between asthma and outcome.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: A language model writes step-by-step reasoning before giving an answer, and a user treats that reasoning as the explanation of the answer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A chain-of-thought is a different thing from an attribution over the input features.
statements.explanation: One is generated text and the other is a score assigned to inputs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model's after-the-fact account of why it answered is a post-hoc rationale that may not reflect the computation.
statements.explanation: Asking the model why afterwards yields a rationale, not a trace of the mechanism.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One faithfulness test is to add a hint to the input and check whether the answer changes while the reasoning does not mention the hint.
statements.explanation: An intervention that changes the answer but not the stated reasoning shows the reasoning is unfaithful.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A plausible chain-of-thought is evidence that it is faithful.
statements.explanation: Plausibility and faithfulness are different properties.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Chain-of-thought is generated text, so it is not by itself a faithful account of the model's computation.
statements.explanation: The text is an output and may not reflect the process that produced the answer.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: An analyst lists four explanation tools: LIME, SHAP, permutation importance and a partial dependence plot, and asks which is which. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: SHAP assigns attributions based on Shapley values.
statements.explanation: SHAP is the Shapley value attribution method.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A partial dependence plot is a local explanation of one prediction.
statements.explanation: It averages over many rows to show an input's average effect, a global view.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Permutation importance measures how much performance drops when one feature is shuffled.
statements.explanation: It is a global importance measure based on shuffling.

statements.label: D
statements.text: LIME fits a local surrogate on perturbed points near one input.
statements.explanation: LIME is a local surrogate method.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Integrated gradients is a global surrogate model.
statements.explanation: Integrated gradients is an attribution method that accumulates gradients along a path from a baseline.

questions.section: Jargon test: explainability
questions.stem: A team lists requests to an explanation tool and wants the exact term for each. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Asking for a ranking of inputs by average reliance across the dataset asks for global feature importance.
statements.explanation: Averaged reliance across the dataset is a global importance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Asking for a rule-based model a regulator can read directly asks for an intrinsically interpretable model.
statements.explanation: Rule-based models are readable by their structure.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Asking whether the explanation reflects what the model really does asks about plausibility.
statements.explanation: That question is about faithfulness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking for the smallest input change that flips a denial asks for a counterfactual explanation.
statements.explanation: A counterfactual states the change that flips the outcome.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking why this one case got its score asks for a global explanation.
statements.explanation: A single case calls for a local explanation.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.source: Sampling, selection, measurement and label bias
questions.stem: An audit lists four situations, and the team labels each with a bias term. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A thermometer that reads two degrees high at one clinic produces measurement bias.
statements.explanation: Measurement bias is systematic error in how a value is recorded.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Training on past customers who were approved for loans, since they have repayment outcomes, produces selection bias.
statements.explanation: The process that decides who enters the data is related to the outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A scale that reads high is an example of sampling bias.
statements.explanation: That is measurement bias; sampling bias concerns who ends up in the sample.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Annotators who label one dialect as toxic more often produce label bias.
statements.explanation: Label bias is systematic error in the assigned target labels.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Label bias is another name for overfitting.
statements.explanation: Label bias is an error in labels, while overfitting is poor generalization.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: An analyst says that labels came from reviewers who judged applicants from one neighbourhood more harshly, so the problem is sampling bias. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The problem described is label bias.
statements.explanation: The target labels carry systematic reviewer error.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sampling bias concerns who ends up in the data, not how labels were assigned.
statements.explanation: Sampling bias is about the makeup of the sample.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Resampling to match population group proportions fixes label bias.
statements.explanation: Resampling changes group makeup but leaves the label errors in place.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Collecting more rows from the same reviewers removes the problem.
statements.explanation: More rows with the same biased labels repeat the bias.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Label bias can exist when the sample matches the target population in group proportions.
statements.explanation: The two problems are independent of each other.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: A hiring model is trained on twenty years of accurate, well-sampled records that show few women hired into engineering. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Collecting a larger random sample removes historical bias.
statements.explanation: A bigger faithful sample reproduces the same inequity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Historical bias can be present when sampling and measurement are sound.
statements.explanation: It does not depend on a flaw in data collection.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Historical bias is a type of measurement bias because the records are inaccurate.
statements.explanation: The records are accurate; the bias lies in the world they describe.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Historical bias requires that the records contain data-entry errors.
statements.explanation: Errors are not needed; accurate records can carry it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This is historical bias: accurate data that reflect a world containing past inequity.
statements.explanation: Historical bias comes from the world, not from collection errors.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: A lender removes race from the inputs of its approval model but keeps zip code, which is correlated with race. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A proxy variable is itself a protected attribute.
statements.explanation: A proxy is an ordinary input that stands in for one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Race is a protected attribute: a characteristic that law or policy shields from discrimination.
statements.explanation: Protected attributes are the characteristics fairness rules refer to.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Removing zip code guarantees the outputs are independent of race.
statements.explanation: Other correlated inputs can still carry the information.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Dropping the protected attribute from the inputs, called fairness through unawareness, can leave a proxy in place.
statements.explanation: Unawareness removes the column but not correlated information.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Zip code here acts as a proxy variable for race.
statements.explanation: A proxy is an input correlated enough with a protected attribute to carry its information.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: A review board states fairness criteria and needs the exact term for each. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal opportunity asks for equal false positive rates across groups.
statements.explanation: Equal opportunity asks for equal true positive rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Predictive parity asks for equal true positive rates across groups.
statements.explanation: Predictive parity asks for equal precision, also called positive predictive value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Calibration within groups asks for equal selection rates.
statements.explanation: Calibration within groups asks that a score mean the same observed frequency in each group.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Demographic parity asks for equal positive-prediction rates across groups.
statements.explanation: It compares selection rates.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equalized odds asks for equal true positive rates and equal false positive rates across groups.
statements.explanation: It matches both error-related rates.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: A review board describes requirements in words and asks which fairness criterion each one names. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Approval rates among repayers and among defaulters both match across groups" names demographic parity.
statements.explanation: That is equalized odds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "The share approved is the same for each group regardless of repayment" names equalized odds.
statements.explanation: That is demographic parity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Among people who truly repay, the approval rate is the same for each group" names equal opportunity.
statements.explanation: Equal opportunity matches true positive rates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "A score of 0.7 should mean about 70 percent observed repayment in each group" names calibration within groups.
statements.explanation: Calibration compares score to observed frequency per group.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Among people approved, the share who repay is the same for each group" names predictive parity.
statements.explanation: Predictive parity compares precision across groups.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: A regulator asks whether a screening tool shows disparate treatment, disparate impact, or both. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Disparate treatment means deciding differently for people because of a protected attribute, such as using race as an input.
statements.explanation: It concerns the basis for the decision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Disparate treatment describes unequal outcome rates regardless of how decisions are made.
statements.explanation: That is closer to disparate impact.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Disparate impact requires proof of intent to discriminate.
statements.explanation: Intent is part of disparate treatment, not disparate impact.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A model that does not take the protected attribute as input is free of disparate impact.
statements.explanation: Proxies can produce unequal outcomes without the attribute as an input.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Disparate impact means a neutral-looking practice produces substantially different outcomes across groups.
statements.explanation: It concerns the effect of the practice.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: Two groups have different shares of people who truly have the positive outcome, and a classifier is imperfect. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A base-rate difference is evidence that the model is biased.
statements.explanation: A base-rate difference describes the data; the model can still be accurate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With differing base rates and an imperfect classifier, calibration within groups and equalized odds generally do not hold together.
statements.explanation: Known results show these criteria are in tension under unequal base rates.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The base rate is the proportion of a group that has the positive outcome.
statements.explanation: It is the prevalence of the outcome in the group.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The base rate is the same as a group's false positive rate.
statements.explanation: False positive rate is a model error rate, not outcome prevalence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A base-rate difference in the data can itself reflect historical bias.
statements.explanation: Past inequity can shape which outcomes appear in the records.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: A company wants to meet several fairness criteria at once and asks why the metrics disagree. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Different metrics encode different notions of fairness, so the chosen metric should be stated with the reason.
statements.explanation: The metric choice is part of the claim being made.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Fairness criteria are compatible in ordinary conditions, so a model meets each at the same time.
statements.explanation: They are generally incompatible when base rates differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fairness trade-off means improving one criterion can worsen another criterion or overall accuracy.
statements.explanation: Criteria can conflict, so gains on one come with costs elsewhere.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Choosing among fairness metrics is a value judgement about context, not just a statistical decision.
statements.explanation: The right criterion depends on the harms involved.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Raising a threshold for one group to equalise true positive rates can change selection rates across groups.
statements.explanation: Adjusting a threshold moves several rates at once.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: An audit finds similar error rates for women overall and for older people overall, but high error for older women. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Good results on each single attribute can hide poor results at the intersection.
statements.explanation: Averages over a single attribute can mask a small subgroup.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reporting metrics by gender and by age separately is an intersectional analysis.
statements.explanation: Separate breakdowns miss the combined subgroups.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Intersectional analysis examines subgroups defined by combinations of attributes.
statements.explanation: Intersections like older women are the unit of analysis.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Intersectional means measuring fairness across different time periods.
statements.explanation: It refers to overlapping group memberships, not time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Intersectional subgroups can be small, so estimates there can be noisy.
statements.explanation: Small groups give wide uncertainty.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: An analyst says: "the model has disparate treatment because the false negative rate is higher for group B, even though group is not an input." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equalized odds would also ask for matching false positive rates.
statements.explanation: Equalized odds covers both true and false positive rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A higher false negative rate means a lower true positive rate for that group.
statements.explanation: False negative rate plus true positive rate equal one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equal opportunity is the criterion that targets a gap in true positive rates.
statements.explanation: It requires matching true positive rates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Disparate treatment fits because group is not an input.
statements.explanation: Treatment concerns using the attribute, which did not happen here.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Unequal error rates with no group input are closer to disparate impact.
statements.explanation: The practice is neutral on its face but outcomes differ.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: A face dataset is collected from social media photos of young adults and then used for people of many ages. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Some texts call this representation bias.
statements.explanation: Representation bias is a near-synonym for sampling bias in this sense.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is sampling bias: the sample's makeup differs from the population where the model will be used.
statements.explanation: Sampling bias is a mismatch between sample and target population.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It is measurement bias because the photos are inaccurate.
statements.explanation: The photos can be accurate; the problem is who is represented.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evaluating separately by age group helps reveal its effect.
statements.explanation: Subgroup evaluation exposes weaker performance on under-represented groups.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding more rows from the same source reduces it.
statements.explanation: More rows from the same source repeat the same skew.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: A risk score is well calibrated across the whole population but its calibration has not been checked for each group. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reliability diagram is a standard way to inspect calibration.
statements.explanation: It plots predicted probability against observed frequency.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Overall calibration guarantees calibration within each group.
statements.explanation: Group-level miscalibration can cancel out in the average.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Calibration is the same as accuracy.
statements.explanation: Calibration compares probabilities to frequencies; accuracy counts correct decisions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calibration means that among people given score p, about a fraction p have the outcome.
statements.explanation: Stated probability matches observed frequency.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Calibration within groups asks for that match separately in each group.
statements.explanation: The condition is applied per group.

questions.section: Jargon test: bias and fairness
questions.stem: A default model is trained only on applicants who were approved in the past, then used to score the whole applicant pool. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Gathering more outcomes from the same approved group reduces it.
statements.explanation: The skew comes from the missing group, not the count of approved cases.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is label bias because annotators mislabelled applicants.
statements.explanation: No mislabelling is described; the issue is who is in the data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Data from approved applicants alone are representative of the whole applicant pool.
statements.explanation: Rejected applicants are missing, so the data are skewed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This is measurement bias because a feature's scale differs between applicants.
statements.explanation: Nothing about measurement is described.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This is selection bias: the data are a non-random subset chosen by a process related to the outcome.
statements.explanation: Past approvals decided who has outcomes.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A prompt to an AI tool says: "make the model more accurate so it's fair." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A model with 95 percent accuracy is fair.
statements.explanation: High accuracy can coexist with large gaps between groups.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Fairness is a synonym for accuracy on the test set.
statements.explanation: Fairness compares outcomes or errors across groups.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A precise rewrite is: "Reduce the gap in true positive rates between groups (equal opportunity) and report overall accuracy."
statements.explanation: It names a specific fairness criterion and keeps accuracy as a separate quantity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Fair" needs a named criterion such as demographic parity or equalized odds.
statements.explanation: The word alone does not say what is being equalised.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Accuracy measures the share of predictions that are correct, which differs from fairness.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is overall correctness, not a group comparison.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A prompt to an analyst says: "check the data is clean." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Data validation checks that data meet stated rules, such as types, ranges and missing values.
statements.explanation: Validation is rule-based checking of data against a schema or expectations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A precise rewrite names the checks, such as schema validation, missingness, duplicates and outliers.
statements.explanation: "Clean" is vague, while named checks are testable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Cleaning the data removes sampling bias.
statements.explanation: Cleaning fixes errors; it does not change who is in the sample.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Provenance is the record of where data came from and how it was changed.
statements.explanation: Provenance documents origin and custody.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A dataset that passes validation checks is guaranteed to be accurate.
statements.explanation: Validation checks stated rules, which do not prove the values are true.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A report says: "the model is 90 percent confident, so it is 90 percent accurate." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct.
statements.explanation: Accuracy is an observed rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Confidence and accuracy are the same quantity.
statements.explanation: One is a stated probability and the other an observed rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Confidence is the probability the model assigns to its prediction.
statements.explanation: Confidence is the model's stated probability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calibration is the match between stated confidence and the observed frequency of being correct.
statements.explanation: A calibrated 90 percent confidence is right about 90 percent of the time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If 90 percent confident predictions are right 70 percent of the time, the model is well calibrated.
statements.explanation: That model is overconfident, so it is poorly calibrated.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: An analyst writes: "this 95 percent confidence interval means there is a 95 percent probability the true effect lies inside it." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The terms credible interval and confidence interval are interchangeable.
statements.explanation: They rest on different definitions of probability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A p-value is the posterior probability that the null hypothesis is true.
statements.explanation: A p-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis, and it is not a posterior probability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A credible interval is a range built from repeated sampling in the long run.
statements.explanation: That describes a confidence interval; a credible interval is a Bayesian posterior range.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 95 percent in a confidence interval refers to the long-run share of such intervals that cover the true value.
statements.explanation: The coverage is a property of the procedure over repeated samples.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The analyst's sentence describes a credible interval, not a confidence interval.
statements.explanation: A direct probability statement about the parameter is Bayesian.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.source: Covariate shift, concept drift, label shift
questions.stem: A message says: "the model degraded because of drift. The mix of inputs shifted, but the relationship between inputs and outcome is the same." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The word "drift" alone states which distribution changed.
statements.explanation: "Drift" is vague; covariate shift, concept drift and label shift name the change.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Label shift means the distribution of outcomes changes while the input distribution given the outcome stays the same.
statements.explanation: It changes P(y) and leaves P(x given y) alone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Covariate shift means the distribution of inputs changes while the relationship between inputs and outcome stays the same.
statements.explanation: It changes P(x) and leaves P(y given x) alone.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and outcome changes over time.
statements.explanation: The conditional distribution of the outcome given the inputs moves.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The case in the message is covariate shift.
statements.explanation: Inputs changed and the input-to-outcome relationship did not.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A manager says: "verify the model works for patients" and wants evidence the model serves its purpose on real patients. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Checking the model against its written specification in a test is verification.
statements.explanation: Verification confirms the build meets its spec.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Validation asks whether the right system was built, meaning it serves its real purpose.
statements.explanation: Validation checks fit to the real need.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Verification asks whether the system was built right, meaning it meets its specification.
statements.explanation: Verification checks against the specification.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evidence on real patients is validation.
statements.explanation: It tests the purpose in the real setting.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A unit test that the code computes a specified formula is validation.
statements.explanation: That is verification against a specification.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A report says: "the test is 99 percent accurate at spotting the disease, so a positive result means a 99 percent chance of disease." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Precision, also called positive predictive value, is the share of positive results that are true cases.
statements.explanation: It answers what a positive result means.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sensitivity of 99 percent gives a precision of 99 percent.
statements.explanation: Precision also depends on how common the disease is.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Specificity is the share of people without the disease whom the test clears.
statements.explanation: It is the true negative rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Sensitivity is the share of people with the disease whom the test flags.
statements.explanation: It is the true positive rate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Precision depends on prevalence as well as on sensitivity and specificity.
statements.explanation: Rare conditions produce many false positives even with a strong test.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A report says: "the p-value is 0.03, so there is a 97 percent chance the effect is real." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A p-value is computed by assuming the null hypothesis.
statements.explanation: The null defines the reference distribution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true.
statements.explanation: It is a probability of data given the null.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
statements.explanation: It assumes the null, so it cannot be the probability of the null.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A p-value of 0.03 means a 97 percent probability that the effect is real.
statements.explanation: The p-value is not a probability that the effect is real.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A posterior probability is the probability of a hypothesis given the data, in the Bayesian sense.
statements.explanation: It conditions on the data.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A prompt says: "make the model robust against attacks and against new data." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Distribution shift means test inputs come from a different distribution than the training data.
statements.explanation: It is a change in the data-generating distribution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Robustness to distribution shift is tested with adversarial examples.
statements.explanation: It is tested with data from a shifted distribution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adversarial robustness is measured on held-out data from the same distribution.
statements.explanation: Same-distribution held-out data tests ordinary generalization.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adversarial robustness concerns small deliberate input perturbations designed to cause errors.
statements.explanation: Adversarial examples are crafted to fool the model.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An adversarial example is naturally occurring noise in the data.
statements.explanation: It is a deliberate perturbation.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: An analyst asks an AI for "the data lineage" but wants to know who collected the dataset and under what licence. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Joins and aggregations applied to a table belong to provenance rather than lineage.
statements.explanation: Processing steps are lineage.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Lineage tracks transformations from a source to a derived table or feature.
statements.explanation: Lineage follows the chain of processing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The question as asked is about lineage.
statements.explanation: It asks about origin and terms, which is provenance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Who collected the data and under what licence is a question about lineage.
statements.explanation: That is provenance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Provenance records origin and custody: who collected the data, when, how, and under what terms.
statements.explanation: Provenance answers where the data came from.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A student says: "the model memorised the training set, so it has high bias." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Overfitting is the result of high bias.
statements.explanation: Overfitting is typically associated with high variance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: High bias means the model is flexible enough to memorise noise.
statements.explanation: High bias means the model is too simple, which is underfitting.

statements.label: C
statements.text: High variance means the model is too simple to capture the pattern.
statements.explanation: High variance means sensitivity to the particular training sample.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Overfitting means low error on training data and high error on held-out data.
statements.explanation: The model fits noise in the training set.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Bias in the bias-variance sense is the same as demographic bias.
statements.explanation: The statistical bias-variance sense is about systematic error of the model's predictions, not about groups.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: An analyst writes: "I tuned the hyperparameters on the test set, then reported the best test score." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tuning on the test set is the same as cross-validation.
statements.explanation: Cross-validation tunes on folds of the training data, not on the held-back test set.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Data leakage is information from outside the training data, such as test labels, influencing the training.
statements.explanation: Leakage breaks the separation between fitting and evaluation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A validation set is used to tune hyperparameters and choose between models.
statements.explanation: It guides model selection.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A test set is held back for the final estimate of generalization.
statements.explanation: It is used once the choices are made.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Tuning on the test set leaks information, so the reported score is optimistic.
statements.explanation: The test data influenced the choices, so it no longer measures unseen performance.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A prompt says: "collect more data to reduce the model's uncertainty about the noisy sensor readings." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Epistemic uncertainty comes from limited knowledge or data and can shrink with more data.
statements.explanation: More data informs the model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: More data reduces aleatoric uncertainty.
statements.explanation: Inherent noise stays the same.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Uncertainty about a parameter from a small sample is aleatoric.
statements.explanation: That is epistemic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Aleatoric uncertainty is noise inherent in the data.
statements.explanation: It remains however much data is collected.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The word "uncertainty" alone does not say which kind, so a rewrite should name aleatoric or epistemic.
statements.explanation: The two kinds respond differently to more data.

questions.section: Jargon test: wrong word, right word
questions.stem: A report says: "ads and sales are correlated, so ad spend is a confounder of sales", and also treats the correlation as proof that ads drive sales. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The correlation coefficient measures how well a nonlinear curve fits the data.
statements.explanation: The standard correlation coefficient measures linear association.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A strong correlation shows that one variable causes the other.
statements.explanation: Association alone does not establish a causal direction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A spurious correlation is an association not due to a causal link between the variables.
statements.explanation: It can arise from chance or a confounder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A confounder is a common cause of both the exposure and the outcome.
statements.explanation: It creates association without a direct causal link.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A correlation of zero shows the variables are independent.
statements.explanation: Zero linear correlation leaves room for a nonlinear relationship.
